title: [Kernel] TD operand loads for batched MoE GEMM (moe_mmk) on XPU
author: oonyshch
body:
### Purpose
Add a Tensor-Descriptor (TD) operand-load path to `moe_mmk` / `expert_triton_kernel` (the batched MoE expert GEMM) and enable it on XPU. On XPU, masked `tl.load` feeding `tl.dot` bypasses the Xe XMX 2D-block-read path; loading both operands via `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` restores it. Output is bit-identical to the non-TD path.

The batched kernel is the one used by **low-latency Expert-Parallel** dispatch (the batched activation format `[E_local, max_tokens, K]`), so its e2e effect must be measured **in that EP context**, not against the single-GPU fused MoE (a different path, rightly faster when a model fits on one GPU). This addresses the earlier review feedback: the correct comparison is **TD-on vs TD-off on the batched EP path**, which is what this PR touches. (Earlier single-GPU GraniteMoE numbers were misleading and are superseded below.)

Gated by `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD` (auto-on for XPU, opt-in on CUDA sm90+). Stacks under the portable low-latency all-to-all EP backend (#46871).

### Test Plan
- Kernel unit tests: `tests/kernels/moe/test_batched_moe.py` (TD vs plain bit-exact, zero-expert
  handling, device enablement, backend selection).
- E2E via `vllm serve` + `vllm bench serve` on **2× Intel Arc B70**, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, batched
  Triton EP path (`--all2all-backend naive_low_latency`), bf16, `--enforce-eager`, seed 42.
  Isolates TD by toggling only `VLLM_TRITON_USE_TD`. (`VLLM_MLA_DISABLE=1` — DeepSeek MLA on XPU
  has a separate pre-existing numerics bug unrelated to this kernel.)
- Accuracy: gsm8k on GraniteMoE (standard attention → clean XPU read) confirms TD is neutral.

### Test Result

### Per-kernel microbench
- Arc B70 (E=8, K=N=2048, bf16): TD −89…−91% latency across tokens/expert.
- RTX 5060 / H200: TD −68…−70% (CUDA), gains scale with expert GEMM size; bit-exact.

### E2E on the batched low-latency EP path — 2× Arc B70, DeepSeek-V2-Lite (TD off vs on)

**Saturation (ShareGPT, 500 prompts):**

| metric | TD0 | TD1 | Δ TD1 vs TD0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| output tok/s | 134.2 | 290.6 | **+116%** |
| median TTFT | 27.1 s | 12.0 s | **−56%** |
| median TPOT | 797 ms | 334 ms | **−58%** |

**Single-stream (`--max-concurrency 1`, realistic low-latency regime):**

| metric | TD0 | TD1 | Δ | no-EP default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| median TTFT | 1033 ms | 600 ms | −42% | 427 ms |
| median TPOT | 353 ms | 270 ms | −24% | 124 ms |

### CUDA cross-check (DeepEP low-latency, Qwen3-30B-A3B, 4× H200)
+72% req/s, −53% TPOT with TD on; per-kernel 1.3–6.1× (scales with K/N); bit-identical.
(Logs: `cuda_td_deepep_ll_logs.zip`, attached below in a comment)

### Accuracy (TD is a bit-exact operand-load change)
GraniteMoE gsm8k (8-shot, 200): default 0.500 / TD0 0.480 / TD1 0.470 — flat within noise, matching the model's published ~0.49.

Takeaway: TD is a large, consistent win on the batched EP path it actually touches (+116% throughput, −58% TPOT on 2× Arc B70; +72% req/s on H200), bit-exact, accuracy-neutral, never a regression. 

Full XPU logs:
[pr46340_bench_logs.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30139331/pr46340_bench_logs.zip)

title: [GDN] Improve kkt kernel of CuteDSL prefill backend
author: gau-nernst
body:
## Purpose This a a follow-up of #43273. In this PR, I only focused on optimizing the matrix inverse pipeline inside the KKT kernel. A quick recap on the KKT kernel timeline This is a bit more detailed than the timeline shown previously in #43273, because the extra steps shown above (`Prepare gate/beta` and `Store Ab/Abg to tmem`) turn out to be the bottleneck! I asked Codex to add some instrumenting code so we can get an actual kernel timeline tcgen05 is so fast that `W MMA + U MMA + next KKT MMA` < `INV warps load and prepare beta/gate`! Furthermore, Ab/Abg preparation looks surprisingly slow, taking around 20-25% the time of inverse logic, which was supposed to be the most expensive. As it turns out again, doing multiplication can be a bottleneck on Blackwell. So how do we overcome it? ### Slow beta/gate preparation Move beta/gate preparations to extra warps! These prep warps can overlap with existing INV warps, and go 1 stage ahead of the INV warps -> when INV warps need beta/gate, those values are already ready in smem buffer -> no waiting ### Slow Ab/Abg prepration after `inverse(I+A)` Currently, we have a clear boundary between doing `inv(I+A)`, and then compute `Ab = inv(I+A) * beta` / `Abg = inv(I+A) * beta * gate`. ``` # current 1. compute inverse for diagonal 16x16 tiles (Newton-Schulz) 2. compute inverse for off-diagonal tiles (block forward-substitution) 3. compute Ab/Abg, and store to tmem ``` This cleanly separates the logic, but not optimal: there is an extra smem roundtrip, and we also unnecessarily store the zeros upper-triangular tiles. Instead, we can fuse Ab/Abg prep with the inverse steps. ``` # new 1. compute inverse for diagonal 16x16 tiles (Newton-Schulz) 1b. while the result is still in registers, compute Ab/Abg and store to tmem 2. compute inverse for off-diagonal tiles (block forward-substitution) 2b. while the result is still in registers, compute Ab/Abg and store to tmem ``` We save the unnecessary Ab/Abg computation for the upper triangular tiles. Before, we have 4x4 16x16 tiles. Now, we only need to compute and store (1+2+3+4) 16x16 Ab/Abg tiles. The new kernel timeline tcgen05 is still mostly idle. We can do pingpong schedule like FlashAttention in the future. ### Other cleanup I also take this opportunity to make small tweaks in the kernels that don't really bring significant changes - Move `elect_sync()` inside the tcgen05 helper functions. From my experience, this gives better codegen, as CuteDSL may generate weird predicated address calculations - Remove swizzled layout for `sA` and `sAi` - Use `TmaInfo` object returnted by `make_tiled_tma_atom` directly, no need to `(atom, tma_tensor, s_layout)` tuples. - Apply `f32x2` math as appropriate using `cutlass.range(vectorize=True)` - Remove adhoc BF16 bit manipulation in favour of built-in PTX like `neg.bf16x2` and `sub.bf16x2` ## Microbenchmarks GB200. FlashInfer as baseline | model_case | input_case | FlashInfer | Old CuteDSL | New CuteDSL | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | Qwen3.6-27B TP1 | 1x8192 | 0.422 ms (1.00x) | 0.369 ms (1.14x) | 0.352 ms (1.20x) | | Qwen3.6-27B TP1 | 1x16384 | 0.714 ms (1.00x) | 0.712 ms (1.00x) | 0.662 ms (1.08x) | | Qwen3.6-27B TP1 | 8x1024 | 0.281 ms (1.00x) | 0.297 ms (0.95x) | 0.271 ms (1.04x) | | Qwen3.6-27B TP1 | 8x2048 | 0.393 ms (1.00x) | 0.561 ms (0.70x) | 0.508 ms (0.77x) | | Qwen3.6-27B TP1 | 8@8192 (mixed) | 0.410 ms (1.00x) | 0.363 ms (1.13x) | 0.336 ms (1.22x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP1 | 1x8192 | 0.426 ms (1.00x) | 0.464 ms (0.92x) | 0.425 ms (1.00x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP1 | 1x16384 | 0.721 ms (1.00x) | 0.912 ms (0.79x) | 0.828 ms (0.87x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP1 | 8x1024 | 0.337 ms (1.00x) | 0.413 ms (0.82x) | 0.371 ms (0.91x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP1 | 8x2048 | 0.483 ms (1.00x) | 0.787 ms (0.61x) | 0.705 ms (0.69x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP1 | 8@8192 (mixed) | 0.463 ms (1.00x) | 0.470 ms (0.98x) | 0.425 ms (1.09x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP4 | 1x8192 | 0.424 ms (1.00x) | 0.242 ms (1.75x) | 0.243 ms (1.75x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP4 | 1x16384 | 0.713 ms (1.00x) | 0.437 ms (1.63x) | 0.430 ms (1.66x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP4 | 8x1024 | 0.175 ms (1.00x) | 0.132 ms (1.33x) | 0.123 ms (1.43x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP4 | 8x2048 | 0.207 ms (1.00x) | 0.190 ms (1.09x) | 0.183 ms (1.13x) | | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B TP4 | 8@8192 (mixed) | 0.379 ms (1.00x) | 0.220 ms (1.72x) | 0.228 ms (1.67x) | Around 10% improvements for TP1, which is huge considering this is just the KKT kernel (there are also the H and O kernels). For TP4, perf is mostly unchanged. ## E2E testing Qwen/Qwen3.6-27B AIME25 (exact match): 0.9167 8k-1 prefill only, GB200, concurrency 64 Branch | TPGS | TTFT ---|---|--- main | 25938 tok/s | 20.00s this PR | 25964 tok/s | 19.98s Pretty much noise, which is expected I suppose ---

title: [KV Offloading] Replace `bool|None` lookup return with LookupResult enum
author: ronensc
body:
## Purpose

Replace the ambiguous `bool | None` return type of `OffloadingManager.lookup()` with a `LookupResult` enum that distinguishes between two previously conflated `None` cases:

- **`HIT_PENDING`** — block exists in the primary tier but its write is still in-flight.
  Should count as a hit in `_sliding_window_lookup`'s consecutive-hit streak.
- **`RETRY`** — block found on a secondary tier (promotion started) or async lookup pending.
  Should NOT count as a hit (breaks streak).

Previously `_sliding_window_lookup` treated both as a miss (`result = False`), which was pessimistic for the `HIT_PENDING` case and could prevent loading blocks that are about to be ready.

The new enum has four members: `MISS`, `HIT`, `HIT_PENDING`, `RETRY`.

### Scope

- `OffloadingManager.lookup()` return type → `LookupResult`
- `SecondaryTierManager.lookup()` return type → `LookupResult`
- `AsyncLookupManager.lookup()` remains `bool | None` — concrete `SecondaryTierManager` implementations (fs, obj) convert at the boundary.
- Scheduler uses `match`/`case` statements to handle all four variants.

Relates to #33689

title: [Feature] Initial support for fault tolerant ep using scale-down
author: fangyuchu
body:
## Purpose

This PR adds **scale-down** to the vLLM fault tolerance (FT) framework for DP+EP
MoE deployments in external-LB mode.

The existing FT framework (`--enable-fault-tolerance`) supports `retry` —
reinitializing the DP process group after a transient fault where all ranks
survive. When a DP rank dies permanently (hardware failure, OOM kill), `retry`
is insufficient: the dead rank's expert slots are unreachable and the EPLB
placement tables reference slots that no longer exist.

**Scale-down** (`POST /v1/fault_tolerance/apply` with `instruction: "scale_down"`)
removes dead DP ranks, masks the corresponding EP ranks at the all2all kernel
level, redistributes orphaned logical experts onto surviving ranks using EPLB
redundant slots, selectively reloads only the reassigned expert weights from
disk, rebuilds the DP Gloo group over the surviving slots, and resumes
inference — without a full restart.

Recovery is **orchestrator-driven**: engines detect faults, report status, and
wait for an explicit command. There is no self-recovery path.

---

## Operator Contract

This section is the interface an external controller (Kubernetes operator,
Dynamo, or any service framework) can rely on.

### Requirements

- **External load balancer mode only**: one engine per API server
  (`--api-server-count=1 --data-parallel-size-local=1`). Validated at startup
  (`arg_utils.py`); the server refuses to start otherwise. Internal LB is not
  supported.
- **MoE model with DP+EP** and an all2all backend that supports timeouts:
  `deepep_low_latency` or `nixl_ep`. Validated at worker creation
  (`WorkerSentinel.__init__`). Without one of these, a dead rank hangs the whole
  cluster and none of this document applies.
- **`scale_down` additionally requires EPLB with `num_redundant_experts > 0`** —
  redundant replicas are what survivors use to cover the removed rank. Validated
  at the worker layer; a deployment without it fails the command with a clear
  `ft_error`.
- **Not supported: prefill context parallelism** (`prefill_context_parallel_size
  > 1`). Rejected at worker creation — the TP sibling barrier and group reinit
  have no PCP equivalents.
- **`scale_down` partial weight reload supports the default weight loader only.**
  The reload goes through `get_model_loader`, and only `DefaultModelLoader`
  implements `get_all_weights`; every other loader raises `NotImplementedError`.
  This is reached only when the redistribution actually reassigns experts.

Startup flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--enable-fault-tolerance` | Turns the feature on. Also forces DP sync onto the Gloo CPU group. |
| `--cpu-distributed-timeout-seconds N` | How quickly a surviving rank declares a silent peer dead. |
| `--fault-tolerance-config='{"engine_recovery_timeout_sec": 120}'` | How long a faulted engine waits for your command before giving up and exiting. |

### Endpoints

**`POST /v1/fault_tolerance/apply`** — send a command. Asynchronous: returns
`202 Accepted` immediately and runs the recovery in the background. Poll
`status` for the outcome. **[implemented]**

The endpoints exist **only** under the `/v1` prefix. Earlier revisions of this
branch also exposed unprefixed `/fault_tolerance/apply|status` aliases; those
have been **removed**.

`retry` — clean up and resume, keeping all ranks:

```json
{"instruction": "retry", "params": {}}
```

`scale_down` — permanently remove dead ranks and continue without them:

```json
{"instruction": "scale_down", "params": {"removed_dp_ranks": [1]}}
```

**`GET /v1/fault_tolerance/status`** — observe everything. **[implemented]**

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "total_engines": 1,
  "engines": [
    {
      "id": 0,
      "status": "unhealthy",
      "fault_info": "RuntimeError",
      "mask": [1, 0],
      "ft_state": "failed",
      "last_ft_request_id": "<uuid>",
      "ft_error": "..."
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `healthy` \| `unhealthy` \| `diagnosing` \| `dead` — engine health. |
| `fault_info` | (only when `unhealthy`) exception type, or `"Recovery failed; full restart required"` on a terminal scale-down failure. |
| `mask` | (only when `unhealthy`) which EP peers this engine lost contact with, `1` = unreachable, in **EP** coordinates. |
| `ft_state` | Lifecycle of the most recent `apply`: `recovering` (in flight) or `failed`. Absent when idle. |
| `last_ft_request_id` | The `request_id` the state refers to. Recorded at **dispatch**, so it identifies the active operation even for a request that is still running. |
| `ft_error` | Why that request failed. Only meaningful once `ft_state` is `failed`. |


### Which engines can accept a command

Commands are accepted **only while an engine is `unhealthy`** — the state it enters
after detecting a fault and before recovery:

| Status | Meaning | Accepts commands? |
|---|---|---|
| `unhealthy` | Detected a fault, waiting for you | **Yes** |
| `diagnosing` | Mask query in flight (transient) | No — keep polling |
| `healthy` | No fault detected | No — `status is HEALTHY` |
| `dead` | The engine process is gone | No — `status is DEAD` |

- **`retry` can be repeated.** If it fails, the engine stays `unhealthy` and
  accepts another attempt (send a fresh `request_id`) until
  `engine_recovery_timeout_sec` expires.
- **A failed `scale_down` is terminal.** Once it passes request validation, any
  failure moves the engine to `dead` and the instance has to be restarted —
  expert migration between ranks cannot be undone.

A `healthy` engine that never becomes `unhealthy` while its peers are faulted is
most likely wedged (e.g. blocked in a collective with no timeout). It will not
accept a command, so the deployment has to be recreated.

Consequence for a controller: if Kubernetes diagnoses a failed rank *before*
vLLM's own timeouts fire, some survivors may still report `healthy` and
`scale_down` will be rejected with `reason: "status is HEALTHY"`. Wait for every
surviving engine to reach `unhealthy` on its own, then dispatch. All survivors
are guaranteed to get there eventually (all2all kernel timeout, or Gloo group
timeout on the control path). A proactive prepare/pause path that lets a
controller start recovery immediately is not implemented.


### Admission and health during a fault

- **[implemented] Admission goes false.** While FT is enabled and engine status
  is anything other than `healthy`, `AsyncLLM.add_request` raises
  `EngineFaultedError` → **HTTP 503**, so load balancers and SDKs retry on
  another instance.
- **[implemented] `/v1/fault_tolerance/status` stays reachable** throughout —
  it is served by the API server process, independent of the engine busy loop.
- **`/health` reports liveness, not FT state.** `check_health()` raises only when
  the engine process itself is gone (`engine_dead or not is_running`), so an
  engine that is `unhealthy` but alive still returns **200**. This is
  intentional: `/health` answers "is this process up", and the FT-specific
  question "should this instance take traffic" is answered by `add_request`
  returning **503** and by `/v1/fault_tolerance/status`. Point readiness at
  `/v1/fault_tolerance/status`, not at `/health`.

### Concurrency and idempotency of `apply`

- **[implemented] One recovery at a time per engine.** A command arriving while
  another recovery is in flight is rejected with
  `reason: "another recovery is in progress"`. This rejection does **not**
  overwrite `ft_state` / `last_ft_request_id` / `ft_error`, so the controller can
  still read which request *is* running — that is the "competing recovery
  reports the active operation" behavior.
- **[implemented] Replay after success is rejected**: recovery leaves the engine
  `healthy`, and the command gate only accepts commands while `unhealthy`, so a
  replay fails fast with `status is HEALTHY`.
- **Send a fresh `request_id` per round.** The `request_id` is recorded in
  `status` and namespaces the round's coordination keys in the per-round
  recovery store; the design does not treat a repeated `request_id` as a
  duplicate to suppress. A competing recovery is rejected and reports the active
  operation through `last_ft_request_id`.

### Rules that matter

- **`removed_dp_ranks` uses original rank IDs.** Ranks keep their startup IDs
  forever; a removed rank stays as an empty slot and nothing is renumbered. The
  set is cumulative-safe: you may include ranks removed in earlier rounds (the
  increment is what gets applied) but it must contain at least one new rank.
- **Recovery is all-or-nothing across engines.** Survivors vote
  (`all_reduce(MIN)` over one success bit on the rebuilt DP group); only
  unanimous success resumes serving.
- **After the first committed `scale_down`, engines never idle.** They keep
  stepping dummy batches when there is no traffic, which doubles as continuous
  fault detection. Expect extra power draw; before the first scale-down, idle
  behavior is unchanged.
- **Invalid commands are rejected up front and are non-terminal.** Bad
  `removed_dp_ranks` or missing store params produce a recorded `ft_error`; the
  controller re-reads status and re-issues.

---

## Design

### Slots model — EP topology never changes

From vLLM's point of view a removed rank remains an **empty slot**:
`parallel_config.data_parallel_size` / `data_parallel_rank` stay frozen at their
initial values and DP rank ids never change. There is exactly one coordinate
system (original) and no densification anywhere. Only the rebuilt Gloo
`cpu_group` uses dense internal ranks over `sorted(alive)`, computed at reinit
time and never written back to config.

The all2all kernel likewise keeps the original EP world size, with dead EP ranks
masked via `update_mask()` (both `deepep_low_latency` and `nixl_ep`). Keeping the
topology fixed is what avoids model re-init, graph recompile, and CUDA graph
re-capture on the recovery path.

### Engine-level flow

1. **Validate** `removed_dp_ranks` (non-empty, in range, excludes own rank,
   leaves ≥1 survivor) and require a non-empty increment over the cumulative
   dead set. Client errors here are non-terminal.
2. **Rebuild the TCPStore** if the store master (lowest alive rank) was just
   removed.
3. **Reinit the engine DP group** over `sorted(alive)` and create the per-round
   recovery store.
4. **Dispatch** to workers via `collective_rpc`, then **vote** — a unanimous
   `all_reduce(MIN)` over one success bit.
5. **Commit only after full success.** `data_parallel_master_ip` is committed
   inside the group reinit; `_dead_dp_ranks` is committed after the vote.

### Worker-level flow

1. Sync GPU, clean worker state (execute_model_state, kv_connector_output,
   input_batch).
2. **Validate the EPLB prerequisite** (EPLB state present with redundant
   experts). This is the platform-specific validation point, keeping the
   engine/client path backend-agnostic.
3. Clean all2all buffers (this also wipes kernel mask state).
4. **Mask** the dead EP ranks — computed from the engine-supplied **cumulative**
   `dead_dp_ranks`. The worker keeps no FT history; masks from earlier rounds are
   replayed from the engine's set, so `clean_buffers` never loses them. `retry`
   runs the same clean-and-replay logic.
5. **Redistribute experts** (see below).
6. **Reinit the Gloo DP group** over the surviving slots and mount the
   cumulative dead set on the DP group coordinator for dead-column
   neutralization.

### Expert redistribution

All operations are **deterministic with stable iteration order** — every
surviving rank produces bit-identical results with no cross-rank communication:

1. Mark dead columns in `physical_to_logical_map` as `-1`.
2. Steal slots from over-replicated experts (donors with >1 replica) to cover
   missing logical experts, interleaving across EP ranks for balanced loading.
3. Rebuild `logical_to_physical_map` and `logical_replica_count`.
4. Rebuild each FusedMoE layer's `_expert_map`.
5. Selectively reload **only reassigned** expert weights from disk.

Both checkpoint layouts are handled: per-expert checkpoints reload only the
reassigned `<layer>.<expert_id>.` weights; **fused** checkpoints (Qwen3-VL MoE,
gpt-oss — one tensor per layer holding all experts) reload the whole touched
layer tensor, which is correct because the weight loader writes each expert
through the rebuilt expert map. A `(layer, expert)` pair matching neither layout
raises a clear `RuntimeError`.

### Recovery commits only on a unanimous survivor vote

After worker dispatch, surviving engines `all_reduce(MIN)` one success bit over
the rebuilt DP group. A failed `retry` leaves the engine `unhealthy` and
retryable. A failed `scale_down` past request validation is terminal — the
engine reports `dead` and exits. Invalid commands are rejected up front with an
observable `ft_error`.

### `request_id` namespaces a recovery round

All engines in one round share the `request_id`, which namespaces that round's
coordination keys in the per-round recovery store so concurrent or stale rounds
cannot cross-talk. When empty it falls back to the engine's local reinit epoch.

---

## Implementation Notes

- **TP sibling lockstep barrier (TP > 1).** `_synchronize_dp_ranks` (v1) and
  `sync_cudagraph_and_dp_padding` (v2) run a per-step Gloo barrier over the TP
  CPU group when FT is enabled and `tp_size > 1`. A sibling whose peer stopped
  arriving fails on the host within `cpu_distributed_timeout_seconds`, never
  leaving an orphaned TP collective (e.g. fused allreduce kernels without
  timeout) on its device stream. The TP CPU group is rebuilt during worker
  `retry`. This and the dead-column fill are the only FT touchpoints on the hot
  path; cost is one loopback Gloo round trip per step.
- **Dead-column neutralization.** Under the slots model the DP allreduce tensors
  keep their original width and a dead rank's column stays `0` after the SUM
  allreduce, which is not neutral for `min` / `all(==1)` aggregations. After the
  allreduce each rank locally fills dead columns (from
  `get_dp_group().dead_dp_ranks`) with aggregate-neutral values. The fill happens
  *after* the allreduce — a pre-fill would be summed across all alive ranks.
  Known gap: the v2 `max_query_len` row is left at `0`, so an all-`None` vote
  reads as `0` when a dead column is present.
- **EPLB async state reset.** An `ft_reset_epoch` on the EPLB state lets the
  async worker detect a recovery and abandon in-flight transfers instead of
  applying stale results; the async thread survives exceptions when FT is
  enabled and stays alive so EPLB can resume after a retry.
- **Side-stream mask query.** Worker `query_mask` runs on a separate CUDA stream
  so a poisoned main stream cannot block the mask read that status reporting
  depends on.
- **Recovery port coordination (bind-and-hold).** Recovery rebuilds several Gloo
  groups whose members span processes. Ports are never pre-allocated via
  `get_open_port`; instead the group's rank-0 member binds a listening socket to
  port 0, publishes the port number through the per-round recovery store, and
  group init takes ownership of the held socket — so a stolen port cannot fail
  group init, which would be terminal for `scale_down`.
- **No idle pause after a committed scale-down.** The DP wave wake-up path
  depends on the DP coordinator, which has no failover, so once the dead set is
  non-empty the engine never idle-pauses and keeps stepping dummy batches. The
  32-step `sync_dp_state` allreduce is kept (it carries the pause consensus and
  doubles as idle-time fault detection), and explicit pause/resume (RL weight
  sync) is unaffected.

---

## Test Plan

**E2E tests** — `tests/v1/fault_tolerance/test_fault_tolerance_e2e.py`, gated on
`has_nixl_ep()`:

1. `test_injected_fault_retry_recovers_all_ranks` (DP=2) — injected fault, all
   ranks `unhealthy`, `retry`, all ranks `healthy` and serving.
2. `test_scale_down_removes_dead_rank_and_recovers` (DP=4, EPLB with 32
   redundant experts) — SIGKILL rank 1's worker; survivors go `unhealthy`, the
   victim's engine goes `dead` and rejects `retry` with a recorded `ft_error`;
   `scale_down(removed_dp_ranks=[1])` to all survivors; all survivors return to
   `healthy` and serve completions.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/fault_tolerance/test_fault_tolerance_e2e.py -v -s
```

**Manual cluster validation** — external LB, 4 independent API servers, one
engine each; DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (MoE, 64 logical experts),
`--data-parallel-size 4 --tensor-parallel-size 2` (EP world 8),
`--enable-expert-parallel --all2all-backend nixl_ep --enable-eplb`
(64 redundant experts, async), `--enable-fault-tolerance`,
`--cpu-distributed-timeout-seconds 30`, `engine_recovery_timeout_sec=500`.

**Manual PD-disaggregated validation** — 2P2D behind a proxy, KV transfer over
NIXL + Mooncake Store; each tier a separate DP=2 × TP=2 deployment (EP world 4
per tier), `MultiConnector` (`NixlConnector` + `MooncakeStoreConnector`).

---

## Test Results

### Manual scale-down validation: PD co-location, TP=2

**PASSED.** Exercises the TP=2 single-worker-kill scenario end to end.

| Phase | Observation | Timestamp |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster ready | 4 ranks (DP=4 × TP=2, EP world 8) initialized, serving baseline traffic | 17:49:24 – 17:50:48 |
| Fault injected | One worker of DP rank 1 (TP1 sibling, EP rank 3) killed during active inference | 17:50:48 |
| First survivor-side error | Survivors' TP1 workers hit gloo `Connection reset by peer` on the per-TP-rank DP group | 17:50:48 |
| Victim DEAD | Engine 1's executor shut down its remaining worker; busy loop cancelled → status DEAD; its API server stays up and keeps answering `/v1/fault_tolerance/status` | 17:50:57 |
| Survivors UNHEALTHY | Engines 0/2/3 raise from the nixl_ep kernel timeout with mask `[0,0,1,1,0,0,0,0]` (EP ranks 2,3 = DP rank 1, both TP workers) | 17:51:18 |
| scale_down dispatched | `POST /v1/fault_tolerance/apply` `removed_dp_ranks=[1]` → 202 on R0/R2/R3 | ~17:51:44 |
| Expert redistribution | 257 (layer, expert) pairs reloaded from disk per worker (652–733 tensors); `num_dispatchers` synced to `active_rank_bound=8` | 17:51:45 |
| Scale-down complete | Gloo DP group rebuilt 4→3 (dense group ranks R0→0, R2→1, R3→2; original `data_parallel_rank` frozen); engines 0/2/3 → HEALTHY, `cumulative dead_dp_ranks=[1]` | 17:51:45 |
| Post-recovery inference | All 3 survivors resume serving `/v1/chat/completions` with HTTP 200 | 17:51:45 – 17:52:07 |

Key observations:

- Recovery itself (mask replay + redistribution + weight reload + group reinit)
  completes in ~1s once dispatched; end-to-end latency is dominated by fault
  detection — immediate for the TP1 siblings via gloo connection-reset, ~30s for
  the surviving engines via the nixl_ep kernel timeout.
- No hangs and no orphaned TP collectives: the TP sibling lockstep barrier keeps
  survivor device streams clean.

### Manual scale-down validation: PD-disaggregated + TP=2

**PASSED.** Same scenario in a prefill/decode-disaggregated deployment (2P2D)
with KV transfer over NIXL + Mooncake Store.

| Phase | Observation | Timestamp |
|---|---|---|
| Cluster ready | 2P + 2D instances up (each DP=2 × TP=2, EP world 4), baseline requests served through the proxy | 14:15:48 – 14:16:55 |
| Fault injected | One worker of the decode tier's DP rank 1 (TP0 sibling, EP rank 2) killed during active decode (1 in-flight request on the victim) | 14:19:31 |
| Survivor detects fault | Surviving decode instance's workers (both TP ranks) raise gloo `Connection closed by peer` on the per-TP-rank DP group; engine → UNHEALTHY | 14:19:31 – 14:19:40 |
| Victim DEAD | Victim engine's executor shuts down its remaining worker; engine → DEAD; its in-flight request is lost with the instance | 14:19:36 – 14:19:40 |
| Mooncake cleanup | Master expires the dead instance's clients and unmounts its segments (clients 8 → 6) | 14:19:41 |
| scale_down dispatched | `POST /v1/fault_tolerance/apply` `removed_dp_ranks=[1]` → 202 on the surviving decode instance | 14:20:09 |
| Scale-down complete | Dead EP ranks [2, 3] masked at the nixl_ep kernel; `num_dispatchers` synced to `active_rank_bound=2`; 0 expert reassignments needed (64 redundant experts = a full second replica of every logical expert, so no weight reload); Gloo DP group rebuilt 2→1; engine → HEALTHY, `cumulative dead_dp_ranks=[1]` | 14:20:10 |
| Post-recovery inference | New requests through the proxy flow prefill → surviving decode instance (NIXL P2P + Mooncake lookup), `/v1/completions` returns 200, steady decode ~30 tok/s | 14:20:25 – 14:20:45 |

Key observations:

- The prefill tier (a separate DP group) is untouched by the decode-tier fault
  and keeps serving throughout.
- Fault detection is immediate (gloo connection reset on the DP group, including
  during a dummy batch on the idle surviving engine); recovery itself completes
  in ~1s once dispatched.
- With `num_redundant_experts` equal to the logical expert count, scale-down
  needs no expert reassignment or weight reload — every logical expert keeps a
  live replica.

title: [2/N][Core] support partial prefix cache hit for hybrid model
author: ZJY0516
body:
## Purpose

This PR builds on the partial prefix-cache primitives from #45939 and completes fine-grained prefix-cache hits for aligned full-attention + Mamba hybrid models. The overall design is described in RFC #45702.

The PR adds:

- a public `prefix_match_unit` that selects prefix-match granularity independently from physical KV-cache block sizes;
- fine-grained lookup in the full-attention and Mamba cache managers;
- token-accurate convergence in the hybrid coordinator;
- scheduler boundaries needed to materialize and resume partial Mamba states;
- copy-on-write for requests that continue from a shared partial block;
- worker-side block copies with scheduler-side lifetime fencing.


It e2e works now

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-FP8 --enable-prefix-caching --mamba-cache-mode align --prefix-match-unit 16
```

Use 2 sequential request to simulate multi-turn:
- 10000 in, 1 out
- 10000 + 200 in, 1 out

```
w/ partial cache hit
"first_latency_sec": 0.3047793720033951, "second_latency_sec": 0.09551339800236747

w/o partial cache hit
"first_latency_sec": 0.2865299719851464, "second_latency_sec": 0.13373498094733804
```

## Design

### Match unit and cache-manager hash views

`Request.block_hashes` is computed at `prefix_match_unit` granularity. Each KV-cache group continues to allocate its existing physical block size.

For example:

```text
prefix_match_unit          = 2
full-attention block_size  = 4
Mamba block_size           = 8

request hashes: H2, H4, H6, H8, H10, ...
```

Managers using physical-block lookup receive a grouped view such as `[H4, H8, ...]`. Managers supporting fine-grained lookup keep the original hash list and may probe `H2` or `H6` inside a physical block.

The configured match unit must divide every cache-group block size. If it is not specified, vLLM derives it from the GCD of the resolved group block sizes.

### Explicit token-length cache hits

Cache-manager lookup now returns both the physical blocks and the exact number of matched tokens:

```text
(blocks_by_group, hit_length)
```

The separate length is required because a hit at `H6` includes the physical block `[4, 8)`, but only tokens `[4, 6)` in that block are valid.

`FullAttentionManager` first matches complete physical blocks from the start of the request, then probes hash boundaries inside the next block from longest to shortest. `MambaManager` keeps its existing right-to-left state lookup, but can now search at match-unit boundaries and return the physical block containing the matched recurrent state.

Managers without fine-grained support continue to return block-aligned hit lengths through the same API.

### Hybrid-coordinator convergence

The hybrid coordinator tracks a token hit length independently from each group's block list. It repeatedly reduces the candidate length until every cache group can cover the same logical prefix.

For example:

```text
full attention: 6-token hit, 2 physical blocks
Mamba:          4-token hit, 1 physical block
------------------------------------------------
coordinator:    4-token hit
```

Full-attention results are downward-closed, so an existing result can be trimmed without another lookup. Physical block lists are trimmed with ceiling division so the block containing a partial tail is retained.

EAGLE also uses the explicit token length. In fine-grained mode it drops one match unit, rather than one physical block, before the result is returned.

The explicit-length contract is also propagated to the Mooncake store coordinator. Its block-pool adapter exposes `hash_block_size` so it can reuse the same manager lookup interface.

### Creating partial tail entries

Full attention registers the final hash-aligned prompt boundary once the containing physical block is available.

Aligned Mamba requires the recurrent state from exactly that boundary. The scheduler therefore stops once at the final match-unit boundary before the end of a partial prompt block. `MambaManager` registers that state only when the step lands on this boundary; it does not retain every intermediate state inside the physical block.

When execution resumes from a partial hit, the first chunk stops at the next physical block boundary. Subsequent chunks return to the existing block-aligned scheduling path.

### Copy-on-write

A request cannot append to a physical block while the prefix cache exposes an entry for an earlier boundary in that block. This PR uses copy-on-write, with two allocation paths.

For a new request hitting a partial entry, the request is redirected to a private block:

```text
request table: shared source -> private destination
copy:          shared source -> private destination
```

The shared cached block remains unchanged and the request continues from the private copy.

An already-running aligned-Mamba request may register a partial entry for its current state and then continue in the next step. Its worker block table is append-only, so that request must remain on the original block. Instead, the cache entry is moved to a new block:

```text
cache hashes: original request block -> cache-owned destination
copy:         original request block -> cache-owned destination
request:      continues writing the original block
```

`BlockPool.move_block_hashes()` re-points all hashes without emitting a remove/store event. The destination is excluded from same-step lookup until the copy has populated it.

### Copy execution and lifetime

Managers queue `(source, destination)` block pairs. `KVCacheManager` converts them to block-ID copies on `SchedulerOutput`, and workers execute them after zeroing newly allocated blocks and before model forward:

```text
zero new blocks -> copy partial blocks -> model forward
```

The worker copies complete block-major storage pages. Storage aliases across layer views are deduplicated, so each backing allocation is copied once.

Both copy endpoints are retained until the non-empty scheduler step carrying the copy has completed. Their release uses the existing deferred-free queue, preventing either block from being recycled while asynchronous execution is still reading or writing it.


---

title: [Perf] Enable + tune FlashInfer fused allreduce at world_size=16 on SM 10.3 (GB300)
author: majunze2001
body:
## Purpose

FlashInfer fused allreduce+RMSNorm is gated by world size in two places, and
neither currently admits `world_size=16`:

- `PassConfig.flashinfer_max_size()` returns `None` unless the world size is in
  `FI_SUPPORTED_WORLD_SIZES` (was `[2, 4, 8]`), and
- it then looks up `FI_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_MAX_SIZE_MB[capability]`, which for SM 10.3
  (GB300) had no `16` entry.

When either is missing, `flashinfer_max_size(16)` is `None`, so both the
`AllReduceFusionPass` and the standalone `FlashInferAllReduce` communicator disable
themselves and TP=16 falls back to a plain all-reduce plus a separate RMSNorm.

This became reachable now that #46001 makes **TEP=16 functional** for DeepSeek-V4
(block-FP8 shared expert sharding). This PR is the perf follow-up that turns the
fused path on at `world_size=16` and supplies the benchmarked threshold — the same
thing #37756 did for `ws=2/4/8`.


## Justification

Benchmarked on a GB300 NVL system — 4 nodes × 4 GPUs in one NVLink domain
(`world_size=16`), bf16, hidden=7168 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), CUDA-graph, 100 trials. ms/op.

### Standalone all-reduce — `benchmark_device_communicators.py`, ws=16

This is the comparison that sets the value: FlashInfer mnnvl vs `pynccl` (the
multi-node fallback). mnnvl wins through 56 MiB, **ties at 64 MiB**, loses above.

| Tensor Size | flashinfer_mnnvl | pynccl | Winner |
|-------------|-----------------:|-------:|--------|
| 28 MB | 0.122 | 0.161 | mnnvl (1.32×) |
| 42 MB | 0.180 | 0.211 | mnnvl (1.17×) |
| 56 MB | 0.238 | 0.249 | mnnvl (1.04×) |
| **64 MB** | **0.271** | **0.271** | **tie** |
| 70 MB | 0.296 | 0.286 | pynccl |
| 84 MB | 0.354 | 0.322 | pynccl |

`64` is the break-even (mnnvl is not worse through 64 MiB) and matches the `ws=2/4`
convention of `64` for "fusion competitive across the swept range." It is also a
lower bound on the true fusion threshold: `FI_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_MAX_SIZE_MB` actually
gates *fused* AR+RMSNorm vs *unfused (AR + a separate RMSNorm kernel)*, and the fused
op does the RMSNorm for free — so the real crossover is at least the AR-only one.
(`56` — the last strict win — is the more conservative alternative; the 56↔64 region
is flat / within noise.)

### Fused AR+RMSNorm — `benchmark_fused_collective.py`, ws=16 (corroboration)

Confirms fusion is strongly beneficial and that the one-shot flag is inert for mnnvl
(one-shot ≡ two-shot at every size):

| Input Size | Standard (compiled) | mnnvl 1shot | mnnvl 2shot |
|------------|--------------------:|------------:|------------:|
| 7 MB | 0.164 | 0.033 (5.0×) | 0.033 (5.0×) |
| 28 MB | 0.386 | 0.125 (3.1×) | 0.125 (3.1×) |
| 56 MB | 0.700 | 0.254 (2.8×) | 0.254 (2.8×) |
| 112 MB | 1.278 | 0.510 (2.5×) | 0.510 (2.5×) |
| 224 MB | 2.419 | 1.017 (2.4×) | 1.017 (2.4×) |

Caveat: in this environment the `nccl_allocator` failed to link (the pip-wheel
`libnccl.so.2` isn't on the linker path), so NVLS/symmetric-memory was disabled and
the `standard` baseline is slower than on a fully-configured node — this inflates the
fused speedup and is why the fused-vs-standard crossover never appears here. The `64`
value is therefore anchored on the standalone-AR table above (mnnvl vs `pynccl`),
which is symmetric-memory-independent, not on this table.

## Relation to existing PRs (not a duplicate)

- **#37756**  — *"Add SM 10.3 all-reduce communicator tuning"* — set these
  same tables for `ws=2/4/8`. This PR extends the identical mechanism to `ws=16`
  using the same two benchmarks. Different world size; not a duplicate.
- **#46001**  — makes TEP=16 *functional* for DeepSeek-V4 (block-FP8 shared
  expert). That PR touches only the V4 model; it does not enable the fused allreduce.
  This PR is the orthogonal perf enablement and depends on TEP=16 being reachable.
- **#40970**  — fixes the FlashInfer allreduce *benchmark* harness; does not
  touch the threshold tables.

`gh pr list --state open --search "FI_ALLREDUCE_FUSION_MAX_SIZE_MB"` and related
searches found no open PR adding a `ws=16` threshold.

## Test Plan

Run on a GB300 NVL system (4 nodes × 4 GPUs = 16 in one NVLink domain), the same two
benchmarks #37756 used:

```bash
# Standalone all-reduce communicator comparison (sets the value)
torchrun --nnodes 4 --nproc_per_node 4 \
    benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_device_communicators.py \
    --num-warmup 10 --num-trials 100

# Fused allreduce+rmsnorm vs standard (corroboration; ws=16 enablement is in this PR)
FI_BACKENDS=mnnvl torchrun --nnodes 4 --nproc_per_node 4 \
    benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_fused_collective.py \
    --hidden-dim 7168 --num-tokens 128 256 512 1024 2048 4096 \
    --quant-modes none --warmup 10 --trials 100
```

Results: tables above. mnnvl all-reduce beats `pynccl` through ~56–64 MiB at `ws=16`;
fused AR+RMSNorm is 2.4–8× over the non-fused path across the swept range.

Lint:

```bash
pre-commit run ruff-check ruff-format --files \
    vllm/config/compilation.py \
    vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/allreduce_rms_fusion.py
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files \
    vllm/config/compilation.py \
    vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/allreduce_rms_fusion.py
```

Not yet run / out of scope: end-to-end compiled (non-eager) TEP=16 serving with the
fused pass active. The TEP=16 functional validation (gsm8k) in #46001 was under
`--enforce-eager`, which bypasses the compilation fusion pass; exercising this path
end-to-end is a follow-up once #46001 lands.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude). A human author has reviewed
every changed line and is responsible for the change end-to-end, including running
the benchmarks and lint above on GB300 hardware.

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Disable dynamic speculative decoding for fixed-K proposers instead of crashing
author: Sunt-ing
body:
## Purpose

Dynamic speculative decoding (`num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size`, added in #32374) lowers the runtime speculative-token count below the configured maximum, down to 0, based on batch size. Four proposers were written before that feature and hard-assert that the runtime count equals the configured maximum:

- `ngram_proposer_gpu.py:341` `assert num_speculative_tokens == self.k`
- `extract_hidden_states.py:119` `assert num_speculative_tokens == self.num_speculative_tokens`
- `suffix_decoding.py:44` `assert num_speculative_tokens == self.num_speculative_tokens`
- `medusa.py:49` `assert num_speculative_tokens == self.num_speculative_tokens`

So enabling dynamic SD with any of `ngram_gpu` / `suffix` / `medusa` / `extract_hidden_states` lets the scheduler legally pick a runtime count below the max and the proposer crashes with `AssertionError` deep inside `LLM.generate()`, after the config was accepted and the target model already ran. Proposers that do support dynamic SD honor the runtime count instead (eagle family overwrites `self.num_speculative_tokens` in `llm_base_proposer.py`; CPU `ngram` uses `assert num_speculative_tokens <= self.k`).

This mirrors the existing contract that dynamic SD is incompatible with some configurations. Following the same pattern as the data-parallel case (`_maybe_disable_dynamic_sd_for_data_parallel` in #45963), this PR disables dynamic SD at config init for these fixed-K methods, warns, and falls back to the static `num_speculative_tokens`, instead of crashing at runtime.

## Test Plan

Real `LLM.generate()` before/after on the 3 GPU-reachable methods (`ngram_gpu`, `extract_hidden_states`, `suffix`), plus a config-level regression test.

E2E repro (crashes on current main, RTX 4090, V1 model runner):

```python
import os
os.environ["VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER"] = "0"
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",
    enforce_eager=True,
    max_model_len=256,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.35,
    speculative_config={
        "method": "ngram_gpu",
        "prompt_lookup_min": 1,
        "prompt_lookup_max": 4,
        "num_speculative_tokens": 4,
        # dynamic SD schedule: batch size 1 -> runtime K=0
        "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size": [(1, 1, 0), (2, 8, 4)],
    },
)
out = llm.generate(["ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha"],
                   SamplingParams(max_tokens=4, temperature=0.0))
print(out[0].outputs[0].text)
```

Regression test:

```
pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dynamic_sd.py -q
```

## Test Result

Config regression test `test_dynamic_sd_disabled_for_fixed_k_method` (parametrized: `ngram_gpu` disabled, `ngram` unchanged) fails on current main and passes with this PR. Full file `tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dynamic_sd.py`: 18 passed.

E2E on RTX 4090, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, V1 model runner. The same `LLM.generate()` call crashes on current main and runs to completion with this PR for both `ngram_gpu` and `suffix`. `extract_hidden_states` and `medusa` have the identical assertion and are handled by the same config guard.

<details>
<summary>Before (current main): AssertionError</summary>

title: [DeepEP V2] Bound num_max_tokens_per_rank in do_expand=False
author: WoosukKwon
body:
## Purpose

In `do_expand=False` (decode / cudagraph) mode, `DeepEPV2PrepareAndFinalize._do_dispatch` left `num_max_tokens_per_rank` unset, so `ElasticBuffer.dispatch` fell back to the buffer's init capacity (`= max_num_batched_tokens`). The recv buffer was therefore sized to the worst case `R * max_num_batched_tokens`, and the expert kernels processed ~`R * 8192` rows even when only a handful of decode tokens were present — which dominated decode step time.

This PR bounds `num_max_tokens_per_rank` to the DP-padded batch size (`max(num_tokens_across_dp)`, uniform across ranks), rounded up to a power of two.

The pow2 bucketing is important: DeepEP JIT-compiles a separate dispatch kernel per distinct `num_max_tokens_per_rank`. Feeding the raw per-step size makes it recompile for every batch size — a `cicc` recompile storm that starves the GPU at high concurrency. Rounding up to a power of two bounds the compiled set to ~`log2(max_num_batched_tokens)` values (compiled once, then cached), while staying small for decode (e.g. 1 token → 1) and capped at the buffer's init capacity for prefill.

Prefill (`do_expand=True`) is unchanged — it keeps the existing `num_max_tokens_per_rank=None` / CPU-sync path.

## Not a duplicate

Searched open PRs for `num_max_tokens_per_rank`, `DeepEPV2`, `DeepEP v2`, and `deepep_v2`. The related open DeepEP v2 PRs — #45282 (NVFP4 dispatch), #40718 (combine_v2), #45193 (topk_ids optional for do_expand), #45321 (Dockerfile version bump) — address different areas. None touch decode-mode recv-buffer sizing.

## Test plan

- Lint/type: `ruff check`, `ruff format`, and `mypy` (via pre-commit) pass on the touched file.
- Benchmarked DeepSeek-V4-Flash on GB200 ×4, `dp=4 -ep`, DeepEP v2 + Triton MoE:
  - **concurrency=1 decode step time: 100.7 ms → 16.4 ms (6.1×)**
  - concurrency=64: no `cicc` recompile storm (previously ~0% GPU utilization during the storm)
  - concurrency=1024: ~+6% throughput
  - GSM8K accuracy unchanged (~95%)

## Note

AI assistance (Claude) was used in preparing this change.

Signed-off-by: Woosuk Kwon <woosuk@inferact.ai>

This test was failing in CI on ROCm due to fp16 numerical mismatches between the reference and the fused kernel. The root cause is that the torch-native reference (forward_native) implicitly upcasts fp16×fp16 to fp32, while the fused CUDA kernel runs in native fp16.

title: [Perf] Skip detokenization in online beam search
author: GuyStone
body:
## What & why

Online beam search builds an internal per-step `SamplingParams` requesting
`logprobs = 2 * beam_width`. The engine then **detokenizes every one of those
`2 * beam_width` logprob token ids into strings on every decode step**
(`LogprobsProcessor` → `tokenizer.decode`). Beam search never uses those
strings — it ranks candidates by `cum_logprob` and detokenizes only the final
selected sequences itself (`tokenizer.decode(tokens)` near the end of
`beam_search`). 

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/837d5b35636d731fecca95c39dd0280a02013ba2/vllm/entrypoints/generate/beam_search/online.py#L208
The per-step detokenization is therefore pure overhead that
grows with beam width, and it starves the GPU between decode steps.

This sets `detokenize=False` on the internal per-step `SamplingParams` in
`vllm/entrypoints/generate/beam_search/online.py`. Final output text is
unchanged (still produced by the explicit `tokenizer.decode` on the winning
beams). `detokenize=False` is only invalid alongside `stop` strings, and these
per-step params set none, so it is safe here.

```diff
         logprobs_num = 2 * beam_width
         sampling_params = SamplingParams(
             logprobs=logprobs_num,
             max_tokens=1,
             temperature=temperature,
+            detokenize=False,
         )
```

Scope is the **online** path only. The offline path
(`beam_search/offline.py`) has the identical pattern and would benefit from the
same one-liner as a follow-up.

## Benchmark — before / after

`vllm bench serve`, Qwen3-1.7B, single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, `--backend
openai-chat`, random dataset 512-in / 32-out, 20 prompts, `--max-concurrency
4`, `--ignore-eos`, fixed `--seed 12345`. Beam search triggered via
`--extra-body '{"use_beam_search": true, "n": <bw>, "temperature": 1.0}'`.
Beam search is non-streaming, so TTFT ≈ E2EL and TPOT/ITL are ~0 — the
meaningful metrics are **end-to-end latency** and **throughput**.

| Beam width | Mean E2EL (baseline → after) | Speedup | Output tok/s (before → after) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 1542.7 ms → **855.3 ms** | **1.80×** | 1652 → 2985 |
| 60 | 6611.7 ms → **2615.3 ms** | **2.53×** | 1161 → 2913 |

The win grows with beam width, as expected for an O(beam_width) per-step cost.

## GPU utilization (nvidia-smi dmon, during the runs)

The GPU was being starved by CPU-side detokenization; removing it roughly
**doubles** SM utilization:

| Beam width | SM util, active samples (before → after) | Peak SM |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 34% → **62%** | 40% → 73% |
| 60 | 22% → **42%** | 54% → 74% |

## nsys profiling (before / after)

Nsight Systems trace bracketing an identical focused bw60 run (12 prompts,
conc 2, seed 777, captured via `nsys start`/`stop`):

| | Baseline | After |
|---|---|---|
| Focused-run wall (bench duration) | 21.13 s | **10.08 s** |
| Total GPU kernel time (`cuda_gpu_kern_sum`) | 3.311 s | 3.319 s |
| GPU busy fraction (kernel time / wall) | **15.7%** | **32.9%** |
| Mean E2EL (focused run) | 3521.8 ms | 1679.1 ms |

The total GPU kernel time is **identical** before and after (~3.31 s) — the fix
removes no GPU work, only CPU work. Same compute in ~half the wall clock, so the
GPU busy fraction doubles (cross-validates the dmon numbers). Host-side CUDA API
time stays dominated by `cudaEventSynchronize` (the engine waiting on the GPU),
consistent with the bottleneck being host-side detok between GPU bursts.
(CPU IP/backtrace sampling was unavailable in this environment, so the trace
attributes the saved time to reduced wall clock / higher GPU duty cycle rather
than naming `tokenizers.decode` directly.)

## Correctness

Identical deterministic beam-search request (`n=4`, `temperature=0`) against the
server before and after the change returned **byte-identical** output for all
beams — confirming `detokenize=False` does not alter results.

## Not a duplicate

No open PR addresses this. Upstream PR vllm-project/vllm#33563 implemented the
same idea and was **approved by a maintainer** ("a good and safe optimization")
but was closed by its author over commit-history issues, deferring to
vllm-project/vllm#29133, which has since also closed. Both touched the older
file layout (`entrypoints/llm.py`, `entrypoints/openai/engine/serving.py`); the
current `entrypoints/generate/beam_search/online.py` still lacks the
optimization. This PR applies it to the current code path.

## Test commands run

```bash
# build (editable, precompiled wheel pinned to a published commit)
VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 VLLM_PRECOMPILED_WHEEL_COMMIT=6cc2c9ba… \
  uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto
# server
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --port 8000 --max-logprobs 256
# benchmark (run per beam width, before and after)
vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --dataset-name random --random-input-len 512 \
  --random-output-len 32 --num-prompts 20 --max-concurrency 4 --seed 12345 \
  --ignore-eos --num-warmups 3 \
  --extra-body '{"use_beam_search": true, "n": 20, "temperature": 1.0}'
```

Lint: `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on the changed file.

## AI assistance

reviewed every changed line and ran the benchmarks and correctness check above.

title: [Perf][ThinkingBudget] reduce search space for thinking tokens
author: walterbm
body:
## Purpose

Currently the thinking token budget logic uses `_find_last_sequence_index` to scan the entire generated sequence on every single generated token.

```python
end_thinking = self._find_last_sequence_index(
       state.get("output_tok_ids", []), self.think_end_token_ids
)
```
This causes the scan time to blow up on longer generations because it's basically a O(n^2) nested loop.

One way to fix this time complexity is to keep track of the sequences that have already been scanned in the TB state and only search for new tokens. This PR  implement that change by adding a new `_find_last_sequence_index_from` helper.

## Test Plan
Created a micro-benchmark to test the difference between current full rescan of `_find_last_sequence_index` vs the new `_find_last_sequence_index_from` per decode step.

```python
import time

from vllm.v1.sample.thinking_budget_state import ThinkingBudgetStateHolder

MARKER = [998, 997]

def full_rescan(n: int) -> float:
    out: list[int] = []
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(1)
        ThinkingBudgetStateHolder._find_last_sequence_index(out, MARKER)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

def incremental(n: int) -> float:
    out: list[int] = []
    cursor = 0
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n):
        out.append(1)
        idx = ThinkingBudgetStateHolder._find_last_sequence_index_from(
            out, MARKER, cursor - (len(MARKER) - 1)
        )
        if idx == -1:
            cursor = len(out)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"{'thinking tokens':>15} | {'full rescan':>12} | {'incremental':>12} | {'speedup':>8}")
for n in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000, 8_000, 16_000, 32_000):
    full = full_rescan(n)
    incr = incremental(n)
    print(f"{n:>15,} | {full:>10.3f}s | {incr:>10.4f}s | {full / incr:>7.0f}x")

```

## Test Result
| thinking tokens | full rescan (`_find_last_sequence_index`) | incremental (`_find_last_sequence_index_from`) | speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1,000 | 0.052 s | 0.0004 s | 148× |
| 2,000 | 0.125 s | 0.0007 s | 180× |
| 4,000 | 0.521 s | 0.0014 s | 374× |
| 8,000 | 2.187 s | 0.0029 s | 743× |
| 16,000 | 8.647 s | 0.0061 s | 1415× |
| 32,000 | 34.744 s | 0.0114 s | 3061× |

title: [Optimization] Skip DP padding tokens in MoE
author: WoosukKwon
body:
For DP/EP with CUDA graphs, a batch can contain a large number of padding tokens. Today, these padding tokens are handled the same way as real tokens, introducing unnecessary compute overhead.

For example, if one DP rank has a 512-token prefill while the other ranks are idle, every DP rank pads its input batch to 512 tokens—the maximum across all DP ranks, since 512 falls within the PW CUDA graph bucket. As a result, the model processes `512 * dp_size` tokens instead of the actual 512 real tokens.

This PR enables skipping these padding tokens by marking their `topk` values as `-1`. MoE kernels and A2A kernels, such as DeepEP V2, can then optionally skip sending/computing those tokens and avoid the associated overhead.

This behavior is currently gated behind the `VLLM_MOE_SKIP_PADDING` environment variable, which defaults to `0`, because some MoE kernels may not support `topk = -1`.

title: [XPU] Optimize XPU worker shutdown logic to prevent resource leak
author: chaojun-zhang
body:
## Purpose:
Optimize the XPU shutdown flow to properly release oneCCL/Level Zero resources when vLLM server stops. 

This also fixes a hang issue where repeated server startups on the same XPU devices would deadlock during oneCCL initialization.

## Problem:
With the default shutdown_timeout=0 (abort mode), worker processes are force-killed without executing cleanup code. On XPU, this leaves Level Zero driver resources unreleased, causing subsequent server startups on the same devices to hang at oneCCL all_reduce.

## Fix:
- Set shutdown_timeout=5 for XPU platform, enabling drain mode so workers can run destroy_model_parallel() and
  destroy_distributed_environment() before exit
- Add gc.collect() + empty_cache() + synchronize() in model runner shutdown for XPU (matching existing ROCm behavior)

- Add XPUWorker.shutdown() with rank/local_rank logging and mem pool release 

How to reproduce (without this PR)
1. pytest -sv tests/basic_correctness/test_cpu_offload.py

title: [ROCm][P/D] MoRIIO toy proxy: support JSON Content-Type for OpenAI clients.
author: lcskrishna
body:
## Purpose

The Quart-based MoRIIO disaggregated toy proxy returns streamed responses with Quart's defaults via `make_response(stream_generator)` without setting a `Content-Type`. 

Quart defaults a streamed response to `text/html; charset=utf-8`, so even on a successful `200` the body is mislabeled.

**Reference Documentation from Quart:** 
https://quart.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/reference/source/quart.wrappers.response.html

This breaks OpenAI-compatible JSON clients. For example, `lm_eval` (`local-completions` backend) calls `response.json()`, which rejects the non-JSON mimetype and discards every response with the following error message: 

```
ContentTypeError(..., status=200, message="Attempt to decode JSON with unexpected mimetype: text/html; charset=utf-8", headers=<... 'Content-Type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8', 'Server': 'hypercorn-h11' ...>)
```

The result is `(no outputs)` for every request and no accuracy score, even though the prefill/decode disaggregation path itself works correctly. The MoRIIO proxy is the only one (Quart-based) that omits it.

This PR aims at supporting Content-Type (application/json) for MoRI IO toy proxy server and also matches with other toy proxies. 

## Changes

Files changed: 

* `examples/disaggregated/disaggregated_serving/moriio_toy_proxy_server.py`

## Test Plan

* Run the following GSM8K lm_eval command in PD Disagg with MoRI IO toy proxy. 

```
lm_eval --model local-completions --tasks gsm8k \ --model_args model=<model>,base_url=http://127.0.0.1:<proxy_port>/v1/completions,num_concurrent=64,max_retries=3,tokenized_requests=False
```

title: [Bugfix] Allow flashinfer_cutlass as a clamped NVFP4 MoE backend
author: lucifer1004
body:
Models that set a SwiGLU clamp (swiglu_limit) -- e.g. DeepSeek-V4-Flash NVFP4 -- restrict NVFP4 MoE backend selection to NVFP4_BACKENDS_WITH_CLAMP, which previously contained only FLASHINFER_TRTLLM. The TRTLLM NVFP4 fused MoE only supports Blackwell datacenter GPUs (capability family 100 / SM100), so on SM120 (e.g. RTX PRO 6000) selection fails with "No NvFp4 MoE backend supports the deployment configuration", with no eligible fallback.

FlashInferExperts (flashinfer_cutlass) already applies the clamp -- it builds gemm1_clamp_limit and passes swiglu_limit into flashinfer_cutlass_fused_moe -- and supports SM120. Add it to NVFP4_BACKENDS_WITH_CLAMP so clamped NVFP4 MoE models can run on workstation Blackwell. FLASHINFER_TRTLLM stays first in AVAILABLE_BACKENDS, so SM100 selection is unchanged. This also matches the explicit-backend error message, which already lists flashinfer_cutlass as a clamp-capable option.

Validated on RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) with DeepSeek-V4-Flash NVFP4 (TP2/EP2): the backend selects flashinfer_cutlass, the server reaches ready, and GSM8K exact_match = 0.965, confirming the clamp is numerically honored.

title: [Bugfix] FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120 compatibility with GLM-5 NVFP4
author: lucifer1004
body:
Models with an index_topk skip pattern (e.g. GLM-5.2, index_topk_freq=4)
build a sparse-MLA indexer only on a subset of backbone layers; the
remaining "skip" layers are constructed with indexer=None and instead
receive the shared top-k indices buffer via MLAAttention
(extra_impl_args["topk_indices_buffer"], see mla_attention.py).

FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120 asserted `indexer is not None` and only read
`indexer.topk_indices_buffer`, so every skip layer crashed at init with
"requires a sparse-MLA indexer". This broke serving of GLM-5.2 (both
NVFP4 and MXFP4) on SM120, even though MLAAttention already passes the
shared buffer for these layers.

Mirror FLASHMLA_SPARSE: take the shared buffer from the indexer when
present, otherwise from mla_args. The existing
`assert self.topk_indices_buffer is not None` still guards the
truly-missing case.

title: [Rust Frontend] [Perf] Make Granite4 string argument scanning incremental
author: reidliu41
body:
## Purpose

  Granite4 tool calls can encode `arguments` either directly as an object or as a JSON string containing the serialized arguments:

  ```json
  {"name":"f","arguments":{"data":"..."}}
  {"name":"f","arguments":"{\"data\":\"...\"}"}
```

  The object form already carries scan state across streaming chunks. The
  string form was still parsed with the one-shot `json_str` helper, which
  cannot remember how much of an incomplete string it has already scanned.
  When a long string-valued argument arrived over many chunks, each retry
  started again from the beginning of the buffered string.

  This change adds a small scan state for the string form: the byte offset
  already scanned and whether the scanner is currently after an escape
  character. Granite4 now resumes string scanning across chunks, then
  decodes the complete JSON string once the closing quote is available.
  The emitted arguments stay unchanged.

 Use a direct reproduction that feeds Granite4 string-valued 
arguments in 7-byte chunks and measures end-to-end parser time.
```
  Before this change:

   payload    string-valued arguments
  ━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    16 KiB                   6.789 ms
  ─────────  ─────────────────────────
    32 KiB                  27.031 ms
  ─────────  ─────────────────────────
    64 KiB                 107.961 ms

  After this change:

   payload    string-valued arguments
  ━━━━━━━━━  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    16 KiB                   0.038 ms
  ─────────  ─────────────────────────
    32 KiB                   0.078 ms
  ─────────  ─────────────────────────
    64 KiB                   0.166 ms
```
  Before the change, doubling the string argument size increased runtime
  by roughly 4x on larger inputs. After the change, runtime scales roughly
  linearly.

  This PR also adds a Criterion benchmark for Granite4 long arguments.
  Local result after this change:
```
  - granite4/long_string_arguments/reuse_parser: about 110 us
  - granite4/long_string_arguments/create_parser: about 108 us
```

title: [Attention][MLA] FlashMLA sparse: DCP on the fp8_ds_mla mixed-batch path + MTP
author: drakosha
body:
DCP support for the `FLASHMLA_SPARSE` backend on the `fp8_ds_mla` KV path, including MTP spec decode under full cudagraphs. `fp8_ds_mla` is what the backend selector picks on Hopper for DSA models with small per-rank head counts (GLM-5.2 / DeepSeek-V3.2 at TP4/DCP4), and this path previously refused DCP outright.

Earlier revisions stacked on #46076 and carried the sparse-indexer DCP machinery (global top-k merge, `--dcp-sparse-indexer-mode`); all of that has since landed in main via #46076 and its follow-ups, so the PR is now backend-side only: +234/−34 across `flashmla_sparse.py`, `flashmla.py` and one test file. (#45426 was our earlier standalone version with its own indexer; this supersedes it and reuses the upstream merge machinery instead.)

## Changes

`flashmla_sparse.py`:
- Opt the backend into the shared DCP decode merge (`can_return_lse_for_decode`): the fp8 mixed-batch kernel now returns decode LSE, sliced together with the head padding and reshaped to the `(tokens, heads)` layout the reducer consumes.
- Under DCP the indexer emits global token ids: keep this rank's shard and convert to local `fp8_ds_mla` slots via `triton_filter_and_convert_dcp_index` with `compact_valid_to_front=False` — the scattered `-1`s stay in place and the fp8 kernel masks them natively, skipping the per-call front-pack. Rows where this rank owns none of the selected tokens get `(0, -inf)`, the identity of the cross-rank LSE merge, so they drop out of the reduce.
- Allow varlen decode under DCP (`supports_dcp_with_varlen` when `cp_kv_cache_interleave_size == 1`): causality comes from the indexer's top-k indices, not kernel metadata. This is what makes MTP + DCP work under full cudagraphs.
- Fail-closed guards instead of silent corruption: `ag_rs` comm backend only; fp8 mixed-batch path only (the split prefill/decode path returns LSE for decode tokens only, and the bf16 sparse path is rejected under DCP); a head-envelope guard rejecting configs where local and DCP-gathered head counts pad to different fp8 decode kernel envelopes (e.g. 128 q-heads at TP8/DCP8).

`flashmla.py` (dense FlashMLA decode): flatten the kernel's `[batch, heads, seq_len]` LSE to `[tokens, heads]` for the DCP reducer — matters under spec decode, where `seq_len > 1`.

Tests: `test_fp8_dcp_head_envelope_guard` in `test_sparse_mla_backends.py`, parametrized over local head counts × DCP world sizes, both accepting and rejecting cases.

## Testing

4×H200, GLM-5.2-NVFP4, TP4/DCP4/EP + MTP, `fp8_ds_mla`, current rebase:

- `test_sparse_mla_backends.py` + `test_indexer_dcp_localize.py`: 140 passed / 0 failed (SM90).
- Full cudagraph capture clean; exact needle recovery at 198k context across all ranks.
- Warm decode 78 tok/s at batch 1, 854 aggregate at batch 32 (786k context window).
- dcp=1/2/4 byte-identical on long (>2048-tok) contexts in earlier revisions of the same merge path.

The branch has also been soaking continuously since mid-July on a production 4×H200 GLM-5.2-NVFP4 deployment (TP4/DCP4/EP + MTP) via nightly-based images carrying this PR.

Related fixes in the surrounding DCP infra that this path exposed were split out and handled separately: #48379 (fp8_ds_mla boot on main, merged), #50823 (block-table width under DCP, merged), #50883 (offload block-size scaling under DCP, open).

AI assistance (Claude) was used; every line reviewed by the submitter, tests run by the submitter.

<details>
<summary>History: pre-rebase description (union indexer mode, perf vs #45426) — superseded</summary>

Earlier revisions added an opt-in `--dcp-sparse-indexer-mode {exact,union}` on top of #46076's global top-k merge, motivated by a ~30% batch-1 decode regression of the exact merge vs our standalone indexer (#45426): 52.0 → 36.4 tok/s warm at batch 1, with union recovering to 43.5 and a follow-up localizer opt to 50.7. After the indexer machinery landed upstream in its final form, the flag and the indexer-side changes were dropped from this PR; the numbers above no longer describe the current diff.

</details>

title: [Docker] Remove redundant flashinfer download-cubin step
author: mgoin
body:
## Summary

The `flashinfer-cubin` wheel — a default CUDA dep in `requirements/cuda.txt` since #37233 — already ships all precompiled cubins into the package directory that FlashInfer's runtime loader reads from (`jit/env.py:_get_cubin_dir` resolves to the package dir when `flashinfer-cubin` is installed). The `flashinfer download-cubin` step in `vllm-base` re-downloads the same files from NVIDIA's artifactory **unconditionally** (`download_artifacts()` has no skip-if-present check), and since #41134 moved it below the per-commit wheel-install layer, that download re-runs on every build (~10 min, ~half the image-build job). This removes the redundant step.

## Validation

Inspected the shipped nightly image (`vllm/vllm-openai@sha256:14469ba3…`):

- `flashinfer_cubin` wheel ships **15,558 `.cubin` files (1.8 GB)** — all listed in the wheel `RECORD`, i.e. provided by `pip install`, not the download step.
- With **`--network=none` and `FLASHINFER_NO_DOWNLOAD=1`**, the runtime loader (`get_artifact`) resolves cubins from disk with checksum verification passing (8/8 sampled). The image needs no network for cubins at runtime.
- `download-cubin` still re-fetched all ~15.6k artifacts in build #73639 despite the wheel already providing them — confirming pure redundancy.
- Compared the full required artifact set against the wheel: **0 missing** — all 15,558 cubins, all 34 unique `.h` headers (incl. the `trtllmGen_*_export/*.h` JIT include paths), and all 7 `checksums.txt` are shipped by the wheel.

Anything genuinely not bundled is JIT-fetched by FlashInfer on first use, the same as for any `pip install flashinfer-cubin` user who never runs `download-cubin`.

## Relation to #46465

Alternative to #46465, which keeps the download and caches it via a dedicated BuildKit stage (+53 net lines). Since the wheel already provides the cubins, the download isn't needed at all — this just deletes it (−7 lines). One of the two should land, not both.

## Notes

AI assistance (Claude) was used to investigate and prepare this change; I reviewed every line and am accountable for it.
