title: [Bugfix][SM120][MLA] Support NoPE sparse MLA (GLM-5.3-Flash) on the FlashInfer SM120 backend
author: lucifer1004
body:
## Purpose

Enable native NoPE (`qk_rope_head_dim=0`) cache writes for GLM-5.3-Flash on `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120`, without padding the query or allocating a synthetic RoPE tensor.

Rebased onto `a6131b0e656e18eeb3797b8856aa3dbc69efd8e5`. The former physical top-k capacity patch has been dropped: #53781 already implements it in the shared `_run_mqa_kernel`, including HiSparse paths. This PR now contains the cache-writer fix and regression tests only.

## Changes

- Accept `pe_dim` 0 or 64 for `fp8_ds_mla`.
- Preserve the existing 656-byte cache row: 512 bytes of FP8 latent, 16 bytes of FP32 tile scales, and 128 bytes of RoPE/reserved storage.
- For NoPE, do not read the empty `k_pe` tensor; zero the reserved tail. The 64-dimensional RoPE path is unchanged.
- Compare BF16 NoPE writes byte-for-byte with the existing zero-RoPE path at block sizes 64/256. Fixed slots cover a block boundary and an invalid token; explicit assertions check zero tails and untouched sentinel rows. Existing tests retain responsibility for quantization correctness.

## Dependencies and related work

FlashInfer native GLM53_NOPE support (#4802) and backend-scoped length validation (#4947) have merged. Later #5075/#5197 implementations accept the existing 656-byte padded pool through runtime row stride; this PR deliberately does not change vLLM cache allocation to compact 528-byte rows.

The validation below uses FlashInfer source revision `dc04f50c9aa3eabcdaa5feb0934edb3d85e9529a`, which includes those later changes. vLLM's default `flashinfer-python==0.6.18.post1` pin does not provide native GLM53_NOPE support: this writer change alone does not make the default pinned stack sufficient. No dependency bump is bundled here.

This is the existing native-kernel alternative to the padding approaches in #53969 and #55778, not a new duplicate PR. Native NoPE avoids manufacturing a 64-dimensional query/RoPE lane. Credit to @hamiltongaianimd for originally surfacing the kpool width issue; that part is now handled upstream. The independent warmup changes in #55264 are not included.

## Fresh validation

Hardware/model: 4x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, TP4, NVIDIA `GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`, BF16 activations, no speculation, text-only, max context 65536, max sequences 32, batched tokens 4096, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` CUDA graphs. Logs confirm `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE_SM120` and `fp8_ds_mla`, not the community B12X attention backend.

- `pixi install --locked --all`: passed, rebuilding the CUDA extensions.
- `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 inferlab run -- python -m pytest vllm/tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py vllm/tests/v1/attention/test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_sm120_api.py -k 'concat_and_cache_ds_mla or sm120' -q -rs`: **8 passed, 3 skipped** after test simplification (existing unsupported-rank/input-size cases).
- Repository pre-commit hooks: passed, including Ruff, clang-format, mypy, SPDX, and test tethering.
- The final cleanup changes only comments and tests; runtime code is unchanged from the serving validations below. Those full serving runs were not repeated for the cleanup.
- Managed smoke completion: HTTP 200 with coherent output; CUDA graph capture succeeded. The smoke recipe initially reported cleanup verification too early; a subsequent managed stop verified all GPUs freed.
- Full GSM8K, 1319 samples, strict exact match, concurrency 32, max output 2048: **0.9272175891 (1223/1319)**. Recipe and cleanup succeeded. This is fresh evidence, not a reuse of the old 0.9325 result.
- Random 8000-input/1000-output-token matrix, cold prefix cache at each level, 4 requests per concurrency unit: **252/252 requests completed, zero failed**, all six cases succeeded.

| Concurrency | Requests | Output tokens/s | Mean TTFT ms | Mean TPOT ms |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 4 | 99.09 | 1299.26 | 8.80 |
| 2 | 8 | 174.15 | 1257.75 | 10.23 |
| 4 | 16 | 281.54 | 1655.10 | 12.55 |
| 8 | 32 | 414.32 | 2140.93 | 17.15 |
| 16 | 64 | 559.25 | 2949.53 | 25.61 |
| 32 | 128 | 706.52 | 4500.77 | 40.64 |

### Validation limitation: distributed autotune

The unmodified all-operator autotune configuration did **not** pass startup. Leader-only sparse warmup populated rank-local tuning entries; the later distributed pass showed asymmetric cache hits and follower Gloo all-reduce timeouts. Skipping only dense `fp4_gemm` exposed the same pattern in CUTLASS MoE GEMM1, whose cache keys include `tp_rank`.

Successful serving/evaluation/benchmark runs explicitly used:

```text
VLLM_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_SKIP_OPS=fp4_gemm,trtllm::fused_moe::gemm1,trtllm::fused_moe::gemm2
```

FlashInfer autotune otherwise remained enabled. This is a disclosed validation workaround, not an autotune fix or a claim that the original configuration passes. These performance numbers are specific to this configuration. No warmup workaround code is included in this PR. FP16 was not qualified; a separate scale-conversion issue also reproduces with the existing 64-dimensional RoPE writer.

Developed with AI assistance; the changes and validation evidence are available for human maintainer review. The human submitter remains responsible for review and the contribution.

title: [Perf] Use SDPA for BLIP-2 Q-Former attention
author: Levius-Fubuki
body:
## Purpose

BLIP-2 Q-Former attention currently materializes the attention scores, applies
scaling and softmax separately, and launches a second matrix multiplication:

```text
before: {matmul: 2, mul: 1, softmax: 1, dropout: 1}
after:  {scaled_dot_product_attention: 1}
```

This PR uses standard `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` for
both Q-Former self-attention and cross-attention. It preserves the existing
scale and training dropout behavior while allowing PyTorch to dispatch fused
attention kernels.

This removes the score-sized attention intermediate and the separate scale,
softmax, dropout, and value-matmul launches. It keeps one portable PyTorch path
with no custom kernel, architecture gate, device branch, or device-specific
tuning.

I searched the open PRs for BLIP-2, Q-Former, and SDPA changes and found no
active PR addressing this attention path.

## Test Plan

### Lint

```bash
ruff check vllm/model_executor/models/blip2.py
ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/models/blip2.py
git diff --check origin/main..HEAD
```

### RTX 4090 default eager encoder benchmark

The performance harness constructs the real
`Blip2ForConditionalGeneration` class with BLIP-2-compatible dimensions and
invokes its real `embed_multimodal` boundary. Both variants use identical,
finite, deterministic weights.

Hardware/software: NVIDIA RTX 4090, CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130.
Timing uses 25 warmups, 200 iterations, and five alternating repeats.

| Dtype | Batch | Scope | Old p50 (us) | New p50 (us) | Speedup |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| FP16 | 1 | Q-Former | 1519.28 | 1049.77 | 1.45x |
| FP16 | 4 | Q-Former | 1521.30 | 1006.97 | 1.51x |
| BF16 | 1 | Q-Former | 1504.88 | 1052.73 | 1.43x |
| BF16 | 4 | Q-Former | 1565.29 | 1088.26 | 1.44x |
| FP16 | 1 | `embed_multimodal` | 2797.99 | 2322.34 | 1.20x |
| FP16 | 4 | `embed_multimodal` | 2744.05 | 2196.03 | 1.25x |
| BF16 | 1 | `embed_multimodal` | 2691.73 | 2248.67 | 1.20x |
| BF16 | 4 | `embed_multimodal` | 2748.79 | 2177.32 | 1.26x |

The Q-Former geometric-mean speedup is 1.48x for FP16 and 1.43x for BF16.
All eight rows passed numerical, finite-value, repeatability, shape, and
input-mutation validation with no performance regression.

Q-Former peak extra allocation decreased from 1,579,008 to 1,237,504 bytes at
batch 1, and from approximately 7.3 MiB to 5.1 MiB at batch 4.

Profiler results replace 80 `aten::bmm` calls and 40 separate softmax calls per
ten Q-Former invocations with 40 `aten::scaled_dot_product_attention` calls.
All candidate calls dispatch to `aten::_flash_attention_forward`.

The harness, raw CSV, gate result, and profiler summary are available in the
[benchmark artifact Gist](https://gist.github.com/Levius-Fubuki/18c576619c30d983466d2f57cd6ee7e6).

## Test Result

`ruff-check`, `ruff-format`, and `git diff --check` passed.

## Limitations

These results come from one RTX 4090 run with deterministic weights, not a
full pretrained BLIP-2 checkpoint or end-to-end request throughput benchmark.

Current BLIP-2 does not implement `SupportsEncoderCudaGraph`, and runtime hooks
confirmed that Q-Former executes on the default eager multimodal encoder path.
No CUDA Graph performance claim is made. If BLIP-2 gains encoder CUDA Graph
support later, batch-1 short-key shapes should be benchmarked again before
enabling capture.

No performance claim is made for other architectures, devices, or PyTorch
versions. Full upstream cross-backend CI still requires a maintainer `ready`
or `verified` label.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used during implementation, testing, benchmarking, and PR
drafting. The human contributor reviewed and takes responsibility for the
change and evidence.

title: [Bugfix][EC Connector] Fail the request, not the engine, when a remote encoding cannot arrive
author: gty111
body:
## Summary

NIXL EC consumers can fall back to local encoding after a remote transfer fails, even when a rewritten request contains only metadata. This can trigger an assertion and terminate EngineCore instead of failing the affected request.

- Preserve local fallback when actual model input is available; otherwise report the unavailable request through `take_unavailable_requests()`.
- Retry and log ACK timeouts, with a 60-second per-request/per-embedding wait budget that survives retries and in-flight waits. Increase the default ACK timeout from 2 to 30 seconds.

title: [Transformers] Generalize merged-column linear fusion
author: BANANASJIM
body:
## Purpose

Adds a generic `MergedColumnParallelFuser` to the Transformers backend's fuser system, as a structural fallback for column-parallel sibling projections that don't fit `GLUFuser`/`QKVFuser`'s specific patterns.

- **New fuser**: matches any set of ≥2 sibling linears fed the same placeholder input, rewrites `l1(x), l2(x), ... -> merged(x).split(sizes, -1)`, and merges them into one `MergedColumnParallelLinear`. Handles any number of projections with independent output sizes.
- **Collision-safe naming**: `merged_name` is a computed property, length-prefixed over the source projection names (`f"{len(name)}_{name}"` joined), so two different projection-name tuples can never produce the same attribute/`packed_modules_mapping` key. GLU/QKV/MLA keep their fixed conventional names (`gate_up_proj`, `qkv_proj`, `fused_qkv_a_proj`) since those always represent the same split.
- **Multi-candidate fusion selection**: `get_fusers` now caches every structurally-matching redefining fuser for a class, not just the first. `Fusers.__getitem__` then validates them per real instance and picks the first that passes, so a heterogeneous model (same Python class, differently-shaped layers) can fall back to the generic fuser on layers the specific one rejects, instead of silently missing fusion.
- **Dedup**: shared the merged-call-splice AST rewrite (`StackedFuser._splice_merged_split`) across `MergedColumnParallelFuser`, `QKVFuser`, and `MLAFuser`, removing three near-identical implementations.
- **Correctness fixes surfaced in review**: `GLUFuser.validate` now rejects mismatched gate/up `out_features` (an AndMul kernel requires an even split) instead of assuming `_get_glu_nodes`'s shared-input check made it redundant — fx's leaf-module tracing never validates shapes, so nothing else caught it.
- **Tests**: added coverage for arbitrary-arity merging, input-mutation rejection, `BroadcastGLU`/unfusable cases, `merged_name` uniqueness across different linear-name tuples, and the heterogeneous same-class fallback (`QKVFuser` vs `MergedColumnParallelFuser` chosen per-instance).

AI assistance was used.

## Test Plan

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/models/transformers/fusers`
- `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/models/transformers/test_backend.py -k 'replace or vocab_tables or input_embeddings or tower_weights or marking'`
- `.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files tests/models/transformers/fusers/test_linear.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/__init__.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/base.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/glu.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/merged_column.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/mla.py vllm/model_executor/models/transformers/fusers/qkv.py`

## Test Results

- Fuser suite: 72 passed, 1 skipped.
- Related backend tests: 11 passed, 24 deselected.
- Pre-commit: all applicable hooks passed, including Ruff, formatting, mypy,
  SPDX, and forbidden-import checks.
- Model evaluation is not applicable because this refactors existing fusion
  behavior without adding or changing a model implementation. Numerical tests
  cover GLU parity and arbitrary-N merged weight loading.

title: [Test] Split test_sampling_mask_preserves_top_k_boundary_ties to remove Triton-kernel-specific assumption Description
author: mayuyuace
body:
## What
`test_sampling_mask_preserves_top_k_boundary_ties` (added in #54901) fails
on Triton-backed platforms (e.g. XPU) with `assert 3 > 3`.

## Why
The test builds its fixture by calling the real `apply_top_k_top_p` on
tied top-k boundary logits, and assumes ties are always preserved
(count > k). That's true for the PyTorch fallback, but the Triton kernel
intentionally trims boundary duplicates to always return exactly k
(same tradeoff already documented in `test_topp_tie_break_deterministic`).
So the test baked in one backend's behavior as a cross-backend contract.

## Fix
Split into two tests, matching what this case actually used to cover
before #54901:
- `test_sampling_mask_matches_processed_top_k_top_p_support`: end-to-end
  check that `SamplingMaskTensors` matches whatever `apply_top_k_top_p`
  produces, with a backend-agnostic assertion.
- `test_sampling_mask_preserves_top_k_boundary_ties`: hand-built logits
  (no `apply_top_k_top_p` call) to reliably test the `max_num_kept`
  overflow/bitmask-fallback path.

No production code changed (test-only).

## Test
`python -m pytest tests/v1/test_outputs.py -v` → 14 passed
(previously 1 failed on XPU).

title: [Kernel][Perf] Register-resident path for per-token-group 8-bit quant
author: chuan932
body:
## Summary

`per_token_group_quant_8bit` stages every group through shared memory because it
reads the group twice: once to reduce absmax, once to quantize. At `group_size`
128 a group of 16-bit input is 256 B, which fits in registers, so both the
staging and the `__syncthreads()` separating the two passes are avoidable.

This adds `per_token_group_quant_8bit_register_kernel` for the unpacked float32
scale layout. It is taken when `group_size == 128`, the input is 16-bit, both
buffers are 16 B aligned, and both are contiguous; everything else keeps the
existing shared-memory schedule.

vLLM already has `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel` with the
same register pipeline, but float32-scale callers cannot reach it: it is
hardwired to UE8M0 exponents packed 4-per-int32 with TMA-aligned strides. Rather
than reshaping those callers, this extends the same idea to the ordinary scale
layout, reusing that kernel's subgroup shuffle mask and UE8M0 exponent bit math
verbatim.

A second, smaller effect of the fixed 256-thread launch: `GetGroupsPerBlock`
falls back to 1 group per block when `num_groups` is odd, leaving 16 active
threads per block. The register path pads the grid and bounds-checks instead, so
it is unaffected — visible below as the `(1, 128)` and `(333, 128)` rows, where
the shared-memory schedule spends ~14 µs almost entirely on launch overhead.

## Not a duplicate

```bash
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "per_token_group_quant"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "per token group quant register"
```

No open PR touches this kernel's schedule. The nearest work is in different
directions:

- #53874, #54857, #43907 — ROCm/aiter **fusions** (folding the quant into GeGLU,
  RMSNorm, or RoPE), not a schedule change to the CUDA kernel.
- #53346, #51477 — UE8M0 correctness fixes in the Triton paths and in fusion
  eligibility.
- #45151, #36297, #46935 — folding per-group quant into another kernel's
  epilogue (attention, BMM, async-TP).
- #48653 — adds FP8 type dispatch for the transformers backend.

This PR changes only how the existing CUDA kernel is scheduled, and leaves the
kernel that other work fuses into intact.

## Performance

H20-3e (SM90), CUDA 13.0. Microbenchmark against the shipped shared-memory
kernel via `torch.ops._C.per_token_group_fp8_quant` /
`torch.ops._C.per_token_group_quant_int8`, µs per call, output buffers
preallocated so allocation is outside the timed region.

FP8 output, UE8M0 scales (the DeepGEMM default), row-major:

| input dtype | shape | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bf16 | (1, 128) | 14.0 | 5.5 | 2.54× |
| bf16 | (333, 128) | 13.8 | 5.3 | 2.62× |
| bf16 | (1024, 6144) | 24.2 | 9.1 | 2.66× |
| bf16 | (8192, 6144) | 183.9 | 59.9 | 3.07× |
| bf16 | (65536, 256) | 62.9 | 22.1 | 2.84× |
| fp16 | (8192, 6144) | 180.3 | 55.5 | 3.25× |
| fp16 | (65536, 256) | 61.8 | 20.7 | 2.99× |

FP8 output across the scale-layout matrix, bf16 input:

| shape | ue8m0 | column-major | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (8192, 6144) | yes | no | 184.1 | 60.1 | 3.06× |
| (8192, 6144) | yes | yes | 194.2 | 64.0 | 3.03× |
| (8192, 6144) | no | no | 175.0 | 76.7 | 2.28× |
| (8192, 6144) | no | yes | 184.8 | 83.2 | 2.22× |
| (65536, 256) | yes | yes | 66.5 | 23.8 | 2.80× |
| (65536, 256) | no | no | 60.1 | 28.2 | 2.13× |
| (65536, 256) | no | yes | 63.4 | 30.4 | 2.08× |

INT8 output (no UE8M0 scales), bf16 input:

| shape | smem | register | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1, 128) | 6.7 | 5.1 | 1.32× |
| (333, 128) | 6.6 | 4.9 | 1.36× |
| (1024, 6144) | 14.9 | 11.7 | 1.27× |
| (8192, 6144) | 118.4 | 76.1 | 1.56× |
| (65536, 256) | 40.8 | 27.9 | 1.46× |

The spread is worth explaining rather than quoting the best number. The register
side converges to ~60–77 µs at (8192, 6144) in all three tables — it is
bandwidth-bound. The differences come from the baseline:

- `c10::Float8_e4m3fn(float)` is a software conversion and costs materially more
  than int8's hardware `cvt`, so the FP8 baseline starts slower (175 vs 118 µs)
  and has more to give back.
- On the register side UE8M0 is ~22% faster than float32 scales because a
  power-of-two scale lets the inner loop multiply by the reciprocal instead of
  dividing per element.

So the ~3× on the UE8M0 FP8 path is three effects stacked (no smem round trip,
reciprocal instead of divide, an expensive baseline conversion), not register
residency alone. INT8 keeps a smaller but consistent 1.26–1.56×.

Reproducing:

```bash
python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_per_token_group_quant.py --dtype fp8
```

Run it on `main` and on this branch and compare the CUDA column (this PR adds
serving-sized shapes to that script's defaults, which previously topped out at
512 groups). The `gs=64` rows do not meet the dispatch condition and should be
unchanged across the two runs, which makes them a useful control.

### End-to-end serving

GLM-5.2-FP8, TP=8 on 8×H20-3e, 256k max model len, chunked prefill at 8192,
concurrency 1, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`. Same server config and same benchmark
script on both sides, run back to back in one window:

| prompt tokens | baseline | with register path | throughput | latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 3591.9 tok/s | 3622.5 tok/s | +0.85% | 2.279 → 2.264 s |
| 16384 | 3560.7 tok/s | 3620.9 tok/s | +1.69% | 4.596 → 4.519 s |
| 65536 | 3351.0 tok/s | 3404.3 tok/s | +1.59% | 19.529 → 19.213 s |
| 131072 | 3078.6 tok/s | 3123.9 tok/s | +1.47% | 42.471 → 41.872 s |

The 8k row gains least because at one chunk the fixed per-request costs (HTTP,
tokenization, scheduling, sampling) are the largest share of wall clock, while
the kernel saving scales with token count. From 16k up it settles at 1.5–1.7%.

That is consistent with the profile attribution: at an 8192-token chunk this
kernel accounts for 22.28 ms per step (15.60 ms over 411 calls with column-major
scales plus 6.68 ms over 150 row-major), and the measured 3.03×/3.07× puts it
near 7.3 ms — about 15 ms off a ~800 ms step, or 1.87% of GPU time. End-to-end
lands slightly under that because the denominator also carries non-GPU work.

Measurement caveat, and it biases against this PR: to avoid rebuilding the
prebuilt `_C_stable_libtorch.abi3.so` in that environment, the served run reached
the kernel through a Python-level redirect of the op call, so every call paid an
extra Python frame and predicate. Built normally the dispatch happens before the
launch, so treat 1.5% as a lower bound. Baseline reproducibility was checked
independently: the back-to-back baseline matched an earlier run from several
hours before to within 0.2% at every length.

## Bit-exactness, and why there are no eval numbers

Output is bit-exact with the shared-memory kernel in every configuration tested
below — quantized bytes and scales compare equal with `torch.equal`, not within
a tolerance. Two details carry that:

- The UE8M0 scale is derived with the same exponent bit math
  (`exp_bits + (mant_bits != 0)`) that `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel`
  already uses, which is equivalent to `exp2f(ceilf(log2f(...)))` on this input
  domain.
- The non-UE8M0 path divides by the scale instead of multiplying by its
  reciprocal. The reciprocal costs an ulp and moves the ~0.05% of values that
  land exactly on an 8-bit boundary. Only the UE8M0 path, where the scale is a
  power of two and the two are equivalent, multiplies.

Because the bytes are identical, an accuracy eval would reproduce `main`'s
numbers exactly and would not be evidence of anything. I have not run one, and
am offering the bit-exactness comparison in its place. Happy to run a specific
eval if a reviewer would rather see it.

## Testing

Extended the existing suite rather than adding a file. `test_per_token_group_quant_fp8`
gained `dtype` parametrization (bf16/fp16) and three shapes that exercise the new
schedule: a single group, an odd token count leaving a partial trailing block,
and a serving-sized shape.

Its assertions are `atol=0.15` against Triton, which cannot see a bit-level
difference, so two dedicated tests pin the path equivalence. Both build a
16 B-misaligned but contiguous input, which falls back to the shared-memory
schedule, and require the two paths to agree exactly:

- `test_per_token_group_quant_fp8_register_matches_smem` (24 cases)
- `test_per_token_group_quant_int8_register_matches_smem` (6 cases) — int8 shares
  the schedule via `per_token_group_quant_int8`, and differs from fp8 in how
  `DST_DTYPE(q)` rounds (truncation toward zero vs round-to-nearest-even), so it
  needs its own guard.

```bash
pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py \
    -k "register_matches_smem"
# 30 passed in 5.30s

pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_per_token_group_quant.py \
    -k "test_per_token_group_quant_fp8 and not packed and not register_matches"
# 256 passed in 8.20s
```

Kernel-level bit-exactness was measured separately, since the installed vLLM in
my test container does not carry this patch: the new kernel was compiled into a
standalone extension and compared byte-for-byte against
`torch.ops._C.per_token_group_fp8_quant`, with a profiler check confirming the
baseline really executes `per_token_group_quant_8bit_kernel<c10::BFloat16,
c10::Float8_e4m3fn, false, true, float>` rather than falling back to Triton.

- FP8: 72/72 configurations bit-exact across input dtype, UE8M0, column-major,
  and shape
- INT8: 10/10 bit-exact
- 48/48 bit-exact driven through the `per_token_group_quant_fp8` entry point
  itself, which adds `tma_aligned_scales=True` coverage (input dtype ×
  column-major × TMA alignment × UE8M0 × 4 shapes)
- Edge inputs (all-`+inf`, all-`-inf`, `NaN`, all-zero, 1e-30, 1e30): identical
  bytes on both paths

`nvcc -arch=sm_90a` compiles the modified translation unit clean, and
`pre-commit run --files <the three files>` passes.

## Validation gaps

Stating these rather than implying full coverage:

- **ROCm is untested by me.** The `USE_ROCM` shuffle branch is copied verbatim
  from `per_token_group_quant_8bit_packed_register_kernel` in the same file, so
  it is an already-shipped pattern rather than new code, but I have no AMD
  hardware to confirm it.
- **INT8 has no end-to-end number**, only the microbenchmark above. The serving
  measurement is FP8, which is what GLM-5.2 and the other block-quantized models
  use.
- The served run reached the kernel through a Python-level redirect rather than a
  full rebuild, as noted under performance. The 48-configuration check above was
  run with that redirect active, so the measured run was numerically identical to
  baseline.

## AI assistance

AI assistance (Kiro) was used for this change, recorded as an `Assisted-by:`
trailer on the commit. I have reviewed every changed line, and ran the compile,
tests, microbenchmarks, and profiling described above myself.

title: [Perf] Read VidCom2 frame budgets once
author: Levius-Fubuki
body:
## Purpose

VidCom2 currently reads each dynamic per-frame Top-K budget with
`ks[i].item()`, then reads the selected-token count with another scalar
reduction. For `T` frames this introduces `T + 1` host-visible scalar reads in
the token-selection path.

This PR copies the small budget vector to a Python list once, preserves the
original one-dimensional unsorted `torch.topk` operation for every frame, and
reuses the budget sum during count reconciliation:

```text
before: T per-frame item() reads + 1 mask.sum().item() read
after:  1 ks.tolist() transfer
```

The budgets are already clamped to at least one, so the previous non-positive
budget branch was unreachable. The change keeps one portable PyTorch path with
no custom kernel, architecture gate, device branch, or device-specific tuning.

This is not duplicating existing work. The following open-PR searches returned
no matching VidCom2 optimization: `VidCom2 topk`, `VidCom2 frame budget`, and
`video prune synchronization`.

## Test Plan

### Regression test

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/multimodal/test_vidcom2.py
```

The new test runs the complete mask function, rejects any per-element
`Tensor.item()` read, and verifies exactly one vector budget transfer. Existing
tests cover retained counts, dynamic frame budgets, empty input, and first-frame
behavior.

### Lint and pre-commit

```bash
pre-commit run --files \
  tests/multimodal/test_vidcom2.py \
  vllm/multimodal/video_prune/vidcom2.py
```

### RTX 4090 complete-function benchmark

```bash
python bench_vllm_vidcom2_single_sync.py \
  --baseline-module ../vllm-vidcom2-single-sync-baseline/vllm/multimodal/video_prune/vidcom2.py \
  --candidate-module vllm/multimodal/video_prune/vidcom2.py \
  --dtype float16 bfloat16 float32 \
  --frames 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 \
  --tokens-per-frame 48 196 576 \
  --q 0.25 0.5 0.75 0.9 \
  --warmups 25 --iterations 100 \
  --output full-matrix.csv
```

Hardware/software: NVIDIA RTX 4090, driver 580.76.05, CUDA 13.2,
PyTorch 2.13.0+cu132. Baseline commit: `c615b1fd`.

| dtype | T | Tokens/frame | q | Old p20/p50/p80 (us) | New p20/p50/p80 (us) | p50 speedup |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|:---|:---|---:|
| BF16 | 1 | 48 | 0.50 | 781.79 / 784.24 / 790.75 | 750.84 / 754.55 / 761.13 | 1.04x |
| BF16 | 2 | 48 | 0.50 | 821.88 / 824.39 / 831.62 | 775.74 / 777.62 / 784.39 | 1.06x |
| FP16 | 8 | 196 | 0.75 | 1134.89 / 1138.19 / 1146.59 | 1024.67 / 1027.04 / 1034.63 | 1.11x |
| BF16 | 32 | 196 | 0.50 | 1996.89 / 2005.31 / 2022.69 | 1589.97 / 1595.34 / 1604.75 | 1.26x |
| FP32 | 64 | 576 | 0.25 | 3228.88 / 3359.86 / 3497.51 | 2202.08 / 2216.91 / 2252.41 | 1.52x |
| BF16 | 128 | 576 | 0.75 | 5158.44 / 5176.38 / 5210.99 | 3582.24 / 3592.81 / 3604.61 | 1.44x |

Across all 288 configurations, the raw geometric-mean speedup was 1.181x and
the median was 1.142x. All masks matched bit-for-bit. One T=1 sample was a raw
timing outlier; five alternating-order trials with 500 iterations reproduced a
1.041x median speedup (1.037–1.041x), leaving no stable regression beyond 3%.

The profiler confirms that Top-K and scatter counts are unchanged while the
per-frame scalar reads disappear:

| T | `item` calls, old → new | CUDA memcpy events, old → new | Top-K calls, old/new | Scatter calls, old/new |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 60 → 0 | 60 → 20 | 60 / 60 | 40 / 40 |
| 8 | 180 → 0 | 220 → 60 | 200 / 200 | 160 / 160 |
| 32 | 660 → 0 | 700 → 60 | 680 / 680 | 640 / 640 |

Each profiler row contains 20 complete mask calls. Other reconciliation-path
copies remain; the removed difference is exactly `20 * T` per-frame budget
reads.

The standalone benchmark, raw CSV, profiler output, outlier recheck, and paired
model-evaluation output are available in the
[benchmark artifact Gist](https://gist.github.com/Levius-Fubuki/d9dc92209a34e02a53cf49f45ae9f5aa).

### Qwen3-VL paired evaluation

The offline evaluation used `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` revision
`89644892e4d85e24eaac8bacfd4f463576704203`. Baseline and candidate requests
were interleaved in one process, prefix caching was disabled, and both mask
functions were also run on the same visual embeddings.

| Source frames | Visual grid | Mask result | Operator old → new | E2E old → new |
|---:|:---|:---|---:|---:|
| 8 | `[4, 8, 8]` | exact, 0/64 differ | 1.061 → 0.836 ms (1.27x) | 647.60 → 645.29 ms (1.004x) |
| 32 | `[16, 4, 4]` | exact, 0/256 differ | 1.549 → 1.196 ms (1.29x) | 644.90 → 644.57 ms (1.001x) |

All ten timed baseline/candidate outputs had identical generated token IDs,
text, and cumulative log probability.

## Test Result

```text
33 passed
```

`ruff-format`, `ruff-check`, typo, SPDX-header, forbidden-import,
new-`torch.cuda` API, and `git diff --check` checks passed locally.

## Limitations

The broad performance matrix uses synthetic post-ViT embeddings on one RTX
4090. The two Qwen3-VL cases validate output stability but do not establish an
end-to-end throughput improvement; the optimized helper is a small fraction of
total inference latency. No performance claim is made for other architectures
or backends.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used during implementation, testing, benchmarking, model
evaluation, and PR drafting. The human contributor reviewed and takes
responsibility for the change and evidence.

title: [Bugfix][V2] Warm up kernels before capturing CUDA graphs
author: aoshen02
body:
## Purpose

Fixes #55336.

`warmup_kernels` runs a scheduler-realistic prefill plus a decode step at
`max_num_seqs`. On the V2 path it is called *after* `capture_model()`, so those
shapes reach the shared workspace arena only once CUDA graphs already hold
pointers into it. `WorkspaceManager._ensure_workspace_size` grows the arena by
replacing the tensor, which frees the buffer the captured graphs baked in, and
the next replay writes into freed memory.

This hoists the V2 warmup next to `kernel_warmup()`, which already runs before
capture for the same class of reason. The V1 sampler warmup is untouched — its
comment documents why it has to follow capture.

Warming up before capture is also what TensorRT-LLM and SGLang do:
`tensorrt_llm/_torch/pyexecutor/cuda_graph_runner.py` warms up ahead of each
capture with the comment *"This also lets us initialize states in the
attn_metadata and resize the shared attention workspace before any graph is
captured"*, and SGLang runs two warmup iterations per shape before capturing.

## Test Plan

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files   # ruff, ruff-format, mypy
```

Serving DeepSeek-V4-Flash on GB200, which aborts during startup on main with

```
RuntimeError: Triton Error [CUDA]: an illegal memory access was encountered
```

under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, `--max-num-seqs 256`, `cudagraph_mode=FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`.
Two setups: 8x GB200 (DP8/EP8/TP1, 43 layers) and a single GB200 with a 4-layer
proxy of the same model. Measured four things: whether this patch alone fixes
the crash, cold-start time, KV cache sizing, and throughput on a healthy
configuration that never hit the bug.

## Test Result

`pre-commit`: passed (ruff, ruff-format, mypy).

**Fix, isolated.** This patch is the only change in the third row; a separate
one-line model-side fix I am upstreaming as #55299 is not sufficient on its own,
which rules it out as the cause of the repair:

| patch applied | `max-num-seqs 256`, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE |
| --- | --- |
| none | illegal memory access during startup |
| #55299 only | illegal memory access during startup |
| **this PR only** | **starts, 14 FULL + 53 PIECEWISE graphs captured** |
| both | starts |

8x GB200, 43 layers: 37 FULL + 53 PIECEWISE graphs captured, zero illegal
memory accesses, batch-invariance probes intact, server serving.

**Cold start** (first log line to health, 8x GB200, 43 layers): 8m19s with this
patch vs 8m10s without, i.e. +1.8%, within run-to-run noise. The workload is
unchanged, only its position moves.

**Memory accounting is byte-identical.** The workspace this bug is about is
allocated either way — the patch only moves *when* — and the KV cache is sized
before `compile_or_warm_up_model` runs, so nothing shifts. Every startup figure
on the 8x GB200 run matches:

| | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| model loading | 41.61 GiB | 41.61 GiB |
| actual usage | 43.17 GiB | 43.17 GiB |
| non-torch | 6.57 GiB | 6.57 GiB |
| peak activation | 3.09 GiB | 3.09 GiB |
| graph capturing | 3.09 GiB | 3.09 GiB |
| available KV cache | 106.92 GiB | 106.92 GiB |
| GPU KV cache size | 279,010 tokens | 279,010 tokens |

**No throughput regression** on a configuration that was already healthy —
DeepSeek-V4-Flash, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=0`, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE,
`--max-num-batched-tokens 8192`, 256 concurrency, 150/3000 in/out:

| | output throughput | TPOT | TTFT |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| main | 16107 tok/s | 15.62 ms | 800 ms |
| this PR | 16109 tok/s | 15.67 ms | 616 ms |

## Notes

AI assistance was used for this change: the fault was located with
instrumentation written by Claude Code, and the patch was drafted with it. The
diff moves one call and I have reviewed it end to end.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Summary

  kernels to CPU (AVX512/AMX), under `csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels/` (`flash_mla.cpp`,

title: [Kimi Perf] Group fp8 mla cahche insertion, 4~6x kernel level performance improvement for small batch
author: yewentao256
body:
## Purpose

Group fp8 mla cahche insertion

Before:

```bash
CUDA launch 1：layer 0
CUDA launch 2：layer 1
CUDA launch 3：layer 2
CUDA launch 4：layer 3
CUDA launch 5：layer 4
```

Now
```bash
One grouped kernel launch
  ├─ token 0, layer 0
  ├─ token 0, layer 1
  ├─ ...
  └─ ...
```

So basically combining 5 layers together, saving a lot of launch time

## Test

Acc covered in current unit test

Perf can be seen in this AI generated script

```bash

import math
import os
import statistics
from collections.abc import Callable
from functools import partial

import torch

from vllm import _custom_ops as ops
from vllm.platforms import current_platform

NUM_LAYERS = 5
BLOCK_SIZE = 16
KV_LORA_RANK = 512
ROPE_DIM = 64
TOKEN_COUNTS = [
    1,
    2,
    4,
    8,
    16,
    32,
    64,
    128,
    256,
    512,
    1024,
    2048,
    4096,
    8192,
    16384,
]


def insert_single(
    kv_c: torch.Tensor,
    k_pe: torch.Tensor,
    caches: torch.Tensor,
    slots: torch.Tensor,
    scales: torch.Tensor,
) -> None:
    for layer in range(NUM_LAYERS):
        ops.concat_and_cache_mla(
            kv_c[layer],
            k_pe[layer],
            caches[layer],
            slots[layer],
            "fp8",
            scales[layer],
        )


def insert_grouped(
    kv_c: torch.Tensor,
    k_pe: torch.Tensor,
    caches: torch.Tensor,
    cache_ptrs: torch.Tensor,
    slots: torch.Tensor,
    scales: torch.Tensor,
) -> None:
    ops.concat_and_cache_mla_grouped(
        kv_c,
        k_pe,
        cache_ptrs,
        slots,
        BLOCK_SIZE,
        caches[0].stride(0),
        caches[0].stride(1),
        scales,
        "fp8",
    )


def measure_us(function: Callable[[], None], repeats: int) -> float:
    start = torch.Event(enable_timing=True)
    end = torch.Event(enable_timing=True)
    start.record()
    for _ in range(repeats):
        function()
    end.record()
    end.synchronize()
    return start.elapsed_time(end) * 1000 / repeats


@torch.inference_mode()
def main() -> None:
    torch.set_default_device("cuda")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    entry_size = KV_LORA_RANK + ROPE_DIM

    print(
        f"device: {current_platform.get_device_name()} "
        f"(CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES={os.getenv('CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES')})"
    )
    print(f"{'tokens':>7} {'5 x single (us)':>17} {'grouped (us)':>14} {'speedup':>9}")
    for num_tokens in TOKEN_COUNTS:
        num_blocks = math.ceil(num_tokens / BLOCK_SIZE)
        repeats = max(20, min(1000, 65536 // num_tokens))
        kv_c = torch.randn(NUM_LAYERS, num_tokens, KV_LORA_RANK, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        k_pe = torch.randn(NUM_LAYERS, num_tokens, ROPE_DIM, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        caches = torch.empty(
            NUM_LAYERS, num_blocks, BLOCK_SIZE, entry_size, dtype=torch.uint8
        )
        slots = torch.arange(num_tokens).unsqueeze(0).expand(NUM_LAYERS, -1)
        scales = torch.linspace(0.05, 0.25, NUM_LAYERS, dtype=torch.float32)
        cache_ptrs = torch.tensor(
            [cache.data_ptr() for cache in caches], dtype=torch.int64
        )
        single = partial(insert_single, kv_c, k_pe, caches, slots, scales)
        grouped = partial(insert_grouped, kv_c, k_pe, caches, cache_ptrs, slots, scales)

        for _ in range(20):
            single()
            grouped()
        torch.accelerator.synchronize()

        single_samples = []
        grouped_samples = []
        for sample in range(7):
            if sample % 2:
                grouped_samples.append(measure_us(grouped, repeats))
                single_samples.append(measure_us(single, repeats))
            else:
                single_samples.append(measure_us(single, repeats))
                grouped_samples.append(measure_us(grouped, repeats))
        single_us = statistics.median(single_samples)
        grouped_us = statistics.median(grouped_samples)
        print(
            f"{num_tokens:7d} {single_us:17.2f} {grouped_us:14.2f} "
            f"{single_us / grouped_us:8.2f}x"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

And we get


title: [ROCm][MoE] Pad the AITER MoE intermediate size at allocation time, and round the expert-group count to a kernel that exists
author: sshlyapn
body:
## Purpose

Two independent startup failures on the ROCm AITER MoE path, both caused by shapes AITER has no compiled kernel for, both focusing on IFM/K2-Horizon-375B-A23B model support. 

### 1. Unaligned per-partition intermediate size - unquantized path only, fp8 AITER alignment is unchanged

AITER's CK 2stages MoE kernel dispatches on `inter_dim <= 192`: below it both stages use 64-wide tiles, above it at least one stage uses a 128-wide tile. CK's `IsSupportedArgument` rejects an intermediate not divisible by that width, so `moe_intermediate_size = 1792` at TP=8 gives `224` and fails with `device_gemm ... does not support this GEMM problem`.

**Fix:** round the intermediate up in `maybe_roundup_sizes`, the existing hook for this (already overridden by five other quant methods). It runs before `create_weights`, so the padded size reaches allocation and the loader — which derives shard offsets from the checkpoint, not the parameter shape — fills only the real rows.

**Alignment rule: `64 if inter_dim <= 192 else 128`, mirroring AITER's own threshold rather than always using 128.** A flat 128 mispredicts 2 of the 19 sizes measured against the real kernel (64 and 192 both pass despite not being 128-aligned) — it is a wrong model that happens to be safe. It also costs: `inter_dim` is a tuned-config lookup key, and across the 148 shipped AITER config files (11279 rows) the threshold rule pads **0** tuned rows while a flat 128 would move **207** off theirs onto the heuristic fallback. Rounding up never crosses the boundary (`96->128`, `160->192`, `192->192` all stay `<= 192`), so the alignment picked is always the one the dispatcher then applies. Dtype-independent: CK derives both tile widths from `sizeof(A0DataType)`, identical for fp16 and bf16.

**Zero-init.** The loader narrows to the checkpoint extent and never writes the tail, so `w13`/`w2` are allocated with `torch.zeros` **when either dim is padded** — unpadded layers keep `torch.empty` and pay nothing. Pad lanes are then bit-exactly inert: `silu(0) * 0 = 0`, and the zero columns in `w2` contribute exactly zero to stage 2. With `torch.empty` the tail holds recycled device memory, which is live weight to the kernel; whether that hurts depends on load-time allocation order, so it presents as sporadic implausible tokens with no error. mxfp4 and quark nvfp4 already allocate zeroed; #55251 is doing the same for fp8.

**Scope.** Gated on `UnquantizedMoeBackend.AITER`, only selected on ROCm with AITER MoE enabled; every other unquantized backend falls through the base hook untouched. The quantized AITER paths have their own overrides with different constants and are not touched — fp8 needs 256.

**Known interaction.** Since `intermediate_size_per_partition` now differs from `..._unpadded`, `experts/rocm_aiter_moe.py` computes a non-zero `intermediate_pad` where it previously got 0. Traced: with `QuantType.No` + bf16 the dispatch falls past every cktile/flydsl branch (all require `q_type == per_1x32`) to the plain `ck_moe_stage1`/`ck_moe_stage2_fwd` partials, which take no pad argument, and `intermediate_pad` only enters the tuned-config key when `config_file is not None`, which vLLM never sets. So it is computed and discarded, and the kernel runs the full padded GEMM including the zero rows — **up to ~14% extra compute on the MoE GEMMs** (448->512 at TP=4, 224->256 at TP=8).


### 2. AITER `biased_grouped_topk` expert-group count

`_aiter_get_num_expert_group` ceil-divides `num_experts` by the 32-per-group limit then walks to the next divisor, which can produce a count with no compiled kernel: AITER instantiates `biased_grouped_topk` only for `NUM_GRP` in `{1,2,4,8}`, so 96 experts gives 3 and fails to launch.

Grouping is a no-op here (`topk_group == num_expert_group`), so any divisor within the limit routes identically — the constraint is purely which kernel exists. Round to the largest supported count that divides `num_experts` and respects the limit. When none fits (320 -> 10, 33 -> 3) the naive value is kept deliberately: it is large enough that the `topk >= num_expert_group` guard at the call site fails and routing falls back to the generic path rather than reaching AITER.


## Test Plan

Both files are CPU-only and gated on `current_platform.is_rocm()`, so they run in any ROCm CI job without a working AITER runtime.

**`tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_moe.py`** — new "Weight alignment" section appended to the existing file rather than a standalone module, following that file's conventions (function-local imports, `default_vllm_config`, `rocm_` naming):

- `test_aiter_moe_alignment_follows_threshold` — the rule, as a table across the boundary.
- `test_aiter_moe_padded_size_stays_in_its_dispatch_branch` — self-consistency: `(intermediate <= 192) == (padded <= 192)` and `alignment(padded) == alignment(intermediate)`.
- `test_aiter_moe_roundup_pads_intermediate` — the hook end-to-end: 96->128, 192->192, 224->256, 448->512, 512->512.
- `test_aiter_moe_roundup_is_not_applied_to_other_backends` — TRITON and FLASHINFER_CUTLASS keep 224.
- `test_aiter_moe_padded_weights_are_zero_initialized` — pad lanes are zero, not allocator garbage.
- `test_aiter_moe_aligned_weights_are_zero_initialized` — zero-init is unconditional, so it holds for an aligned size too.
- `test_aiter_moe_bias_matches_padded_weight` — `w13_bias.shape[1] == w13_weight.shape[1]` with `has_bias=True`; the defect the post-load approach had.
- `test_aiter_moe_padding_is_numerically_inert` — reproduces the loader's gate/up placement into a zeroed padded parameter, asserts the MoE output is bit-identical to the unpadded reference.

**`tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_num_expert_group.py`** (new) — five tests over `_aiter_get_num_expert_group`: the two invariants the router asserts unconditionally, that a supported count is chosen whenever one fits, a table of known expert counts, and that the fallback is taken deliberately when none fits.

## Test Result

`gfx950` (MI355X), torch `2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f`, on `29af8bd672`.

```
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_num_expert_group.py -q   49 passed, 2 skipped
pytest tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_moe.py -q                 1 failed, 63 passed
both files                                                         1 failed, 112 passed, 2 skipped  (72s)
```

**The one failure, `test_aiter_fused_moe_mi3xx_fp8_accuracy`, is pre-existing and unrelated** — verified by running it alone against an unmodified checkout of the parent commit in a separate worktree, same box and image, where it fails identically.

title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Resolve n_predict from text_config for Qwen3.5 multimodal MTP

### Purpose
In Qwen3.5/3.6 multimodal wrapper checkpoints (such as `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` and `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B`), `mtp_num_hidden_layers` is located in `text_config` rather than directly on the outer wrapper config. `SpeculativeConfig.hf_config_override` previously inspected only the top-level `hf_config`, leaving `n_predict` as `None` and causing downstream divisibility checks to be bypassed.

title: [Bugfix][Qwen4Exp] fix state index strides in fused PLE conv
author: peakcrosser7
body:
## Purpose

Fix corrupted and repetitive output from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next when multiple prefill requests are processed together by the fused PLE short-convolution kernels.

The failure typically appears as repeated tokens such as `Theductductduct...`. It reproduces on the device-resident PLE path and does not depend on PLE CPU offload.

This change keeps the fused kernels enabled. It does not add a PyTorch fallback, disable CUDA graphs, or revert the PLE fusion.

## Root Cause

In Mamba align-cache mode, pure-prefill state indices are obtained from column zero of the Mamba block table:

```python
state_indices_tensor_p = state_indices_tensor_p[:, 0]
```

The result is a **one-dimensional, non-contiguous tensor**. With MTP=3 its logical elements have a stride of four because each block-table row contains the base state plus three speculative states.

The fused PLE convolution and writeback kernels loaded request `r` with `state_idx_ptr + r`, implicitly assuming a contiguous tensor. Request zero was read correctly, while later requests read adjacent columns from the wrong block-table row and wrote convolution state to the wrong cache slot. The corrupted state then caused repetitive output during decode.

## Design
Passing the stride avoids materializing a contiguous index tensor and adds no allocation or device copy.
- Pass `state_indices.stride(0)` to both fused PLE convolution kernels.
- Load each state slot from `state_idx_ptr + r * state_idx_stride`.
- Cover the production-shaped two-prefill case in both supported convolution state layouts, using query lengths `(16, 676)`, 10,240 channels, and a block-table-like state-index stride of four.

## Not a duplicate

Searched the open PRs for [Qwen4Exp PLE state indices](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+Qwen4Exp+PLE+state+indices), [Qwen4 PLE short conv](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+Qwen4+PLE+short+conv), and [PLE stride](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Aopen+PLE+stride).

The related PRs do not fix this state-index addressing bug:

- [#54517](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54517) introduced the fused PLE kernels whose state-index loads are fixed here.
- [#55272](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55272) removes `torch.compile` from the NVIDIA implementation but retains the same fused kernel pointer arithmetic.
- [#55309](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55309) fuses the PLE residual and QSA output gate but does not change state-index addressing.
- [#54371](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54371) implements UVA PLE offload and n-gram parallelism. This bug also reproduces with offload disabled and is in the common fused short-convolution path.

## End-to-end Reproduction

Start a TP4 server with MTP3. PLE CPU offload should remain disabled:

```bash
vllm serve \
  Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 \
  --served-model-name qwen3.8-flash-next \
  --port 8237 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
```

Save and run the following client. It submits a long and a short prompt together so that the scheduler forms a multi-request pure-prefill batch:

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import requests

URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8237/v1/chat/completions"
FILLER = (
    "The grass is yellow. The sky is blue. The sun is red. "
    "Here we go. There and back again. "
)


def chat(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = requests.post(
        URL,
        json={
            "model": "qwen3.8-flash-next",
            "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            "max_tokens": 128,
            "temperature": 0.7,
            "top_p": 0.8,
            "top_k": 20,
            "seed": 1234,
            "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False},
        },
        timeout=300,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]


for attempt in range(5):
    long_prompt = (
        f"Attempt {attempt}. The pass key is 11111. Remember it. "
        "11111 is the pass key. " + FILLER * 25 + "What is the pass key?"
    )
    short_prompt = f"Attempt {attempt}. 明天中午吃什么?"
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        long_future = pool.submit(chat, long_prompt)
        short_future = pool.submit(chat, short_prompt)
        long_output = long_future.result()
        short_output = short_future.result()

    print(f"attempt={attempt} long={long_output!r} short={short_output!r}")
    assert "11111" in long_output
    assert "ductduct" not in long_output + short_output
```

Before this fix, the script failed on the second pair in the reproduced run:

```text
attempt=1 long='Theductductductductduct...'
AssertionError
```

With this fix, all five pairs return the expected pass key and no repeated `duct` sequence.

## Test Plan

```bash
python -m pytest -q tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py
```

End-to-end validation uses TP4/DP1, MTP3, BF16 activations, chunked prefill, prefix caching, torch compilation, and full/piecewise CUDA graphs.

## Test Result

- Full Qwen4Exp PLE test file: 35 passed.
- New strided-index regression: both SD and DS state layouts passed.
- A/B validation with the old unit-stride addressing: both new regression cases failed, with 90.3% of output elements mismatched.
- Minimal end-to-end reproducer before the fix: failed in attempt 1 with `Theductductduct...` and an `AssertionError`.
- The same minimal reproducer after the fix: 5/5 request pairs passed.
- Extended eager bad-case validation after the fix: 20/20 request pairs passed.
- Extended compiled/CUDA-graph bad-case validation after the fix: 20/20 request pairs passed.

> AI assistance was used for root-cause analysis, implementation, test drafting, and PR-description drafting. I reviewed the resulting changes and test results.

title: [Bugfix] Autotune FlashInfer deferred MoE decode kernels before CUDA graph capture
author: mingg26
body:
## Purpose

Split out the MoE half of #54507 into a standalone fix. This is not duplicate work: #54507 covers both the MLA and MoE decode-autotune cache-miss bugs, while this PR isolates only the MoE part so it can be reviewed and merged independently.

Kimi-K3 decode defers MoE finalization so the consumer can fuse the final top-k reduction. That changes the monolithic FlashInfer MoE output signature from `(tokens, hidden)` to `(tokens, 0)`. The existing generic full-model autotune dummy does not exercise this deferred-finalize path, so FULL decode graph capture misses the `(B, 0)` cache entries, falls back to `MoERunner tactic=-1`, and captures that default tactic into the serving graph.

This change collects `defer_moe_finalize_max_num_tokens` from live deferred-finalize MoE layers and appends the bounded values to the existing FlashInfer autotune token counts. Each token count runs through the normal full-model dummy path with `get_hybrid_num_tokens_buckets(num_tokens)`, so the deferred path is exercised without any MoE-specific dispatcher calls.

The maximum-token pass runs first and tunes the widest bucket set. The later bounded passes reuse those cache entries for unchanged FlashInfer operations because the cache key contains the mapped profile, not the complete bucket list. Only signatures reached through the small-token control flow, including the deferred MoE `(B, 0)` signature, require additional tuning. The remaining overhead is the ordinary smaller full-model forward and cache lookup.

In the K3 B12 validation in #54507, the tuned path and the `tactic=-1` fallback launch exactly the same two MoE BMM kernels under Nsight Systems. This fix therefore changes the autotune result from a miss to a hit without changing the selected MoE kernels in that workload; it is performance-neutral there while removing a real cache-miss/default-tactic bug.

## Test Plan

1. Unit: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/test_flashinfer_autotune_warmup.py -q`
2. Static checks: `pre-commit run --files vllm/model_executor/warmup/kernel_warmup.py vllm/utils/flashinfer.py tests/model_executor/test_flashinfer_autotune_warmup.py`
3. Hardware cache-hit check: serve a truncated Kimi-K3 (4 layers, full 896 experts, dummy weights) on 2x4 GB300, TP8, `cudagraph_mode=FULL`, `--enable-flashinfer-autotune`, and `FLASHINFER_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG`; count `[AutoTuner]: Using fallback tactic` lines for `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` during final graph capture before and after this fix.

## Test Result

Unit:

```text
test_flashinfer_autotune_token_counts_include_deferred_moe_limits PASSED
test_flashinfer_autotune_token_counts_are_bounded_and_deduplicated PASSED
test_flashinfer_autotune_uses_token_buckets_for_each_dummy_run PASSED
3 passed
```

Hardware cache-hit validation from the initial implementation (fallback-tactic lines during final FULL graph capture, rank 0):

| op | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `trtllm_fp4_block_scale_moe` (deferred MoE, shapes `(B, 0)`, B in 1..32) | 128 | 0 |
| `trtllm_batch_decode_mla` (MLA, out of scope here) | 38 | 38 |

The refactor changes how warmup reaches the deferred path, from a direct MoE dispatcher call to the normal full-model dummy pass. The target `(B, 0)` profiles and expected capture-time cache hits are unchanged.

All pre-commit hooks pass on the changed files.

---

AI assistance disclosure: this change was split out of #54507 and adapted to current main with AI assistance from Kimi Code and OpenAI Codex. The human submitter remains responsible for reviewing the final diff and validating the reported results.

title: [perf] wire FA and FlashMLA for sm90 GLM5Next NoPE SparseMLA
author: JaredforReal
body:
Wire up two additional sparse-MLA attention backends for GLM5Next NoPE (head_size=512, e.g. GLM-5.3-Flash) on SM90: `FLASHMLA_SPARSE` and `FLASH_ATTN_MLA_SPARSE`. FlashInfer SM90 remains the default; the new backends are opt-in via `--attention-backend`.

## Changes

- `cmake/external_projects/vllm_flash_attn.cmake`: pin vllm-flash-attn to `9cd61de` (vllm-project/flash-attention#172, merged: FA3 OnlyQv forward for head_size==0). The FlashMLA pin is unchanged: the existing pin already supports d_qk=512 sparse prefill/decode (vllm-project/FlashMLA#17, dense 512 decode, landed independently).
- `flashmla_sparse.py`: admit head_size 512 for SM90 rope-free (NoPE) models with a bf16 KV cache, and skip `concat_mla_q` when the rope part is empty. The SM100 bf16 priority order is unchanged; quantized DS-MLA cache formats and rope-carrying 512 models fall through to FlashInfer/TRITON.
- `flashattn_mla_sparse.py`: for `qk_rope_head_dim == 0`, pass a zero-filled 64-wide q and the latent prefix as k so FA3 computes QV-only scores — works on stock FA3 builds, no only_qv kernel required (credits to @Leoyzen's #56665 approach).
- `tests/v1/attention/test_flashmla_nope_sm90_backend_selection.py`: CPU-only selection-matrix tests for the above gates.

No duplication of existing PRs: the backend wiring is new; the FA3 kernel support landed in vllm-project/flash-attention#172 and FlashMLA dense-512 in vllm-project/FlashMLA#17.

## Benchmarks

Setup: `zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash` (bf16, ~306 GB), 4× H200 (SM90), TP=4, FlashInfer 0.6.18. `vllm bench serve`, random dataset, `--ignore-eos`, `--max-model-len 36000`, warmup with a different seed, two fresh-server runs per backend (cross-rep variance ±0.1%). Both workloads exceed `index_topk` (2048), so prefill and decode both exercise each backend's sparse-MQA kernel.

| Backend | out tok/s (run1/run2) | Δ vs FI | TTFT mean (ms) | TPOT mean / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Not related to the attention kernels; tracked as a separate core-infra issue.

title: [Bugfix] Annotate MTP draft KV cache groups positionally on the hybrid grouping path
author: Navjot10
body:
## Purpose

Hybrid attention + Mamba models using MTP, such as Qwen3.5 and Qwen3-Next, can reach the general KV-cache grouping path without identifying the drafter's group. Since #52771, `OffloadingConnector` deliberately treats unannotated groups as non-draft. The missing annotation therefore leaves the actual drafter-containing group without volatile trailing-chunk handling and produces a warning at startup.

Enable the existing trailing-layer annotation rule for `method="mtp"` on both the packed and general grouping paths, guarded by an exact partition of registered layers. For these hybrid layouts, identify the drafter-containing attention group, including when it also contains target layers, so the offloader excludes its volatile trailing chunk while Mamba groups remain unannotated. Preserve the existing `deepseek_v4` and `deepseek_v41` model checks so their `method="dspark"` path continues to identify the draft group. Other EAGLE/DSpark models retain their existing annotation behavior.

This extends the positional rule from #52047 and complements #52771 by supplying the missing group annotation. The separate #56026 proposes identifying all groups under a distinct drafter prefix. This PR retains the positional rule's limitation: when trailing drafter caches span several groups, it identifies only the group containing the last registered layer.

## Validation

- Rebased onto `49e0427ca5183a56ccb112e5be1300feb2873ca9`.
- `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py -q`: **125 passed**.
- Regression coverage includes DeepSeek V4 MTP, DeepSeek V4 DSpark, DeepSeek V4.1 DSpark, the Qwen hybrid path, unrelated EAGLE/DSpark configurations, and the exact-partition guard.
- [GitHub pre-commit](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/actions/runs/35396934298) passed on `bcd8d7384103691eb00bc4f542de50fb69fc37c3`, including typos and mypy for Python 3.10–3.13.
- **4×NVIDIA B300 CUDA validation:** **125 unit tests passed** and **1 end-to-end test passed**, with no failures, errors, or skips. Full five-shot GSM8K: **95.07% accuracy** over **1,319 questions**, **3.980 mean acceptance length**, and **0.000 invalid-answer rate**. This passes upstream's effective accuracy minimum of 84% (`0.92 - 0.08` tolerance) and acceptance-length minimum of 1.2. [Detailed results](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55390#discussion_r4051206336).

<details>
<summary>GPU runtime and commands</summary>

Used the exact vLLM wheel for base `49e0427ca5183a56ccb112e5be1300feb2873ca9`, with this PR's Python change overlaid and the patched tests run outside the source checkout. The patch and loaded-module hashes match `bcd8d7384103691eb00bc4f542de50fb69fc37c3`. Runtime: Torch 2.13.0, CUDA 13.0, four B300 GPUs.

The upstream `tests/evals/gsm8k/configs/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark-confidence-TEP4.yaml` retains TP4 + expert parallelism and all evaluation settings. The only configuration additions pin the model/tokenizer/code/draft revision to `62af8fffb2f7030cac4de2f0169f5b8d1101b646`. The config-list file contains that pinned YAML.

title: [Perf][GDN] Build cudagraph-capture metadata without a device sync
author: njhill
body:
`build_for_cudagraph_capture` derived the host-side draft counts with `(num_accepted_tokens - 1).cpu()`, a device-to-host copy that drains the whole stream before the metadata can be built. The method is not capture-only: a DP rank with nothing scheduled runs it on every dummy step, because `_dummy_run` re-stages FULL-graph metadata with `for_capture=True`.

Derive `num_decode_draft_tokens_cpu` from `query_start_loc_cpu` instead in the GDN and short-conv builders; the device tensor is still built for the kernels. Add a test asserting no `.cpu()` copy happens in the capture path and that the metadata matches the device-derived reference.

This was found by @ywang96

title: [Bugfix] Fix Kimi K3 NVFP4 MoE weight conversion OOM
author: wzhao18
body:
## Purpose
Currently when running Kimi k3 nvfp4, it throws ~15000 lines of warning like the following due to fragmented memory during quantization post processing. In some cases, it also fatally fails with OOM.
```
[rank6]:[W904 12:06:06.083917542 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:3933] memory allocation failed with OOM on device 6 while trying to allocate 20971520 bytes (free: 16252928, total: 287428640768).

```

This PR fixes it by optimizing nvfp4 MoE weight post processing memory usage. It preallocate the final FlashInfer TRT-LLM shuffled tensors and populate them one expert at a time. This avoids allocating tensors for per-expert result, which fails under `_scoped_allocator_max_split(max_split_size_mb=20)` as large blocks cannot be split up.

title: [Perf][Multimodal] Avoid duplicate text embedding in Qwen2.5-Omni
author: waizuichougou
body:
## Purpose

`Qwen2_5OmniThinkerForConditionalGeneration.embed_input_ids` embeds the text
input before it knows which multimodal merge path is required. For a regular
multimodal request, the method then calls the parent implementation, which
embeds the same text input again. For an audio-in-video request, the custom
interleaved path also embeds the text input again. The first embedding result
is discarded in both cases. This is a performance-only change and does not
alter multimodal embedding placement behavior.

This change determines whether interleaved audio/video merging is required
before embedding text. The regular path delegates directly to the parent
implementation, while the interleaved path performs its custom merge with
one text embedding. The empty-multimodal path also delegates to the parent
implementation without changing the resulting tensor.

### Duplicate-work check

The open pull-request list and recent multimodal performance changes were
checked for work covering duplicate text embedding in
`Qwen2_5OmniThinkerForConditionalGeneration.embed_input_ids`. The nearby
logits-state caching optimization addresses a different sampling-stage
hotspot, so this change does not duplicate it.

## Test Plan

### Validation

```bash
python -m pytest -q tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_qwen2_5_omni_embed.py
ruff check vllm/model_executor/models/qwen2_5_omni_thinker.py \
    tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_qwen2_5_omni_embed.py
ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/models/qwen2_5_omni_thinker.py \
    tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_qwen2_5_omni_embed.py
git diff --check
```

The existing multimodal regression test is extended with call-count assertions
for the standard and audio-in-video paths. No new test file is added.

### Qwen2.5-Omni embedding-stage benchmark

The actual vLLM Qwen2.5-Omni model class was benchmarked on an NVIDIA A100.
The language embedding used the Qwen2.5-Omni-3B vocabulary size (151,936),
hidden size (2,048), and `bfloat16` dtype. This isolates the changed
`embed_input_ids` stage while keeping the model's real token dimensions and
multimodal merge logic. The benchmark does not include the vision/audio
encoders or language-model layers, which are unchanged by this PR.

For each input shape, 30 warm-up calls were discarded. Nine timed samples were
collected, each averaging 30 calls, and the table reports the median time per
call. The unmodified and patched versions used the same inputs and settings.

## Validation Result

### Existing tests and checks

- `tests/models/multimodal/processing/test_qwen2_5_omni_embed.py`: **15 passed**
- `ruff check`: passed
- `ruff format --check`: passed
- `git diff --check`: passed

### Qwen2.5-Omni embedding-stage benchmark

`Change` is `(patched / unmodified - 1)`; negative values are improvements.
The embedding-call column is measured per `embed_input_ids` invocation.

| Input tokens | Multimodal tokens | Unmodified (µs) | Patched (µs) | Change | Text embedding calls |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128 | 32 | 189.542 | 153.088 | **-19.2%** | 2 → 1 |
| 512 | 64 | 190.635 | 155.307 | **-18.5%** | 2 → 1 |
| 1,024 | 256 | 199.612 | 161.519 | **-19.1%** | 2 → 1 |

| 4,096 | 1,024 | 238.967 | 198.417 | **-17.0%** | 2 → 1 |
| 8,192 | 2,048 | 315.972 | 254.839 | **-19.3%** | 2 → 1 |

The result is consistent across short and long multimodal sequences. The
existing output-placement assertions remain unchanged, while the discarded
duplicate embedding is removed from every non-interleaved and interleaved
multimodal call.
