title: [Bugfix][Kimi-K3] Keep transient checkpoints out of prefix-cache eviction
author: Sy0307
body:
## Summary

Keep transient KDA/Mamba prefill checkpoints out of the ordinary prefix-cache eviction set when sparse retention is explicitly active.

This change targets Kimi-K3's hybrid attention path.

## Problem

FlashKDA creates internal checkpoints so the current prefill can continue from a recurrent-state boundary without an additional scheduling step. A checkpoint in the middle of a prompt is useful to the current request, but it is not necessarily a reusable shared-prefix boundary.

Before this change, such a checkpoint could be re-keyed and registered as a normal prefix-cache block. It then participated in the same GPU LRU eviction pool as reusable hot prefixes:

```text
middle checkpoint -> hash -> prefix-cache LRU -> evicts hot prefix
                                             -> later local hit becomes a miss
                                             -> extra load or prefill work
```

Before/after cache lifecycle:

```text
Before:

  KDA prefill
      |
      +--> temporary checkpoint
      |        |
      |        +--> hash + ordinary LRU
      |                     |
      |                     +--> competes with hot prefix
      |                                  |
      |                                  +--> local prefix miss

After:

  KDA prefill
      |
      +--> temporary checkpoint ------------------> current request can use it
      |                                              |
      |                                              +--> no ordinary LRU entry
      |
      +--> shared-prefix-boundary checkpoint ------> reusable prefix cache
                                                     |
                                                     +--> may be retained/shared
```

This is particularly problematic when `prefix_cache_retention_interval == 0`: intermediate checkpoints are not intended to be retained as dense semantic checkpoints, but their temporary hash could still make them eviction candidates.

## Fix

Pass the active retention interval into checkpoint publication. When sparse retention is active and the checkpoint is neither at the end of the prompt nor at the shared-prefix boundary, treat it as request-local state:

```text
middle checkpoint -> current request may use it
                  -> temporary hash is removed
                  -> no ordinary prefix-cache LRU entry
                  -> reusable hot prefixes remain protected
```

Prompt-end and shared-prefix-boundary checkpoints retain the existing publication behavior. This change does not disable KDA checkpoint computation or change the state written by FlashKDA.

## Performance

On a representative B200 Kimi-K3 hybrid workload using TP8/PP2/direct DCP8, the isolated production-style comparison was:

| Configuration | Output throughput |
| --- | ---: |
| Checkpoint disabled (diagnostic baseline) | 1013.00 tokens/s |
| Checkpoint enabled with transient-checkpoint retention fix | 1091.80 tokens/s |

The fixed configuration improved throughput by 7.78% over the checkpoint-disabled diagnostic baseline while retaining the internal checkpoint feature. A separate run with the GEMM-AR option disabled measured 1108.89 tokens/s; that result is included only as context and is not an isolated measurement of this patch.

These measurements are workload-specific and are not used as a claim that this small cache-lifecycle change explains every difference between software stacks. The primary regression signal is the cache-manager reproduction: temporary checkpoint publication changes which blocks compete in the local prefix-cache eviction pool.

## Why this is not a duplicate

- PR #55760 changes the default sparse/dense retention policy for Mamba + EAGLE; this change keeps the explicit sparse-retention behavior but fixes transient checkpoint publication.
- PR #56615 fixes MooncakeStore boundary pairing between Mamba/KDA and attention KV; this change is limited to local prefix-cache block retention.
- PR #56525 guards cache hits until the writing scheduler step is committed; this change addresses eviction eligibility, not write visibility.
- PR #52527 adds observability for sparse-retention misses; this change modifies the cache lifecycle.

## Validation

Focused prefix-cache tests should be run with:

```bash
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py -q
```

The change is intentionally small and preserves the current-request checkpoint path. Model-scale performance validation is still required on a representative hybrid KDA workload.

This change was prepared with AI assistance; the author should review the complete diff and test results before merging.

title: [MM] Add Triton kernel for mm_input_normal.
author: noooop
body:
## Purpose `mm_input_norm` is a memory-bandwidth-bound operator: one multiply-add per element, so runtime is dominated by DRAM traffic. This PR adds a Triton fusion kernel that performs the whole per-channel affine transform in a single pass, replacing the eager path that materialized an fp32 intermediate. The Triton fused kernel is **significantly faster** than the eager, `BatchNorm1d`, and `torch.compile` baselines on the same workload, because it reads the input once and writes the output once — no intermediate DRAM round-trip. https://github.com/noooop/snippet/tree/main/kernel_bench/mm_input_normal This basically saturates my local 4090's VRAM bandwidth ～850GB/s. ``` ./nvbandwidth -t device_local_copy_sm -b 1024 Running device_local_copy_sm. memcpy SM local GPU(column) bandwidth (GB/s) 0 0 1695.46 SUM device_local_copy_sm 1695.46 ``` 1. **Single-pass fusion** — `y = x * weight[c] + bias[c]` computed in one kernel launch, at the input's native dtype (`uint8`/`fp16`/`bf16`/`fp32`). 2. **Preallocated output** — the caller can pass a larger buffer; only the `[:N]` region is written, so buffers can be reused across calls without a per-call allocation. 3. **`float32` compute for free** — arithmetic is done in fp32 inside the kernel regardless of I/O dtypes. This matches the eager path numerically but costs no bandwidth, since the intermediate never leaves registers. ## Test Plan pytest tests/models/multimodal/generation_ppl_test/test_qwen.py pytest tests/model_executor/layers/test_mm_input_norm.py ## Test Result pass ---

title: [watermark] compatibility validation
author: TQCB
body:
## Summary

- centralize engine and request compatibility policy in `VllmConfig._check_supports_watermarking(config) -> bool`
- treat omitted or `true` request watermarking as enabled by default, with `false` as the sole explicit opt-out
- warn once and fall back to unwatermarked generation when the engine or request mode cannot apply watermarking
- cover missing engine configuration, greedy decoding, trace replay, and beam search with the same warning-and-fallback policy
- centralize request-time resolution in engine admission, applying the result only to the request-local copy so reused caller parameters cannot carry a decision across requests or engines
- validate supported speculative-decoding methods and reject incompatible draft, rejection, parallel-drafting, and custom-sampler configurations
- keep explicit seeds and parallel sampling (`n > 1`) supported, with documented caveats for plain Gumbel diversity and seeded fallback sampling
- preserve the optional request value across OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, speech, realtime, batch, beam-search, and direct engine paths until centralized admission resolves it
- explicitly opt internal bookkeeping requests out: language detection, generative scoring, KV-transfer cleanup, and mixed prefill/decode warmup
- add CPU contract tests plus accelerator smoke tests for seeded parallel sampling, prefix caching, grammars, tool calling, TP/PP/DP, mixed batches, API propagation, and internal request paths

## Request behavior

- `watermarking=None`: request watermarking by default
- `watermarking=True`: request watermarking explicitly
- `watermarking=False`: opt out

If watermarking cannot be applied, vLLM warns once for that incompatibility and continues with the request unwatermarked. Transcription, translation, and realtime requests therefore warn once and continue unwatermarked with their default greedy decoding.

title: [Bugfix][KVConnector] Make ExampleHiddenStatesConnector abort-safe
author: ys2025-AI
body:
Fixes `ExampleHiddenStatesConnector` abort-path crash.

## Purpose

`ExampleHiddenStatesConnector.request_finished()` crashes `EngineCore` when a
request is aborted while still **waiting** (i.e. before it was ever scheduled) —
the common case when an API client times out and cancels queued requests.

`_request_filenames` is only populated in `build_connector_meta()` for
`SchedulerOutput.scheduled_new_reqs`. A request aborted before its first
schedule never reaches that code, but `Scheduler.finish_requests()` still calls
`request_finished()` for waiting requests, where the unconditional
`self._request_filenames.pop(req_id)` raises:

```
example_hidden_states_connector.py request_finished
    filename = self._request_filenames.pop(req_id)
KeyError: 'cmpl-b98ee80d8ff99a38-0-8e7006c7'
```

The `KeyError` becomes `EngineCore encountered a fatal error`; every API server
process then dies and clients see a storm of `APIConnectionError`.

This is the connector-side counterpart of the scheduler-side stale-completion
crash tracked upstream:
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/46240
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/46304
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53079

### Changes

1. `request_finished` uses `pop(req_id, None)`; when no filename was recorded
   (aborted before scheduling) it drops residual `_pending_saves`/`_lock_fds`
   state and returns `(False, None)` — no hidden states to save, no blocks to
   delay.
2. `request_finished_all_groups` no-ops when the per-group block table is
   missing instead of indexing out of bounds.
3. `get_finished` only reports `finished_sending` for requests it actually
   tracked (a submitted DtoH copy); abort/never-scheduled requests no longer
   trip `assert req_id in self.requests` in `_update_from_kv_xfer_finished()`.
4. `get_finished_count()` returns `1`: only TP rank 0 writes hidden states, so
   exactly one completion notification is expected per request; without this,
   `KVOutputAggregator` waits for `world_size` notifications.

(3) and (4) are coupled: (3) alone would never complete a request; (4) alone
would let non-writer ranks report before rank 0's copy finishes, freeing KV
blocks too early.

## Test Plan

New CPU-only unit test
`tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hidden_states_connector_abort.py`:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hidden_states_connector_abort.py -q --noconftest
```

Covers:

- `request_finished` on a never-scheduled request returns `(False, None)` (no `KeyError`)
- `request_finished_all_groups` handles a missing group table
- `get_finished` does not report an untracked/aborted request
- `get_finished` reports a tracked request once its copy completes
- `get_finished_count() == 1`

## Test Result

```
$ python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hidden_states_connector_abort.py -q --noconftest
5 passed, 15 warnings in 18.92s
```

End-to-end: on vLLM 0.26.0 + vllm-ascend (Ascend NPU) during online DSpark
hidden-state training, aborting queued requests (client timeouts) previously
fataled `EngineCore` with the `KeyError` above; with this change the engine
survives abort storms and training runs to completion. Reproducer: send a batch
of long-prompt requests, let some time out and get aborted while queued.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Insert MiniMax-M3 sparse-PA K/V without a contiguous copy
author: akii96
body:
## Summary

- Pass the strided K/V slices straight to AITER `reshape_and_cache` on the MiniMax-M3 sparse-PA path instead of calling `.contiguous()` on them first.
- Add `_kv_insert_operand`, which returns the tensor as-is when the kernel's layout requirements are met and copies otherwise.
- No kernel change, no AITER dependency, no new env var, no change to the NVIDIA path.

## Motivation

`MiniMaxM3SparseAttention._insert_aiter_sparse_pa_kv` gets K and V as column slices of the fused `[q | k | v | index_q | index_k]` projection. Column slices are strided, so they are never contiguous, and the two `.contiguous()` calls copy both tensors on every sparse layer of every forward pass.

Those copies are not needed. `reshape_and_cache` already takes the row pitch as a kernel argument and indexes with it (AITER `csrc/kernels/cache_kernels.cu`):

```cpp
int key_stride = key.stride(0);
...
const int64_t src_key_idx = token_idx * key_stride + i;   // i over num_heads*head_size
```

In other words the kernel does not care how far apart two tokens are, only that each token's heads sit next to each other in memory. A `qkv[:, a:b].view(n, H, D)` slice is always laid out that way, whatever `H` is, which is why the copy buys nothing.

`_kv_insert_operand` skips the copy only when it can confirm that layout, and copies in every other case: a tensor of a different rank, one whose heads are not back to back, or one where tokens are so far apart that the gap would not fit in the kernel's `int` stride argument. So the worst case is the behaviour we have today.

## Existing work and non-duplication

- #53833 (with ROCm/AITER#4813) routes to a new fused AITER op and says it will "retain the existing vLLM preprocessing plus `reshape_and_cache` / index-scatter path when an older AITER build does not provide the operation". This PR fixes that retained fallback, so the two do not overlap and can land in any order.
- #54535 (with ROCm/AITER#5143 and #52664) integrates the consolidated AITER QK-norm op and falls back the same way.
- #55007 was the closest in spirit, a small vLLM-only change in this same function, and it states that "the main K/V cache writer remains AITER `reshape_and_cache`; this PR changes only the BF16 index-cache insertion boundary". It left the K/V boundary alone, which is what this PR covers.
- #54682 and #54681 are about the decode indexer and top-k, not cache insertion.

title: [ROCm][Perf] Enable HCA dual-stream overlap for DeepSeek-V4
author: shen-shanshan

## Purpose #51794 enabled multi-stream overlap for CSA layers on ROCm but left HCA layers (main compressor present, no indexer) single-stream, because the ROCm attention subclass dropped its aux streams whenever no indexer exists. On `gfx950` the HCA main compressor is a large fraction of the attention-layer decode time and is fully independent of the query/KV chain: both branches only read the layer input (`hidden_states`) plus their own weights and state, and nothing on the default-stream chain consumes the compressor's outputs until the sparse attention. For HCA layers the attention forward now forks inside the gated region: - **Default stream:** fused wqa/wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert. - **Aux stream 0:** HCA main compressor (fused wkv/wgate score GEMM + DeepseekCompressor). The streams join before the sparse MLA attention, which reads the compressed KV cache and the SWA window. The serial MHC fused post+pre prelude keeps running on the default stream ahead of the fork; the fork's start event orders the aux chain after it. ## Trace Comparison (take `conc=4` as an example) Before: After (**7.47%** faster for HCA layer): ## title: [Bugfix][Mooncake] Report request-level KV load failures under HMA
author: NickLucche
body:
Implements my suggestion back in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50388#pullrequestreview-4827494872, reverting PR https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50388 in doing so.

## Background

#50388 fixed a hard crash (`ValueError: too many values to unpack`) that hit the scheduler whenever a KV load failure was reported on a hybrid (HMA) KV cache layout. The crash happened in `_report_failed_recv` when unpacking multi-group block ID tuples, and the fix taught the scheduler how to unpack them.

The unpacking was never really the problem, though. Under HMA the scheduler tracks a single merged KV cache group while block IDs are only unique *within* a group, so a block-level failure report is ambiguous by construction — there is no correct way for the scheduler to interpret "block N failed" when the same block ID exists in multiple groups. Patching the unpack just moved the ambiguity around.

Nixl ran into the same situation earlier and solved the simple way in #35264: when HMA is required, `_report_failed_recv` skips block-level reporting entirely and the request is reported as a whole via `KVConnectorTransferResults.failed_recving`. The scheduler already handles `failed_recving` for `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` requests under both the recompute and fail policies, so no scheduler-side changes are needed.

## What this PR does

Reverts #50388 and mirrors the Nixl approach in the two connectors that could still hit the crash:

- **MooncakeConnector (P2P)**: the worker determines `_is_hma_required` the same way its scheduler does, and under HMA routes failed receives to a request-level queue surfaced through a new `get_transfer_results()` on the worker, which the connector delegates to. Requests that failed before any blocks were assigned locally are still aborted as before.
- **MooncakeStoreConnector**: all mooncake store loads are asynchronous, so load failures land on requests in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS`. The worker passes the HMA flag into `KVCacheStoreRecvingThread`, and the three failure sites (oversized key, partial batch, exception) report the request via `failed_recving` instead of invalid block IDs. The worker aggregates these across receive threads.

Non-HMA layouts keep the existing block-level failure reporting unchanged.

## Testing

Added unit tests for both connectors covering the HMA case (failure reported as `failed_recving`, no invalid blocks touched) and the non-HMA case (block-level behavior preserved), alongside the existing mooncake and load-failure-recovery suites.

To be explicit: this reverts #50388 on purpose rather than building on it, because the block-level reporting path it fixes cannot be made correct under HMA — the group information is simply not there at the point of failure. If reviewers feel strongly about keeping the scheduler-side unpack robustness anyway, that could be reintroduced separately, but I'd rather not keep dead ambiguity-handling code around.

This PR was prepared with AI assistance; I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above.

title: [Metrics][KV Offload] Add vllm:kv_offload_config_info - generic info metrics for offloading the offloading connector
author: amirfr3
body:
## Purpose

An offloading spec holds static configuration that no metric reports. The CPU cache
exports usage only (`vllm:kv_offload_cpu_cache_usage_perc` and the read/write
variants). A secondary tier exports nothing. So an operator cannot read the capacity,
the mount path, or the eviction policy of a tier from `/metrics`. Every spec that
adds such a fact today must also add its own metric, its own label list, and its own
emission call.

This adds `vllm:kv_offload_config_info`, a gauge with the constant value `1`, and two
hooks. The spec declares the label names. The manager fills the values.

```python
class OffloadingSpec(ABC):
    @classmethod
    def config_info_keys(cls, extra_config: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return ()


class OffloadingManager(ABC):
    def config_info(self) -> Sequence[Mapping[str, str | int | float | bool]]:
        return [{}]
```

`SecondaryTierManager` carries both methods, with the same defaults. Its
`config_info()` returns one mapping, because one tier gives one series.

### One series for each tier

The metric name carries no tier identity. One `tier` label tells the series apart. The
label value comes from `TieringMetricsTracker.tier_label()`, so it equals the `tier`
label that the tiering counters and histograms already carry. An operator joins the
two metrics on that label.

| Source | Name the tier declares and fills | Series in `/metrics` |
|---|---|---|
| a standalone CPU manager | `cpu_num_chunks` | one series, no `tier` label |
| the primary tier of a tiering manager | `cpu_num_chunks` | `tier="0:primary"` |
| secondary tier 0, tier type `example` | `example_info` | `tier="1:example"` |
| secondary tier 1, tier type `example` | `example_info` | `tier="2:example"` |

Two tiers of one type add a series. They add no label name. A new tier keeps the label
set of the other tiers, so an existing query survives.

A tier cannot know its own index, so a tier declares and fills its own names only.
`TieringOffloadingSpec.config_info_keys()` declares the union of the names of every
configured tier, plus `tier`. `TieringOffloadingManager.config_info()` adds the `tier`
label to each mapping. The label name is the constant `TIER_LABEL` in
`vllm/v1/kv_offload/tiering/base.py`, and the tiering metrics use the same
constant. The manager also writes an empty value for each name that another tier
owns, because every series of one metric carries every label.

This shape replaces the earlier revision of this pull request, which put the tier
index in the label name, as `tier1_fs_path`. The helper `config_info_prefix()` that
built such a name is gone.

The gauge is per-engine, like the other offloading gauges. Each engine reports its own
managers, not the instance total.

**This pull request publishes two facts, as a start.** `CPUOffloadingManager`
publishes `cpu_num_chunks`, the number of chunk slots in the CPU tier. The in-tree
`example` secondary tier publishes `example_info`, the value of its `custom_param`, as
a worked example for a tier author. #53902 adds the other CPU facts. The tiering
compose is here, so an out-of-tree secondary tier gets its series today.

A `ConfigInfo` dataclass in `vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py` holds the facts of one
manager. Each field name is a label name, so one class gives both the declared names
and the filled values. `CPUOffloadingInfo` and `ExampleTierInfo` use it.

### Why the spec declares and the manager fills

`OffloadPromMetrics` runs in the API-server process. That process holds the spec
class and the `kv_connector_extra_config` dict. It never builds a spec, and it never
holds a manager. So `config_info_keys()` is a classmethod, and it takes the same dict
that the spec itself receives. The manager holds the built configuration, so it owns
every value. A new fact costs one dict entry there.

Notes:

1. The gauge exists from `__init__`, next to every other offloading metric, so the
   metric never appears late. A labelled gauge makes no child until `.labels()` runs,
   so an engine that never reports exposes no series.
2. `_observe_info()` cannot raise on a disagreement. It builds the value tuple from
   the declared names alone, so the arity always matches. An exception in
   `_get_prometheus_metric()` ends the output handler. Every in-flight request then
   waits forever while the process stays up.
3. `_observe_info()` renders each value with `str()`, so a `bool` reads `True`. That
   matches `CacheConfig.metrics_info()` in `vllm/config/cache.py`.

### The spec is the authority

The two sides need not agree on the order, because the frontend reads each declared
name out of the payload. On a name disagreement:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| the spec declares a name, and no tier fills it | the label value is `""` |
| a tier fills a name that the spec never declared | the frontend drops it |
| either case | one `warning_once` line for each engine |

The check runs once for each payload, and not once for each tier, because the
declaration holds the names of every tier. A name that one tier owns reads empty on
the other tiers by design. So the check cannot see a name that one tier declares and
then leaves unfilled. The docstrings of `OffloadingManager.config_info()` and
`SecondaryTierManager.config_info()` tell an implementer to assert the agreement in a
test, which catches that case in CI.

### How the info reaches the API-server process

1. `OffloadingConnectorScheduler.get_stats()` calls `manager.config_info()` one time.
   It writes the result to the stats payload under `_StatsKey.INFO`. A `_info_sent`
   flag stops a repeat. A Prometheus child keeps the values it received, so one send
   is enough.
2. `is_empty()` counts `INFO`. `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` drops an empty
   scheduler payload, and the first payload usually carries no observation.
3. `aggregate()` copies `INFO` from `other`. The scheduler payload is the `other` in
   `kv_connector_stats.aggregate(scheduler_kv_connector_stats)`. Without this copy
   the info dies on every step that also transfers, and `_info_sent` blocks a second
   try.
4. `reduce()` ignores `INFO`, because the info belongs to Prometheus alone.
   `KVConnectorLogging.log()` now skips an empty summary, so an info-only payload
   adds no bare `KV Transfer metrics: ` line to the interval log.
5. `_observe_info()` aligns each tier mapping with the declared names, under the rules
   in **The spec is the authority**. It reports one series for each mapping.

`INFO` holds label names, not metric names, so it is no metric section. A tier that
rewrites its own metric names now walks the new `OffloadingConnectorStats.metric_sections()`,
and not `stats.data.values()`. `KVCRSecondaryTierManager` is the one such tier in tree.

### `multiprocess_mode="mostrecent"`

`_create_metric` never passed `multiprocess_mode`, so every offloading gauge took
`Gauge`'s default `sum`. Stats attach to one client's outputs per step, so `sum`
multiplies a per-engine constant by the number of frontends under
`--api-server-count > 1`. The default now lives on `OffloadingGaugeMetadata`, which is
`Gauge`-only, so a counter or a histogram cannot set it. Counters and histograms stay
as they are, because their deltas reach exactly one frontend per step. This also
corrects the seven offloading gauges that exist today, all of them per-engine
snapshots.

### Relation to #53902

#53902 adds three fields to `CPUOffloadingInfo`: `cpu_blocks_per_chunk`,
`cpu_kv_bytes_per_chunk`, and `cpu_capacity_tokens_at_max_len`.

## Test Plan

- **Unit tests** - 26 new tests, over five sections of the change.

  - **The declaration in `OffloadPromMetrics.__init__`** - the spec keys become the
    gauge label names, and only a gauge takes `multiprocess_mode`.
  - **`_observe_info()`** - the frontend reads the payload by name, reports one series
    for each mapping and each engine, blanks a declared name that no tier fills, and
    drops a name that the spec never declared.
  - **The transport to the frontend** - `is_empty()` passes an info-only payload,
    `aggregate()` keeps the info, `metric_sections()` leaves the info out, an
    info-only payload writes no log line, and the real scheduler sends the info once.
  - **The CPU manager** - `CPUOffloadingManager` fills the names that
    `CPUOffloadingSpec` declares.
  - **The tiering compose** - the spec declares the union of the tier names, the
    manager fills one mapping for each tier under the `tier` label, each tier reads
    its own config dict, and a tier cannot declare the reserved `tier` label.

  Files: `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_metrics.py` holds 17,
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/test_tiering_offloading.py` holds 8, and
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_manager.py` holds 1.

- **Full offloading suites** - every test under `tests/v1/kv_offload` and
  `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector`, on macOS and on Linux. Each
  failure also occurs on `main`, or needs a GPU.

- **Real server** - one NVIDIA H100 80GB, `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`, and
  `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a CPU primary tier plus one `example` secondary tier.
  The run scrapes `/metrics` after three completion requests.

- **Data-parallel run** - two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, which also starts
  two API server processes. The scrape returns one series for each engine. This run
  covers an earlier revision of the branch.

- **Model evaluations: not applicable.** Metrics only. `get_stats()` writes one
  constant mapping to a payload that the scheduler already emits on every step. No
  scheduling decision, no KV-cache placement, no transfer path, and no model output
  changes. Nobody ran an evaluation, because no output can differ.

- **Not verified.** No run of the unit tests used a GPU. The 32 tests in
  `tests/v1/kv_offload/cpu/test_gpu_worker.py` need CUDA or XPU, so they fail on both
  CPU-only hosts. This pull request does not change the GPU worker.

## Test Result

Full offloading suites:

```
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_offload \
    tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector \
    --ignore-glob='*test_swa_eviction*' -q -rs
```

| Host | Revision | Result |
|---|---|---|
| macOS, no GPU | `e358020cd5`, on `main` `8cc9aa5ad3` | `1056 passed, 74 failed, 15 skipped` |
| macOS, no GPU | `main` `ccfd1cea75` | the same 74 test ids fail |
| Linux pod, no GPU, `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu` | `ae199eedc2`, an earlier revision | `1088 passed, 32 failed, 25 skipped` |

- **macOS, 74 failures.** 32 are in `cpu/test_gpu_worker.py`, and 42 are in
  `cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py`. The same 74 test ids fail on `main`, so the
  platform causes them, and this pull request does not.
- **Linux, 32 failures.** All 32 are in `cpu/test_gpu_worker.py`, and each one stops
  at `assert gpu_tensor.is_cuda or gpu_tensor.is_xpu`. On Linux,
  `cpu/test_shared_offload_region.py` passes 51 of 51.
- **Linux, 25 skips.** The host has no CUDA, ROCm, or Triton (11), no `fs_io_C` (11),
  and no `kvcr` backend (1). Two more skips come from an empty backend parameter.
- **Revisions.** After `ae199eedc2`, the branch changed only docstrings and added
  the `TIER_LABEL` constant.

**Real server.** One NVIDIA H100 80GB, an earlier revision without `TIER_LABEL`:

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --gpu-memory-utilization 0.2 --max-model-len 2048 \
    --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
    "kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use":2147483648,"block_size":16,"eviction_policy":"lru",
    "secondary_tiers":[{"type":"example","custom_param":67}]}}'
```

The scrape after three completion requests:

```

vllm:kv_offload_config_info{cpu_num_chunks="",engine="0",example_info="67",model_name="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B",tier="1:example"} 1.0
```

- The two tiers give two series, and the `tier` label tells them apart.
- `cpu_num_chunks="1170"` is on the primary tier, and `example_info="67"` is the
  `custom_param` of the `example` tier.
- A name that the other tier owns reads `""`, because every series of one metric

- No series appears before the first request, because the info travels with the
  first scheduler payload.

**Two engines**, two H100 80GB, `--data-parallel-size 2`, which also starts two API
server processes. This scrape covers an earlier revision of the branch:


The `engine` label makes the two label sets different, so the `mostrecent` multiprocess

title: [Kimi-K3] Use the fused K/V pack kernel on the decode-context-parallel prefill path
author: brandonfzhang
body:
## Purpose

Kimi-K3 prefill with a long context runs in chunks. For every chunk of every MLA layer, the model projects the gathered latent cache into per-head keys and values, casts them to FP8, and lays them out as the contiguous key and value tensors the attention kernel expects.

#51772 fused that cast-and-layout step into one kernel (`fused_kimi_k3_mla_kv_concat_quant_fp8`, or `fused_kimi_k3_mla_kv_concat` for a bf16 query) for the normal prefill path, but left decode context parallelism (DCP) out of scope. With `decode_context_parallel_size > 1` the Kimi-K3 layer delegates chunked-context prefill to the shared MLA implementation, whose per-chunk tail still does the work as four separate PyTorch operations: two FP8 casts and two strided slice copies.

This PR routes the DCP path through the same fused kernels the non-DCP path already uses.

## What changes

- `MLACommonImpl._context_parallel_compute_prefill_context` takes an optional `fused_mla_kv_concat_fn(kv_nope, k_pe, use_fp8_prefill) -> (k, v)`. When it is given it replaces the cast + split + concat tail; when it is not, the method runs exactly the statements it runs today. No other model passes it.
- `MultiHeadLatentAttention` (Kimi-K3) passes `self._fused_mla_kv_concat`, which makes the same two kernel calls its non-DCP loop already makes.

No new environment variables, no runtime signature probing, no logging: the fused kernels are what every Kimi-K3 deployment already runs on the non-DCP path, so the DCP path simply follows it.

## Microbenchmark: fused kernel vs. the stock tail, across shapes

Per reviewer request, the fused kernel was timed against the stock four-operation tail over every local head count Kimi-K3 can have (96 heads / TP) and chunk sizes from 1 to 131072 tokens, on three GPUs. Cold L2 (a 256 MB buffer is cleared before every call), median of 100 CUDA-event timings, outputs checked byte-exact against the stock path on every row before timing (all exact, no mismatches). Numbers are `stock_us / fused_us`; vLLM 0.31.0 release wheel, torch 2.13 + CUDA 13.0.

**H100 NVL (SM90), FP8 KV cache + FP8 prefill query (the production Kimi-K3 configuration):**

| heads \ tokens | 1 | 16 | 128 | 512 | 1536 | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 | 32768 | 65536 | 131072 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96 (TP1) | 2.33 | 2.22 | 2.27 | 2.14 | 2.40 | 2.35 | 2.37 | 2.35 | 2.17 | 2.09 | – |
| 48 (TP2) | 2.41 | 2.33 | 2.17 | 2.13 | 2.14 | 2.46 | 2.35 | 2.37 | 2.21 | 2.17 | 2.11 |
| 24 (TP4) | 2.54 | 2.32 | 2.22 | 2.24 | 2.11 | 2.26 | 2.45 | 2.35 | 2.37 | 2.23 | 2.16 |
| 12 (TP8) | 2.39 | 2.33 | 2.32 | 2.22 | 2.09 | 2.15 | 2.26 | 2.45 | 2.36 | 2.37 | 2.30 |
| 6 (TP16) | 2.49 | 2.36 | 2.36 | 2.25 | 2.28 | 2.18 | 2.17 | 2.28 | 2.46 | 2.36 | 2.37 |

Geomean 2.29x, min 2.09x, no row below 1.0x. With the rope key already in FP8 (plain FP8 cache gathered without dequantizing): geomean 2.35x, min 1.98x. bf16 query (bf16 cache): geomean 2.11x, min 1.76x.

Absolute times at TP8 (12 heads), FP8 path, H100 NVL: 1536 tokens 24.5 us -> 11.7 us; 16384 tokens 145 us -> 59 us; 65536 tokens 525 us -> 222 us.

**RTX 5080 (SM120, Blackwell), FP8 path:** geomean 1.32x, min 1.11x (at 1536 tokens / 48 heads), no row below 1.0x; FP8 rope key: geomean 1.30x, min 1.06x.

**L40S (SM89, below the kernel's SM90 target, included for completeness):** FP8 path geomean 1.42x, min 1.02x, no row below 1.0x; FP8 rope key: geomean 1.44x, min 1.05x. Only the bf16-query path on this card has rows below 1.0x (worst 0.91x, at 512 to 16384 tokens with 48 to 96 heads); that path is bf16 cache + bf16 query, which no Kimi-K3 deployment on Ada would run, and the non-DCP path already takes it unconditionally.

**GB300 (SM103), the production deployment container (vLLM nightly, torch 2.13 + CUDA 13.0), FP8 path**, same head-by-token grid, cold L2, median of 100, byte-exact on every row:

| heads \ tokens | 1 | 16 | 128 | 512 | 1536 | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 | 32768 | 65536 | 131072 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96 (TP1) | 9.85 | 10.69 | 9.67 | 5.84 | 3.92 | 4.67 | 4.95 | 5.06 | 5.04 | 4.83 | 4.76 |
| 48 (TP2) | 12.04 | 11.48 | 9.52 | 7.91 | 4.71 | 4.13 | 4.76 | 4.92 | 5.07 | 5.09 | 5.09 |
| 24 (TP4) | 12.03 | 11.42 | 9.44 | 10.38 | 6.81 | 3.70 | 4.13 | 4.68 | 4.98 | 5.03 | 5.06 |
| 12 (TP8) | 12.51 | 10.24 | 10.15 | 9.75 | 8.45 | 5.89 | 3.80 | 4.25 | 4.78 | 4.85 | 4.97 |
| 6 (TP16) | 12.74 | 10.57 | 9.52 | 10.81 | 9.66 | 7.55 | 5.95 | 4.00 | 4.21 | 4.63 | 4.79 |

Geomean 6.48x, min 3.70x, no row below 1.0x. Absolute times at TP8 (12 heads): 1536 tokens 96 us -> 11 us; 16384 tokens 157 us -> 37 us; 65536 tokens 582 us -> 120 us. The small-chunk ratios are large because the stock tail is four eager launches (about 85 to 90 us of fixed cost on this host) while the fused kernel is one.

Conclusion: the fused kernel is faster than the stock tail on every Kimi-K3 shape on every GPU on which the FP8 path is deployed (3.7x or more on GB300, 2x or more on H100), so no shape heuristic is added. The gain is bandwidth: the stock tail writes and re-reads an FP8 copy of the whole projection output; the fused kernel reads it once and writes the two outputs directly.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark script (stand-alone; run inside a vLLM install)</summary>

```python
import statistics, torch
from vllm.models.kimi_k3.nvidia.ops.fused_mla_key_concat_kv_cache import (
    fused_mla_kv_concat, fused_mla_kv_concat_quant_fp8)

FP8, NOPE, ROPE, V = torch.float8_e4m3fn, 128, 64, 128

def stock_fp8(kv_nope, k_pe):           # the generic impl's DCP tail
    kv8, pe8 = kv_nope.to(FP8), k_pe.to(FP8)
    k_nope, v = kv8.split([NOPE, V], dim=-1)
    k = torch.empty((*k_nope.shape[:-1], NOPE + ROPE), dtype=FP8, device=kv8.device)
    k[..., :NOPE] = k_nope
    k[..., NOPE:] = pe8
    return k, v

def fused_fp8(kv_nope, k_pe):
    k_nope, v = kv_nope.split([NOPE, V], dim=-1)
    return fused_mla_kv_concat_quant_fp8(k_nope, k_pe, v)

def time_cold(fn, l2, iters=100):
    s, e = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    for _ in range(10): fn()
    t = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        l2.zero_(); s.record(); fn(); e.record(); torch.cuda.synchronize()
        t.append(s.elapsed_time(e) * 1e3)
    return statistics.median(t)

l2 = torch.empty(256 << 20, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
for H in (96, 48, 24, 12, 6):
    for T in (1, 16, 128, 512, 1536, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131072):
        kv = torch.randn(T, H, 256, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
        pe = torch.randn(T, 1, ROPE, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda")
        (k0, v0), (k1, v1) = stock_fp8(kv, pe), fused_fp8(kv, pe)
        assert torch.equal(k0.view(torch.uint8), k1.view(torch.uint8))
        assert torch.equal(v0.view(torch.uint8), v1.view(torch.uint8))
        a, b = time_cold(lambda: stock_fp8(kv, pe), l2), time_cold(lambda: fused_fp8(kv, pe), l2)
        print(f"H={H:3d} T={T:6d} stock={a:8.1f}us fused={b:8.1f}us {a/b:.2f}x")
```

</details>

## End-to-end

Kimi-K3 FP4 on two GB300 nodes (TP8 x DCP8, FP8 KV cache, TRTLLM ragged prefill backend), 3600-second agentic-coding replay at 70 concurrent sessions, same build on both sides except for this routing. Across three paired runs of this A/B the fused pack improved p90 normalized interactivity by 6 to 11% and p90 inter-token latency by about 7%. Throughput moved between -0.6% and +9.2% across those runs, which is inside the roughly 5% run-to-run drift we measured for identical builds on this route, so we do not claim a throughput win; the robust gain is in the latency tail, which is where long multi-chunk requests live.

**Accuracy.** GSM8K-style probes use prompts far shorter than the scheduler chunk and never reach the DCP context path, so we ran a paired teacher-forced perplexity test on ten public-domain texts of 30k to 36k tokens each (330,944 tokens total), scored token by token on a server with the fused pack and one on the stock tail: perplexity 1.014803 vs 1.014815 (-0.0012%), 19 top-1 flips out of 330,944, consistent with batching nondeterminism between two independent server starts. The kernel output itself is byte-identical to the stock tail (checked on every microbenchmark row above and in the unit test).

## Test Plan

```
pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_mla_prefill_context.py
pytest tests/v1/attention/test_mla_context_chunks.py tests/kernels/attention/test_kimi_k3_mla_fused_epilogue.py
```

`test_mla_prefill_context.py` gains `test_dcp_context_fused_pack_matches_generic_tail[auto|fp8]`: it drives `MLACommonImpl._context_parallel_compute_prefill_context` on a GPU with the collectives stubbed, once without the hook and once with Kimi-K3's `_fused_mla_kv_concat`, and asserts the prefill backend receives identical `(q, k, v)` and the merged partial and lse are identical (`atol=0, rtol=0`), for both bf16 and FP8 queries.

## Test Result

See the latest comment on this PR for the run on the current head.

## Scope

- The fused kernels are compiled for SM90+ as part of vLLM and are already what every NVIDIA Kimi-K3 deployment runs on the non-DCP path. No architecture check is added.
- #52239 restructures the gather half of the same DCP method; this change touches the tail after `kv_b_proj`, so the two are complementary.

AI assistance was used to prepare this change.

title: [Model][DSv4.1] Store the whole KV in MXFP8 (FlashMLA V4.1 record)
author: zyongye
body:
## Purpose

DeepSeek-V4.1 has been reusing DeepSeek-V4's paged `fp8_ds_mla` record. FlashMLA has a V4.1-specific one that quantizes the RoPE dims too; this switches DeepSeek-V4.1 onto it on SM100.

| | V4 (`ModelType::V4`) | **V4.1 (`ModelType::V41`)** |
|---|---|---|
| data row | 448 B fp8 e4m3 NoPE + 128 B bf16 RoPE | **512 B fp8 e4m3, RoPE included** |
| scale row | 7 UE8M0 of 64 dims + 1 pad byte | **16 UE8M0, one per 32 dims (MXFP8)** |
| bytes/token | 584 | **528** |
| page (TMA) stride | 576 B | **512 B** |

Both records put a page's whole data region ahead of its whole scale region, so a page is `block_size * bytes_per_token` rounded up to the TMA stride. Because `block_size` is always a multiple of 32, every V4.1 page is an exact multiple of 512 — the padding the V4 record needed disappears, on top of the 9.6% smaller record.

Gated on SM100: `ModelType::V41` is absent from FlashMLA's SM90 sparse-decode feature set, so SM90, ROCm and the FlashInfer SM120 path keep the V4 record. No new cache dtype and no new flag — `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` resolves to `fp8_ds_mla` as before and the record follows the arch, exactly as `fp8_ds_mla` already means 656 B for V3.2 and 584 B for V4.

### What changed

- **FlashMLA pin** → `vllm-project/FlashMLA@b6ef01c`, following the fork's tree reorganization (`csrc/sm*` → `csrc/kernels/sm*`, API implementations split into `.cpp` files). `api.cpp` now registers `fused_norm_rope_attn_rope_cast_*` and the two permute kernels, so their instantiations must be compiled for `_flashmla_C` to link; the source list mirrors the fork's `setup.py` minus the dense backward, which is training-only.
- **Writers**: the fused SWA insert takes a `kv_mxfp8` argument (one UE8M0 scale per lane pair instead of per four, and the RoPE lanes quantize instead of storing bf16); the compressed-cache insert gets an MXFP8 kernel that applies RoPE *before* choosing scales, since the RoPE dims are now quantized.
- **Readers**: the Triton gather and the CuteDSL gather are parameterized by record instead of hard-coded to 448/64, and both pick it from `k_cache.shape[-1]` — the per-token width the KV cache spec already publishes — so the V4 record keeps working unchanged on the same code path.

### The indexer page has to move with them

`_get_bytes_per_block` makes a block's stride the **sum** of every page in the group, and DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 packs the SWA cache, the compressed-KV cache, the indexer cache and the compressor ring into one block. Divisibility by the TMA stride therefore only holds if *every* contributing page carries the same padding — which is what the indexer cache's 576 B alignment was for, rather than any constraint of its own kernel.

Leaving the indexer at 576 while the main caches moved to 512 produced a block stride of 212160 (a multiple of neither) and tripped FlashMLA's `block_stride_bytes % TMA_K_STRIDE == 0` assertion in the startup profile run, after a clean weight load. Every per-spec page size looked correct in isolation. This PR ties the indexer's alignment to the same gate.

## Relationship to other open PRs

- **#56344 (`[Perf] Deepseek V41 Attention MegaKernel`, same author)** integrates FlashMLA PR #221's fused norm+RoPE+attention megakernel behind `--attention-config '{"dsv4_fused_attention": true}'` and adds an `nvfp4_ds_mla` dtype pairing a 528 B SWA cache with a 288 B fp4 compressed cache. This PR is the narrower, unconditional half: it moves DeepSeek-V4.1's *existing* `fp8_ds_mla` cache to the V4.1 record with no opt-in and no new dtype, and it does not touch the attention path. The two overlap on `flashmla.cmake` (that one pins `c112cc1`, this one `b6ef01c` — one commit later, a test-only change in the fork) and on the V4.1 writers/readers; whichever lands first, the other rebases onto it. #56344 does not currently touch `DeepseekV4IndexerCache.get_kv_cache_spec`, so the alignment fix above is worth carrying across either way.
- **#56441 (`[Perf][DSpark] Add KV-only context insertion across V4.1 cache formats`)** touches the same three `csrc/libtorch_stable/` files to add a KV-only wrapper op. The changes are disjoint in intent (its wrapper drops the dummy query; this adds a record selector) but will conflict textually on the op signature and bindings.

Not duplicating either: neither makes the V4.1 MXFP8 record the layout DeepSeek-V4.1 actually runs with by default, and neither carries the indexer-alignment fix.

## Test Plan & Result

```
pytest tests/kernels/test_compressor_kv_cache.py \
       tests/kernels/test_fused_deepseek_v4_qnorm_rope_kv_insert.py   # 271 passed, 11 skipped
pytest tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py                 # 392 passed, 378 skipped
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla.py \
       tests/kernels/attention/test_flashmla_sparse.py                # 10 passed, 144 skipped
pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py -k mla \
       tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py \
       tests/kernels/test_cp_gather_fp8.py                            # 97 passed, 12 skipped
pytest tests/v1/worker/test_dsv4_packed_zeroer_geometry.py \
       tests/v1/attention/test_indexer_deepseek_v4_slot_mapping.py    # 20 passed
pre-commit run --files <changed files>                                # all hooks pass
```

Three new tests cover the record: a byte-exact check of the compressed-cache insert against a reference quantizer derived from FlashMLA's `tests/quant.py`, an insert→gather round trip (which also exercises the CuteDSL path), and the CUDA op's MXFP8 branch against the Triton encoder.

## Model evaluation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (revision `517ef625`), TP4 on one GB300, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 128 --max-model-len 65536`, no speculative decoding. Baseline is the same weights/TP/node on the V4 584 B record.

| task | V4 record (584 B) | **V4.1 MXFP8 (528 B)** |
|---|---|---|
| gsm8k, greedy 5-shot completions, n=1319 | 0.9272 / 0.9310 | **0.9333** flexible · **0.9340** strict |
| gpqa_diamond, thinking, T=1.0 | 0.904 / 0.899 (epoch 1) | **0.9028** (epoch 4, n=792) · pass@4 0.9495 |

0 request errors on both. GPQA truncated 3/792 rows; answered-only accuracy 0.9062. Quantizing the 64 RoPE dims costs nothing measurable.

Comparability caveat: the baselines were taken with the `deepseekv41-flash-0909` image at gpqa `epoch_num: 1`, this run with a local build at `epoch_num: 4`, so the arms differ in image and epoch count as well as in the record. The gsm8k arm at temperature 0 is the tight comparison and it is clean.

Engine-level evidence beyond the scores: FlashMLA hard-errors on any byte count that is not 584/528/288 for `d_qk=512`, so a clean startup — memory profiling, KV allocation (161.73 GiB, 11,589,848 tokens) and full CUDA-graph capture of the sparse decode path — is itself proof the 528 B record was accepted as `ModelType::V41`.

## AI assistance

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). The FlashMLA pin bump, the record change across the writers/readers, the indexer-alignment fix, the new tests and the evaluation runs above were produced in that session and reviewed by me.

title: [Perf][DSpark] Collapse DeepSeek-V4.1 draft states before SP all-gather
author: Juntian777
body:
## Purpose

Under sequence parallelism, the DeepSeek-V4.1 DSpark draft gathers BF16 `[T_local, 4, H]` residual streams and FP32 `[T_local, 4]` pre-mix coefficients before collapsing them into `[T, H]`. The draft returns only the collapsed pre-norm head states; it does not export a full-HC MTP buffer at this boundary.

Collapse each token's streams locally, then gather only `[T_local, H]` and trim SP padding. This reduces the hidden-state gather payload by 4x for `hc_mult=4` and removes the pre-mix gather, reducing this tail from two collectives to one. The target model already follows this ordering when it does not need to export full HC states. Normalization remains in `compute_logits`.

This is a communication optimization, not an output-correctness fix. SP currently requires PP=1, EP enabled, TP>1, and either a MegaMoE backend or DP>1.

### Duplicate-work check

No existing issue was identified for this optimization; issue-number duplicate checks are not applicable. Open-PR searches covered `dspark collapse`, `DeepSeek sequence parallel`, `"hc_collapse_triton"`, and `"dspark" "gather" in:title`. No matching fix was found. Reviewed related PRs: #50658 projects Kimi-K3 target auxiliary states; #56438 handles V4.1 pipeline/SP stage boundaries; #51244 adds V4 kernel fusions; #56513 changes the ROCm delayed mHC projection. None applies this NVIDIA V4.1 draft-tail reorder.

## Test Plan

- Extend the existing mHC kernel suite with a single-GPU dummy test comparing concatenate-then-collapse against collapse-each-shard-then-concatenate. Cover TP4/TP8, T=1/7/32, padding, and ranks with no valid tokens. Require exact BF16 equality (`atol=0, rtol=0`).
- Run the existing collapse correctness, custom-op/compile, and draft-head tests.
- Use a standalone measurement harness (not included in the PR diff) to benchmark the exact tail (`mhc_post_tilelang` + collapse + production `sp_all_gather`) before and after, using random tensors and no model weights. Check eager and captured outputs bitwise before timing. Include an NCCL-only control.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py \
  -k 'hc_collapse or v41_dspark_head' -v

# Retrieve the standalone harness from the measurement commit.
git show 16dc4cc4d05f86cf8fd0c7413e327395337d2371:benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_dspark_sp_collapse.py \
  > /tmp/benchmark_dspark_sp_collapse.py

.venv/bin/python -m torch.distributed.run --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
  /tmp/benchmark_dspark_sp_collapse.py

.venv/bin/python -m torch.distributed.run --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \
  /tmp/benchmark_dspark_sp_collapse.py --nccl-only

.venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia/dspark.py \
  tests/kernels/test_mhc_kernels.py

git diff --check
```

## Test Result

- **25 passed**, 177 deselected. Includes all six new single-GPU shard-order cases; 14 existing Torch deprecation warnings.
- TP4: all six shapes passed bitwise checks in eager execution and CUDA graph replay, for both default SP dispatch and NCCL-only. Repeated the default-dispatch run with the same result.
- Changed-file pre-commit hooks and whitespace check passed.
- Full-model evaluation and end-to-end serving benchmarks were not run. Validation is limited to tail-output equivalence and the scoped microbenchmark; no acceptance-rate, model-quality, or serving-throughput claim is made.

### Scoped tail performance

One node, 4x NVIDIA GB200 connected by NV18 links. PyTorch 2.13.0+cu132, CUDA 13.2, NCCL 2.29.7, Triton 3.7.1, TileLang 0.1.12, FlashInfer 0.6.18. BF16 streams/output, FP32 mixes, H=5120, hc_mult=4. Measurement commit: `16dc4cc4d05f86cf8fd0c7413e327395337d2371` (the standalone benchmark was subsequently removed from the PR; implementation and tests are unchanged), based on `00972dfd72988942138a7a6089eaee08580210b8`.

CUDA graph internal events exclude CPU launch gaps. Each measurement flushes 128 MiB of L2 and uses a device-side all-reduce rendezvous before replay, outside the timed interval. Four pointer-distinct workspaces, 20 warmup replays, 50 samples per variant, alternating A/B order. Report the median of each sample's slowest rank. Compilation, allocation and input generation are outside timing; all production gather staging/copies remain inside. The benchmark also reports logical receive bytes per rank and payload/time; this is not a measurement of physical link bandwidth.

All times below are microseconds for the entire tail. Default-dispatch figures are from the repeat run.

| Global T | Local padded T | Default before | Default after | Speedup | NCCL before | NCCL after | Speedup |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 24.61 | 18.88 | 1.30x | 42.78 | 31.68 | 1.35x |
| 7 | 2 | 26.82 | 18.94 | 1.42x | 42.82 | 31.81 | 1.35x |
| 32 | 8 | 43.14 | 19.60 | 2.20x | 45.50 | 32.91 | 1.38x |
| 128 | 32 | 108.69 | 20.78 | 5.23x | 62.38 | 35.81 | 1.74x |
| 512 | 128 | 163.89 | 28.80 | 5.69x | 96.96 | 52.93 | 1.83x |
| 2048 | 512 | 168.43 | 88.14 | 1.91x | 180.82 | 90.94 | 1.99x |

The first default-dispatch run measured 1.29x/1.40x/2.10x/5.13x/5.76x/1.88x for the same ascending token counts. These are microbenchmark results, not end-to-end speedups.

Backend selection is part of the measured production wrapper: at T<=128, both versions' state gathers use MNNVL Lamport; at T=512, the original full-state gather falls back while the smaller collapsed gather still uses MNNVL; at T=2048, both state gathers fall back. The original pre-mix gather uses MNNVL throughout. The NCCL-only control disables custom gathers. Real distributed measurements cover TP4; TP8 is covered by single-GPU sharding-equivalence tests only.

AI assistance was used (OpenAI Codex) for implementation, tests, benchmarking, and this description.

title: [Bugfix] Make GPU sync checks safe under torch.compile
author: khluu
body:
## Summary

`gpu_sync_debug`'s patched tensor-copy wrappers currently read a `ContextVar`
before checking whether Dynamo is tracing. A full-graph compile therefore fails
with an unsupported `ContextVar.get()` instead of bypassing sync checks as
intended.

This change:

- checks `torch.compiler.is_compiling()` before accessing either `ContextVar`;
- routes the original C++ `Tensor.to` descriptor through a weak-referenceable
  Python callable registered with `torch.compiler.allow_in_graph`, so Dynamo
  treats the call as opaque while AOT/Inductor can still lower it;
- adds a full-graph `torch.compile` regression with device and dtype derived
  dynamically from another tensor;
- runs the two new Voxtral CUDA-graph parameter cases in explicitly spawned
  processes so neither prior pytest CUDA state nor the other graph mode can
  contaminate them.

## CI incident and test-selection evidence

Daily main build #88920 first exposed this in
`test_voxtral_realtime_cudagraph[FULL_DECODE_ONLY]` in the H200 Multimodal
Models (Extended Generation 1) job. PR #51167 added the compiled Voxtral path,
but that exact job was blocked in both its PR build #88857 and post-merge main
build #88899, so the failure was not exercised before the daily run.

I searched open vLLM issues and PRs for the exact `ContextVar.get` / Voxtral
full-graph failure and did not find an existing fix.

## Validation

- `pre-commit run --files vllm/utils/gpu_sync_debug.py tests/utils_/test_gpu_sync_debug.py tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_voxtral_realtime.py` — passed all applicable hooks
- `git diff --check` — passed
- Local pytest was not run because this regression requires CUDA and this development host has no GPU.
- Exact H200 build #88941 passed Async/Inputs/Utils/Worker but exposed the
  saved C++ `Tensor.to` descriptor as Dynamo-unsupported in the Voxtral
  full-graph test.
- Replacement #88962 proved that registering the method descriptor directly
  is invalid at import time because `allow_in_graph` stores a weak reference.
- Replacement #88969 passed Async/Inputs/Utils/Worker and the original Voxtral
  `FULL_DECODE_ONLY` compile/CUDA-graph surface at literal head `c2fbacb1`.
  The following `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` parameter then hit the normal startup
  guard with only 25.73/32.5 GiB free after the prior in-process compiled
  runner retained about 6.5 GiB; later failures were cascades from that state.
- Replacement #89000 passed Async/Inputs/Utils/Worker, but the default CUDA
  isolation helper chose `fork` after the parent pytest process had initialized
  CUDA. Both Voxtral cases therefore failed before engine compilation with
  `Cannot re-initialize CUDA in forked subprocess`.
- #89010 used an invalid copied full SHA and failed in bootstrap; it contains
  no test evidence.
- #89011 also passed Async/Inputs/Utils/Worker, then reproduced the same two
  pre-compilation CUDA-fork failures. Its literal head still contained the
  helper's default mode because the intended one-line `spawn` edit had not
  been staged into the prior commit.
- Current exact replacement #89026 runs only the same two H200 lanes at
  literal signed head `f7f21d97caecf810db069402ed02c4624311af32`, which
  explicitly passes `method="spawn"` to the isolation helper.

No model evaluation is required because the production change only alters
debug-wrapper control flow while Dynamo is tracing. The exact affected
