title: [Online quantization] Extend re-quantization API to MOE (showcase `NVFP4 modelopt/CT/quark` to any online MOE method)
author: fxmarty-amd
body:
## Overview

Followup to https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55684 that implemented the interface for linear layers.

## Claims

This PR implements the RFC https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59062 for MOE layers, showcasing:

- compressed-tensors NVFP4 MOE -> any online MOE quant method
- modelopt NVFP4 MOE quant method -> any online MOE quant method
- quark NVFP4 MOE quant method -> any online MOE quant method

We share the re-quantization logic with linear layers (same as https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55684), no duplication.

This adds a clean API for features like #51274.

Details & testing to be added later.

Left to do:

- [x] Add modelopt NVFP4 dequantize_weight in this PR
- [x] broaden test
- [x] The generic source/target API ignores the source method's size-rounding contract.
- [x] cleanup

Left to other PRs:

- [ ] Requantization unnecessarily requires a runnable backend for the source format
- [ ] Early fail in case the source method does not implement `dequantize_weight` (for now, this fails during loading)
- [ ] Move from current implementation of **loading all original quant method weights before requantizing, to requantizing on the fly weight by weight**. This will be needed to avoid memory overhead in cases like e.g. `FP8 -> MXFP4`.
- [ ] Requantization to `nvfp4_per_token` (not tested in this PR, needs an other PR for Nvidia GPUs)
- [ ] Adopt this API
    - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51274 => mxfp4 -> int4 conversion.

## Validation

Run all added tests:

```bash
pytest -s -vvvvv tests/quantization/test_online.py \
```

title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Always attempt NIXL agent removal during peer teardown
author: nej1gotnochill
body:
## Overview

Fixes the stale NIXL peer-registration state in the P2P tiering transport that can permanently wedge the data plane after a peer-down/reconnect cycle such as SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, while the control plane keeps reporting HIT. Fixes #60205.

## Problem

`NixlTransport.remove_remote_peer()` runs two independent teardown operations in sequence: releasing the remote descriptor-list handle, then removing the remote agent. If `release_dlist_handle()` raises, the exception aborts the method before `remove_remote_agent()` is attempted, so the NIXL remote agent stays registered after the peer is gone — leaving a stale registration behind.

`_publish_peer()` has the same problem on its superseded-registration path: both teardown calls share a single `try` block, so a release failure skips the agent removal for a registration that is being discarded.

**Reporter's reproduction (#60205), condensed:** disaggregated prefill/decode, `TieringOffloadingSpec` over UCX/NIXL. After SIGSTOP of one EngineCore and SIGCONT, the control plane recovers (sessions reconnect, heartbeats and lookups keep returning HIT), but transfers to/from that rank fail permanently — `NIXL_ERR_REMOTE_DISCONNECT`, then `NIXL_ERR_NOT_FOUND` on every poll. Fetches time out after 30 s and recompute; healthy ranks keep working; only a group restart fixes the wedged rank.

## Fix

Move both teardown calls into one small `_release_remote_handles()` helper that runs each operation under its own `try`/`except`, and call it from both `remove_remote_peer()` and `_publish_peer()`. Failures from either teardown operation are logged rather than aborting teardown midway, so `remove_remote_agent()` is always attempted. The `_peer_lock`/`_peer_gen` handling in `remove_remote_peer()` on `main` is unchanged.

## Evidence from the reviewer

The reviewer reproduced the stale-registration wedge on real NIXL/UCX: two pods on different nodes, nixl 1.5.0, `rc_mlx5` over InfiniBand, DRAM-only transfers, using the same call sequence as `NixlTransport`, with every WRITE checksum-verified at the target:

- Teardown plus a same-name re-add after a 249-second SIGSTOP/SIGCONT cycle recovers cleanly; the re-add does not reuse a stale endpoint.
- With the peer frozen, the WRITE raises `NIXL_ERR_REMOTE_DISCONNECT`. If `remove_remote_agent` was also skipped (the pre-patch path when `release_dlist_handle` raises), the SIGCONT plus re-add reports OK, but every WRITE after that still fails with `REMOTE_DISCONNECT` (3 attempts over ~2 min). This matches #60205.
- Calling `remove_remote_agent` unconditionally, then re-adding, recovers it.

## Important qualification

The regression tests simulate `release_dlist_handle()` raising. Why it raised in the original incident is not confirmed.

## Scope boundary

This PR does not claim to stop in-flight writes, change transfer polling semantics, or fix the server notification ordering — `remove_remote_peer()` does not stop an in-flight WRITE. Server notification ordering and transfer-terminal handling are covered by #59790; `poll()`/`NOT_FOUND` handling stays out of scope and will be decided jointly with #59790/#49632.

## Root cause and design

**Root cause.** `remove_remote_peer()` released the dlist before removing the remote agent with no error handling — if `release_dlist_handle()` raised, `remove_remote_agent()` never ran, orphaning the NIXL registration with no Python reference left. `_publish_peer()` shared one `try` block across both calls with the same skip-on-raise behavior.

**Why teardown failures are logged, not raised:** `remove_remote_peer()` runs inside `manager._reap_dead_sessions()`, which has no exception guard up to `get_finished_jobs()`; raising would abort the reap loop and propagate into the scheduler. The EC connector's NIXL transport follows the same log-and-continue pattern.

## Testing

Commands (run from the repo root):

```
python -m pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/ -q --confcutdir=tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p        # 277 passed
python -m ruff check <changed files>                                                                      # passed
python -m ruff format --check <changed files>                                                             # passed
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD                                                                       # clean
```

New regression tests, both verified to fail against unpatched upstream `nixl.py` (negative control: 2 failed, exit 1) and pass with the fix:

- `test_remove_peer_removes_agent_even_if_release_fails` — a release failure during peer removal must not skip `remove_remote_agent()`.
- `test_superseded_registration_removes_agent_even_if_release_fails` — a release failure while discarding a superseded registration in `_publish_peer()` must not skip `remove_remote_agent()`.

Runs are CPU-only with a mocked NIXL agent, in WSL2 Ubuntu, Python 3.12, torch 2.14.1+cpu.

**Outstanding limitation:** no GPU/RDMA/UCX hardware validation was performed by the contributor. The hardware reproduction above was performed by the reviewer, not locally.

## Disclosure

This contribution was prepared with AI assistance (Codebuff).

title: [Bugfix][Core] Count unscheduled running requests toward max_loras
author: sricursion
body:
## Overview

Count the LoRA adapters of all running requests, not only those scheduled in the current step, when deciding whether a waiting request fits within `max_loras`. Without this, a skipped running request lets a request with another adapter in, and the next batch holds more than `max_loras` adapters and trips an assertion in `Scheduler.schedule()`.

Fixes #60301

## Claims

- With `--max-loras N`, a waiting request whose adapter would exceed `N` once a currently skipped running request resumes is no longer admitted early. This happens with pipeline parallelism and also on a single GPU, e.g. when a multimodal request is skipped because the step's encoder budget is used up.
- Fixes `AssertionError` in `schedule()` (`assert len(scheduled_loras) <= self.lora_config.max_loras`), which escapes the engine core busy loop and kills the engine.
- No behavior change when every running request is scheduled in the step.
- One-line source change (the iterable the set is built from) plus its comment; `create_scheduler` in the scheduler test helpers gains a `lora_config` argument.

## Validation

Repro on `main` (`bf049ddb8f`), CPU, `Scheduler` with `max_loras=1`, stepping `schedule()` and `update_from_output()` the way a pipeline-parallel engine does (a step's output returns only after the next `schedule()`):

1. `r1` (LoRA 1, 8-token prompt) is scheduled; its output is still in flight.
2. `r2` (LoRA 2) arrives. `r1` has nothing to run in step 2, so `scheduled_loras` is empty and `r2` is admitted.
3. `r1`'s output returns. Step 3 schedules `r1` (decode) and `r2` (next prefill chunk) together.

Before:

```
max_loras: 1
step1: {'r1': 8}
step2: {'r2': 16} running: ['r1', 'r2']
  File ".../vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 877, in schedule
    assert len(scheduled_loras) <= self.lora_config.max_loras
AssertionError
```

After:

```
max_loras: 1
step1: {'r1': 8}
step2: {} running: ['r1']
step3: {'r1': 1}
distinct LoRAs in batch: {1} max_loras: 1
```

Randomized check (12 requests with LoRA ids drawn from {none, 1, 2, 3, 4}, random prompt lengths and arrival steps, `max_loras=2`, PP=2, `max_num_batched_tokens=16`, 200 seeds, requests complete after 4 tokens):

| | seeds finished | `AssertionError` in `schedule()` | max adapters in one batch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | 176 | 24 | 2 |
| this PR | 200 | 0 | 2 |

Regression test `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_max_loras_counts_running_request_awaiting_output`:

```
# main
E       AssertionError: assert {'b': 8} == {}
E         Left contains 1 more item:
E         {'b': 8}
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:358: AssertionError
1 failed, 1 passed, 199 deselected

# this PR
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_max_loras_counts_running_request_awaiting_output PASSED
```

Existing tests (CPU, `pytest -p no:cacheprovider`):

```
pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py
  45 failed, 175 passed
pytest tests/v1/core
  59 failed, 877 passed, 4 errors
```

All of these failures and errors are pre-existing: the same 59 test ids fail and the same 4 tests error on `main` (rerun there by node id). They are multimodal and e2e tests (`Llava`/`Qwen2.5-VL`/`Qwen3.5` architecture inspection fails, engine and server fixtures cannot start) in an environment without GPU or compiled kernels. None involve LoRA.

Re-checked after rebasing onto `e37e51dd24` (current `main`):

- `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_max_loras_counts_running_request_awaiting_output` fails with `scheduler.py` reverted to `main` (`AssertionError: assert {'b': 8} == {}`) and passes with the fix.
- The scheduler-level repro in #60301 hits the assertion on `main` and runs to completion with this PR; the randomized check gives the same numbers as in the table (24 of 200 seeds fail on `main`, 0 with this PR).
- `pytest tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_async_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py`: 343 passed, 46 failed. The same 46 tests fail on `main` (45 `LlavaForConditionalGeneration` inspection errors because `torchvision` is not installed here, 1 subprocess timeout in `test_kv_cache_utils.py`); none involve LoRA.
- `pre-commit run --hook-stage manual --files tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py tests/v1/core/utils.py vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`, which runs every hook CI runs (including `mypy` for Python 3.10 to 3.13): all hooks pass.

## Details

Root cause: `Scheduler.schedule()` seeds `scheduled_loras` from `scheduled_running_reqs` (`scheduler.py:869-877` on `main`) and the waiting loop admits a request only if its adapter fits in that set (`:918-929`). A running request is skipped in a step when it has nothing to schedule yet: with PP>1 once its prompt is fully scheduled but the output is pending (the `num_new_tokens == 0` case documented in the running loop), and through the other `continue` paths of the running loop (`next_decode_eligible_step` cadence for V2 + PP + async, DP prefill deferral, EC connector and encoder budget waits). Its adapter is then missing from the set, a request with another adapter is admitted, and once the skipped request is scheduled again both end up in one batch. The running loop does not consult `max_loras`, so the existing `assert` is the first thing to notice.

Fix: seed the set from `self.running`. Every request enters `self.running` through the waiting-loop admission check, so the number of distinct adapters among running requests stays at most `max_loras` and the assert holds. This is how the V0 scheduler counted (`curr_loras` was built from all running sequence groups), and what `LoRAConfig.max_loras` ("Max number of LoRAs in a single batch") requires. The variable keeps its name since it is still the set the waiting loop extends as it admits requests.

Scope and limits: the check is more conservative only when a running request that holds an adapter is skipped in the step; that request's adapter slot is kept until it finishes. Two tests cover it: the pipeline-parallel case and, without PP, a running request skipped because earlier requests used up the step's encoder compute budget (suggested in review). Both fail on `main` and pass with this change. Open priority-preemption PRs (#40087, #45558, #45561, #54530) read and update `scheduled_loras` but do not change how it is seeded.

Not a duplicate: I searched issues and PRs on `vllm-project/vllm` for `max_loras`, `scheduled_loras`, `LoRA scheduler`, `LoRA pipeline`, `LoRA async`, `max_loras assertion` and `no free lora slots`, and open PRs for `scheduler.py lora` and `LoRA schedule running requests`. Nothing reports or fixes this. Closest hits: #15422 (merged, introduced the current seeding), #14495 (closed feature request about "No free lora slots" for over-full batches, predates #15422), #17003 (usage question), #10840 (closed, a V0 LoRA scheduling policy), and the open priority-preemption PRs above.

This PR was co-authored with Claude.

End-to-end validation in review: on 2×H20 (Qwen3-0.6B, 3 LoRAs, PP=2, `max_loras=1`) `main` dies with `EngineDeadError` from this assert in all four MRV2/V1 × sync/async combinations and this PR completes with outputs matching per-request runs; the single-GPU encoder-budget case (Qwen3.5-4B, `max_loras=2`) reproduces and is fixed as well.

title: [Bugfix] Don't Eliminate Clones for graph I/O Aliases
author: alex-jw-brooks
body:
## Overview

Currently, the compile clone elimination doesn't check for aliases to graph inputs and outputs, which can unexpectedly clobber values if we take a snapshot of an input that doesn't have any writes & leverage in place kernels (e.g., all reduce for TP>1) and return it outside of the compile boundary for later processing. 

I don't think that there are many models in vLLM that do this with the current compile boundaries, but an example of this case came up yesterday in vLLM Omni, since the thinker snapshots the embeddings, which get `.clone`d and forwarded to the talker (more details in: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/pull/8532), where the audio gets mangled with TP=2 and compile, because the fused allreduce & rms norm runs in place and the clone on the embeddings is right inside the compile boundary.

This PR skips elimination when the clone is returned from the graph and its source aliases a graph input or another output (assuming the clone has no writes). It also adds a regression test for piecewise and full-graph compilation.

title: [ROCm][MoE] Split AiterExperts by weight-quantization key
author: divakar-amd
body:
## Summary

 Split AITER experts by weight quantization key. Splits the single catch-all `AiterExperts` modular-kernel class into five narrower leaf classes, one per weight-quantization scheme:

- `AiterUnquantizedExperts` — `(None, None)`
- `AiterFp8BlockExperts` — `(kFp8Static128BlockSym, kFp8Dynamic128Sym)`
- `AiterFp8TensorExperts` — `(kFp8StaticTensorSym, {Static,Dynamic}TensorSym)`
- `AiterFp8ChannelExperts` — `(kFp8StaticChannelSym, kFp8DynamicTokenSym)`
- `AiterMxfp4Experts` — `(kMxfp4Static, {None, kMxfp4Dynamic})`, gfx950-only 

`AiterExperts` becomes a shared, non-instantiable base class. All other methods (`apply()`, `workspace_shapes()`, device/activation/parallel-config gating, weight-conversion dispatch) stay on the base since they're already scheme-agnostic at runtime — only `_supports_quant_scheme()` meaningfully diverges per scheme, so that's the only thing that moved into the leaves. This is intentionally scoped narrowly: `apply()`'s internal `quant_method` derivation, the `asm_moe_tkw1` dispatch, and MXFP4's `gate_mode`/bias selection all remain in the shared base, still keyed off runtime `quant_config` flags rather than owned per-leaf. Moving `quant_method` down is a reasonable follow-up; `gate_mode` is more tangled (it checks `activation == SITU` before weight-quant key) and likely stays shared. Issue #54966's "own apply()/scale contract per leaf" isn't done by this step — only the scheme-gating (`_supports_quant_scheme`) is.

This mirrors the pattern already used by the Cutlass family (`CutlassExpertsFp8Base`, `CutlassExpertsNvfp4`, `CutlassExpertsMxfp4`), where `AiterExperts` was the remaining monolithic outlier. Part of #54966

## Test plan

MI300 (gfx942), `dv_DistriDPBasic` container, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3`:

```
pytest -x -v tests/kernels/moe/test_modular_kernel_combinations.py -k "aiter"
pytest -x -v tests/kernels/moe/test_rocm_aiter_moe.py
pytest -x -v tests/kernels/moe/test_mori_moe.py
pytest -x -v tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_layer.py -k "mori or aiter"
pytest -x -v tests/kernels/moe/test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py
```

All green. Also ran the full `tests/kernels/moe/` suite as a broader regression sanity check (ROCm/AITER-only change; no CUDA or other-backend code paths touched); all observed failures traced to a pre-existing, unrelated triton-version environment issue (`is_hip_gfx1250` import error) or full-suite resource contention, not this change — confirmed by rerunning the affected tests standalone.

**MI350 (gfx950)**, same test files — all green, including the three gfx950-only numeric MXFP4 tests:

- `test_aiter_mxfp4_quant_scheme_support_matches_gfx950` — PASSED
- `test_aiter_fused_moe_mi350_mxfp4_w4a16_accuracy` — PASSED, 100% match (16384/16384) against the dequantized MXFP4 reference
- `test_aiter_fused_moe_mi350_mxfp4_w4a16_determinism` — PASSED

**Merged with main (resolving the conflict in `test_modular_kernel_combinations.py`)** and re-ran the full test plan on MI355 (gfx950), twice, on two disjoint GPU sets (`HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3` and `4,5,6,7`), identical results both times:

- `test_modular_kernel_combinations.py -k "aiter"`: 48 passed, 6 failed, 6 skipped. The 6 failures (`test_aiter_moe_padding_matrix[{none,hidden}-{fp8_channel_token,fp8_tensor_tensor,fp8_tensor_token}]`) are a pre-existing AITER CK `device_gemm` GEMM-shape limitation on gfx950 for non-block fp8 schemes at the unpadded `intermediate_size=384` shape, unrelated to this split — these are brand-new tests added by main (#59333/#59334) hitting real gfx950 hardware behavior for the first time; they reproduce identically on a clean `main` checkout on this hardware.
- `test_rocm_aiter_moe.py` + `test_mori_moe.py` + `test_topk_softplus_sqrt.py`: 1756 passed, 4 skipped.
- `test_moe_layer.py -k "mori or aiter"`: 3 passed, 20 skipped.

## Known limitations / follow-up

- `AiterMxfp4Experts`'s harness registration (`mk_objects.py`) doesn't currently produce any modular-kernel test case — `MK_QUANT_CONFIGS` has no `quant_dtype="mxfp4"` entry, so it's registered but unreachable. Real MXFP4 modular-kernel coverage is tracked separately in #60886.
- This PR only moves `_supports_quant_scheme()` to the leaves (see Summary); other scheme-specific runtime dispatch stays in the shared base for now.

## Bugs found and fixed along the way

- Merging main brought in two new tests (#59333/#59334: `test_aiter_moe_padding_matrix`, `test_aiter_moe_token_padding_garbage_rows`) that build a `Config` with `fused_experts_type=AiterExperts` directly. Since the split makes `AiterExperts` a non-instantiable base no longer registered in the harness, this fails `config.is_valid()` (`expert_info(AiterExperts)` → `AssertionError`). Fixed both call sites to pick the correct per-scheme leaf class from the quant config instead.
- `modular_kernel_tools/common.py`'s `_maybe_convert_weights_for_experts` gated the gfx950 AITER weight-preshuffle workaround (#60633) on `fe_name == "AiterExperts"` — a literal class-name string match that no longer matches any instantiated class after the split, silently turning off the preshuffle and falling back to JIT-compiling `preshuffle_off` for every AITER harness case (the exact slowdown #60633 fixed). Switched to `issubclass(fe_type, AiterExperts)`.
- Separately, main added a `model_config.sleep_mode_offload_cudagraph` read in `VllmConfig.use_cumem_cudagraph_pool` that the modular-kernel harness's fake `model_config` (a bare `SimpleNamespace`) didn't have, breaking any multi-GPU modular-kernel test. Added the missing fields with their real `ModelConfig` defaults.
- That same `model_config` bug was independently found and fixed in #61260, which also discovered that it was never actually caught in CI: the only AMD job covering this file runs on the single-GPU `mi300_1` pool, so `test_modular_kernel_combinations_multigpu` (which needs `world_size=2`) self-skips via its own GPU-count check on every run. #61260 added a dedicated `mi300_2` job for these cases; that job is now included in this PR (latest commit) instead, so #61260 is being closed in favor of landing it here.

#### Why this isn't a duplicate

No PR performs this exact split. #59333/#59334 (merged into main after this PR was opened) do instantiate `AiterExperts` directly in two new tests — as noted above, merging main surfaced this as a real incompatibility, now fixed by picking the correct leaf class in both tests.

#### AI assistance disclosure

This change was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code),

title: [Spec Decode] Rename AR speculators to StandaloneAR / TargetDependentAR
author: TheEpicDolphin
body:
`AutoRegressiveSpeculator` is the base class for EAGLE, MTP, and Gemma4. When `PlainDraftModelSpeculator` was added in #43091 to support vanilla draft-model speculation, the base-class name became misleading: both are autoregressive.

This PR renames them to make the actual distinction explicit:
- EAGLE, MTP, and Gemma4 are **target-dependent** autoregressive speculators. They consume target model state (hidden states, and for Gemma4 its KV cache). Thus, `AutoRegressiveSpeculator` was renamed to `TargetDependentARSpeculator`.
- The vanilla draft model is a **standalone** autoregressive speculator: it
  needs nothing from the target beyond the accepted/bonus token ids. This, `PlainDraftModelSpeculator` was renamed to `StandaloneARSpeculator`.

title: [Spec Decode][MRV2] Suffix decoding speculator for Model Runner V2
author: nishantrevur
body:
## Overview `method="suffix"` today needs Arctic Inference, runs on the CPU, forces Model Runner V1 and disables async scheduling. With this PR it runs on Model Runner V2 with a GPU speculator, with async scheduling and without Arctic; V1 keeps using Arctic. This is the "suffix" item in #47172. The speculator builds on `ngram_gpu` (#40704) and borrows from #52097 (thanks @zip95297). Related fix on main: #61509 (adaptive verification's startup profiling was counted as CUDA graph memory). @njhill rebased this onto the speculator config refactor and simplified it: seeded requests are no longer special-cased, and the runner hooks are `BaseSpeculator` methods. ## Claims - `method="suffix"` runs on Model Runner V2: GPU-resident, no host sync on the propose path, async scheduling, no Arctic dependency. V1 is unchanged except for the default `num_speculative_tokens` (below). - Acceptance is on par with Arctic: 1.937 tokens per step vs Arctic's 1.923 (k=8) and 1.948 (k=24) on a 21K-request replay. - With adaptive verification, throughput matches or beats Arctic on V1 at every concurrency for Qwen2.5-7B (offline and online serving) and for Qwen2.5-1.5B from concurrency 64 up; at 1.5B concurrency 8 and 32 Arctic is ahead (below). Without adaptive verification, verifying every slot loses from concurrency 32 up, as with `ngram_gpu`. - GSM8K accuracy matches no speculation. - `num_speculative_tokens` now defaults to 8 for suffix decoding (was `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth`, 24), because V2 verifies every slot. ## Validation The results below were measured before @njhill's rebase and simplification. That change only affects requests with an explicit `seed`, and none of these benchmarks send per-request seeds, so they still apply. #61509 has since merged, so the "with #61509" figures are what adaptive verification gets on current main. **Tests** ```bash pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_suffix_speculator.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_adaptive_verification.py # 49 passed pytest tests/test_config.py -k "speculative or suffix or heterogeneous or model_runner" # 68 passed pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_ngram_gpu.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_custom_speculator.py # 58 passed pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/ngram_suffix/test_ngram_suffix.py -k suffix # 3 passed ``` The e2e tests ran with the CI model's weights (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on one L4, before the simplification (which doesn't touch greedy decoding): - The V2 GSM8K correctness test passes (76.3%). At the old default k=24 it ran out of memory: V2 profiles one logits row per request, while every step computes 1 + k. - The V2 cross-request test gives 0.74 → 4.47 accepted tokens per draft on the repeated pass. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it's 1.32 → 5.12, and 1.28 → 1.28 with the corpus off, which the test's `second > 2 * first` check rejects. - The Arctic acceptance test (V1) passes. **Runtime checks** - **No new host syncs:** `VLLM_GPU_SYNC_CHECK=error` with and without adaptive verification, including ingestion. - **TP=2:** corpus, index, statistics and drafts are identical on both ranks after 312 requests, with and without adaptive verification, on the default ring and on a 2,048-token ring where bursts of up to 48 finished requests wrap over themselves. **Acceptance.** Replay of 21,299 greedy Qwen2.5-1.5B requests with 5.1M output tokens (UltraChat, Alpaca, GSM8K, Spec-Bench, code edit, rewrite and templated JSON), in waves of 64, with a 1M-token corpus and k=8. Mean tokens per step. Arctic runs via `arctic_inference` and also sees responses still being generated. The kernel matches the replay on all 1,280 sampled drafts. | Drafter | All | Code edit | Rewrite | Templated JSON | |---|---|---|---|---| | Own history only | 1.651 | 5.50 | 4.74 | 1.65 | | **This PR** | **1.937** | 5.45 | 4.69 | 4.25 | | Exact corpus search + same vote (upper bound) | 1.956 | 5.45 | 4.69 | 4.28 | | Arctic (V1), k=8 | 1.923 | 5.12 | 4.07 | 3.89 | | Arctic (V1), k=24 | 1.948 | 5.89 | 4.37 | 4.11 | **Throughput.** Offline `LLM.generate` on this PR's final code. Output tokens/s relative to no speculation. - **Setup:** concurrency = `max_num_seqs`; prompts from a pinned pool with the replay's category mix (its GSM8K and Spec-Bench prompts also appear in the replay); greedy, `max_tokens=256`, k=8. - **Backends:** FlashAttention 2, except adaptive verification on `TRITON_ATTN`, which is compared against no speculation on `TRITON_ATTN`. - **Runs:** one per point; runs with another process on the GPU were discarded and rerun. | Model | Concurrency | `ngram_gpu` | Arctic (V1) | This PR | This PR + adaptive verification | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Qwen2.5-7B | 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 | 1.28 / 1.14 / 0.73 / 0.52x | 1.31 / 1.29 / 1.24 / 1.03x | 1.46 / 1.32 / 0.82 / 0.59x | **1.39 / 1.36 / 1.24 / 1.18x** | | Qwen2.5-1.5B | 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 / 128 / 256 | 1.45 / 1.25 / 0.84 / 0.55 / 0.50 / 0.44x | 1.41 / 1.43 / 1.17 / 1.00 / 0.91 / 0.82x | 1.66 / 1.47 / 0.97 / 0.64 / 0.56 / 0.52x | **1.56 / 1.29 / 1.15 / 1.05 / 0.99 / 0.91x** | - **Where Arctic wins:** 1.5B at concurrency 8 and 32, by 11% and 5% in absolute tok/s. Adaptive verification trims too much there (open question 2). - **Backend difference:** at 1.5B concurrency 128 / 256, `TRITON_ATTN` without speculation is 1.13 / 1.21x faster than FA2. Against the FA2 baseline the other columns use, adaptive verification is 1.12 / 1.10x. - **With #61509:** the 7B KV cache with adaptive verification grows from 21–46K to 50–70K tokens. 7B throughput becomes 1.38 / 1.32 / 1.30 / 1.15x, within run-to-run noise except at concurrency 32. **Online serving** (`vllm bench serve`, Qwen2.5-7B, prompts not in the 256-request warm-up, up to 256 output tokens, `--generation-config vllm`). Output throughput vs no speculation: | Config | Concurrency 1 / 8 / 32 / 64 | |---|---| | `ngram_gpu` | 1.26 / 1.11 / 0.73 / 0.53x | | Arctic (V1) | 1.42 / 1.37 / 1.24 / 1.10x | | This PR | 1.49 / 1.35 / 0.87 / 0.65x | | **This PR + adaptive verification** (vs no-spec on `TRITON_ATTN`) | **1.44 / 1.44 / 1.30 / 1.23x** | Median TTFT at concurrency 1 is 125 ms with this PR (with or without adaptive verification) and with `ngram_gpu`, vs 73 ms without speculation and 74 ms for Arctic on V1, which runs without async scheduling. That is about one decode step, so it's a V2 spec-decode cost rather than a suffix one.
GSM8K, workloads and correctness checks **GSM8K** (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, all 1,319 questions, 5-shot, `max_num_seqs=128`). Accuracy matches within noise (binomial SE about 1 point); at this load speculation doesn't speed it up: | Config | Greedy | Temperature 0.7 | Wall time (greedy) | |---|---|---|---| | No speculation (FA2) | 83.0% | 81.7% | 193 s | | No speculation (`TRITON_ATTN`) | 83.4% | 82.3% | 156 s | | Arctic (V1) | 83.4% | 83.2% | 252 s | | This PR | 82.8% | 83.6% | 387 s | | This PR + adaptive verification (`TRITON_ATTN`) | 82.9% | 81.6% | 157 s | **Workloads.** Offline, throughput vs no speculation (adaptive verification vs no-spec on `TRITON_ATTN`). Concurrency 32, except long context: | Workload | This PR | + adaptive verification | Arctic (V1) | |---|---|---|---| | VLM: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, 360 distinct camera frames, templated JSON reports and captions | 1.38x (3.18 tok/step) | 1.50x | 1.56x | | RL rollouts: Qwen2.5-1.5B, GSM8K, n=8, temperature 1 | 0.94x | 1.40x | 1.16x | | Multi-turn chat: Qwen2.5-7B, UltraChat history | 0.78x | 1.15x | 1.03x | | RAG + summarization: Qwen2.5-7B, Spec-Bench | 0.86x | 1.16x | 1.10x | | Long-context decode: 24K-token prompts, concurrency 3 | 1.38x | 0.29x; **1.46x with #61509** | 1.19x | At long context, adaptive verification's startup profiling cost the KV cache 1.9 GiB (43K instead of 80K tokens), so prefixes were evicted and re-prefilled. #61509 fixes that accounting on main. **Correctness** (this PR's final code; greedy outputs vs no speculation, 48 distinct prompts; fp32 Qwen2.5-0.5B on `TRITON_ATTN`, since FA2 has no fp32): | Check | This PR | + adaptive verification | `ngram_gpu` | |---|---|---|---| | Plain greedy | 45/48 | 45/48 | 46/48 | | Repetition/frequency/presence penalties | 43/48 | 44/48 | 43/48 | | Structured outputs (JSON schema, regex, choice), `max_tokens=2`, logprobs | identical | identical | regex 11/12, rest identical | | Stop strings with `min_tokens`; `ignore_eos` to 300 tokens | 48/48; 45/48 | 47/48; 45/48 | 47/48; 45/48 | | 24 distinct 800–1,800-word prompts with chunked prefill (`max_num_batched_tokens=512`); 8 prompts ending 40 tokens before `max_model_len` | 24/24, 8/8 | 24/24, 8/8 | 24/24, 8/8 | | Preemption (small KV cache, 144 requests, 355–509 preemptions) | 128/144 | 125/144 | 126/144 | - **Baseline noise:** two no-spec runs, async vs sync scheduling, differ on 1/48 plain prompts. - **Logprobs:** deltas on identical outputs are at most 5e-3, the same as `ngram_gpu`. - **Sampling** (Qwen2.5-1.5B bf16, temperature 1, top-p, top-k, n=16, each method with its own seed): total-variation distance of per-position token marginals vs a no-spec run is 0.153 / 0.079 / 0.131. A second no-spec run gives 0.161 / 0.059 / 0.128, `ngram_gpu` 0.148 / 0.056 / 0.131. - **Aborts** (`vllm serve`, 48 streams aborted mid-generation): the server stays healthy. Greedy requests sent afterwards match those sent before 8/8 without adaptive verification. With it, 7/8 in fp32 (one flip at a 0.0004-nat near-tie) and 2/8 in bf16 7B: the number of verified slots changes the batch shapes.
## Details **How it works** - **Own history:** the longest suffix match within the request's prompt and output, up to `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth`. Same kernel layout as `ngram_gpu`. - **Cross-request corpus:** finished responses go into a GPU token ring (`suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens`, default 1M). A hash index on each request's last 2 and last 4 tokens returns up to 16 candidate positions. Each is verified and extended to its full suffix match, so the index is only an entry point for suffix matching, and hash collisions or overwritten documents only cost a candidate. - **Frequency vote:** for each candidate match length, the candidates matching at least that long vote on the continuation, as in SuffixDecoding. The highest-scoring chain wins, ties going to the longer match; then the longer of the own-history and corpus matches wins. - **Adaptive verification** (`enable_adaptive_verification`): per-slot confidences, learned online by source, match length and position, let the runner trim slots that aren't worth verifying. - **Ingestion:** one GPU program per (document, block). Each program replays the batch's placement to find its offset and skips positions that a later document of the same batch overwrites. Every position is written by exactly one program, so the result is exact and order-independent even when a burst is larger than the ring. A 256 × 4,096-token burst at the default 1M ring takes 0.58 ms. - **TP consistency without collectives:** finished ids are ingested in sorted order, index inserts use `atomic_max` over `(document << 32 | position)`, and the statistics are integer counters. - **Memory at the defaults:** 36 MB (4 MB corpus plus a 32 MB index). Suffix decoding also keeps the runner's token history on the GPU (`max_num_seqs × max_model_len × 4` bytes, e.g. 32 MiB at 256 × 32K).
How a corpus lookup works (diagram) ``` Request history: ... "report" "the" "camera" "at" "the" "north" "gate" └──── last 4 ────┘ └─ last 2 ┘ 1) LOOK UP hash(last 4), hash(last 2) -> buckets, 8 slots each (slot = newest occurrence in each of the last 8 documents) 2) EXTEND BACKWARDS each candidate against the request (up to 24 tokens): request: report the camera at the north gate corpus: log: the camera at the north gate -> match length 6 stale or colliding candidate -> length 0, dropped 3) VOTE + DRAFT candidates matching >= L tokens vote on the next k tokens; the chain with the highest summed probability wins 4) COMPARE with the longest match in the request's own history; the longer match wins, empty slots get the last token ``` Ingestion when a request finishes: `[last 3 prompt tokens | response]` is appended to the ring, and each position with at least 2 (4) tokens before it in the document is indexed under them: `table[hash][doc % 8] = max(existing, (doc, pos))`.
**Why a hash index** | Index | Propose cost (L4) | Notes | |---|---|---| | Suffix tree (Arctic, V1) | CPU, per request | Host sync, so no MRV2 or async scheduling | | Suffix array (#52097) | 1.3–4.5 ms as an eager library call (prototype measurement on a shared L4); #52097 reports 0.4–1.9 ms with its CUDA-graph path (L20, k=16) | Background rebuilds, epochs and a CPU collective for TP | | Brute-force GPU scan | 0.3–1.2 ms at batch 128 (prototype measurement) | Exact; cost grows with batch × corpus | | **Hash index + vote (this PR)** | **11–35 µs** GPU time for batch 1–256 (CUDA-graph microbenchmark), the same at 1M and 4M corpus tokens. As the engine runs it (eagerly): 89–95 µs per step at 4K context for batch 1–256, 231 µs at 128K context with 32 requests (`ngram_gpu`: 75–78 and 111 µs) | No rebuilds. The index alone is within 0.4% of an exact longest-match search; with the vote, about 1% below exact search + vote | One difference from Arctic: corpus matches need at least 2 tokens (so `suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth` must be at least 2 for the corpus), while own-history matches can be 1. Storing the last 3 prompt tokens with each response lets a response's first tokens be drafted from the corpus. **Taken from #52097 and @zip95297's MRV2 port** (`zip95297/vllm-dev`, branch `zip95297/suffix-gpu-mrv2`): GPU cross-request matching with no host sync; an `on_requests_finished` hook in `finish_requests` that ingests from `RequestState` and skips preempted requests (from the MRV2 port); sorting finished ids for TP consistency; the replay-based acceptance evaluation. **Changes outside the speculator** - `SuffixSpeculatorConfig` (`suffix/config.py`): suffix's default `num_speculative_tokens` is `min(8, suffix_decoding_max_tree_depth)` on both runners. On V1 it caps Arctic's dynamic draft length; set 24 for the previous V1 behavior. - `BaseSpeculator`: new no-op `add_request`, `on_requests_finished` and `reset_state` methods, which the runner and MRV2's kernel warmup call directly. The suffix speculator uses them to reset per-slot stats, ingest finished requests, and drop the warmup requests from the corpus. Dense `all_token_ids` for suffix. **Limitations** - Seeded sampling isn't reproducible with suffix decoding: drafts come from previously finished requests, and with adaptive verification the number of verified slots depends on the batch. The same seeded request sent alone twice gave identical output 0/4 (fp32; 4/4 without speculation). With `suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens: 0` and adaptive verification off it's 4/4. - The corpus is shared across requests regardless of `cache_salt` or LoRA adapter, like Arctic's global tree on V1 (documented; set `suffix_decoding_corpus_tokens: 0` to isolate). - Adaptive verification needs full CUDA graphs and an attention backend that replays variable-length decode batches. On L4 that is `TRITON_ATTN`: vLLM's FA2 backend declares uniform-batch support only. Until #61509 lands, its startup profiling also costs KV capacity, which matters at long context. - Under async scheduling a finished request can carry up to about 2k+1 tokens past the stop point into the corpus. ## Open questions 1. **Adaptive verification by default?** It is what makes suffix decoding pay off from concurrency 32 up. It isn't on by default here because it fails at startup on backends that can't replay variable-length decode graphs (FA2, the pre-Hopper default), so a default needs a fallback to off. Happy to add that here, or in a follow-up. 2. **Low-concurrency trimming.** Adaptive verification trims too much at low concurrency on small models: Qwen2.5-1.5B at concurrency 8 is 1.29x with it vs 1.47x verifying every slot (7B: 1.36x vs 1.32x). Tune it here (for example with a more optimistic prior) or later? 3. **Corpus default.** 4M tokens adds about 2–3% acceptance, but the index grows from 32 MB to 128 MB. 4. **Tokens past the stop point.** Pass the scheduler's final length down to ingestion? 5. **Arctic-only options** (`max_spec_factor`, `min_token_prob`) are ignored on V2 (documented). Warn as well? ## Follow-ups - Exclude filler slots from spec-decode metrics for GPU drafters (as #52097 does on V1 and its MRV2 branch does; see also #44056 and #50518). With adaptive verification, trimmed slots are still counted as drafted. - Index responses while they're still being generated. That may be why Arctic is ahead on the templated VLM workload. - CUDA-graph the propose path (@zip95297's bucketized draft graphs). - aarch64 benchmarks. ---

(Mandatory for agents, optional for humans). - [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR. - [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity. - [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI. - [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples. - [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.
**Not duplicating existing work:** the only other suffix decoding drafter PR is #52097 (`suffix_gpu` on V1), whose author is collaborating here; searches for "suffix decoding", "suffix_gpu" and "SuffixSpeculator" find no other MRV2 implementation. AI assistance (Claude) was used to investigate, prototype, write and test this change. cc @njhill @zip95297 @benchislett @TheEpicDolphin

title: [Perf] Support minimum KV splits configuration for TokenSpeed MLA decode
author: wzhao18
body:
## Overview

The TokenSpeed MLA decode kernel supports passing an optional flag `min_split_kv` to force a minimum number of KV splits, which can accelerate performance by up to 4x speedup under certain workloads, see https://github.com/lightseekorg/tokenspeed/pull/1693.

Expose the split floor through `AttentionConfig`:

```bash
--attention-config '{"tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv": 8}'
```

The default is `1`, preserving automatic scheduling. Values are validated in `[1, 256]`; the setting only applies to TokenSpeed MLA decode.

## Claims

- Configure the decode split floor per engine through the existing attention configuration API.
- Reserve workspace for the configured floor and pass `min_split_kv` directly to the decode kernel; `1` preserves automatic scheduling.

## Validation

Configuration-interface update (October 9, 2026):

- `pre-commit run --files vllm/config/attention.py vllm/envs.py vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/tokenspeed_mla.py tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py tests/v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py`: passed.
- `pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual --files <changed files>`: passed.
- Isolated source validation with `.venv/bin/python /private/tmp/pr60345_validate.py`: passed actual `AttentionConfig` default/boundary validation, invalid-value rejection, hash differentiation, and JSON/dotted argument parsing; all 12 existing CPU decode contract cases passed using the actual forward method, including direct forwarding of `min_split_kv` at both `1` and `8`. GPU backend imports were isolated for macOS.
- Added coverage to the existing CLI suite and updated decode tests for the workspace interface. Full pytest collection (`pytest tests/engine/test_arg_utils.py -k test_attention_config -q`) stopped at the unavailable `tblib` dependency in `tests/conftest.py`.
- CUDA/DCP kernel tests and model evaluations were not rerun on this macOS host. The following benchmark and accuracy results are prior validation of the same kernel setting, before the configuration-interface change.


### E2E agentic benchmark result
Kimi K3 nvfp4 2xDCP8 + 1xDEP16 c320: **1.64x e2e speedup**

```
baseline: Throughput per GPU: 11942 tok/s
decode with min_split=8: Throughput per GPU: 19678 tok/s
```

### Accuracy Eval
Tested Kimi K3 nvfp4 DCP8 + DEP16 GSM8k:
```

Num shots: 5
Max tokens: 256
Temperature: 0.0
Seed: 42
Accuracy: 0.935
Invalid responses: 0.001
Total latency: 45.735 s
Questions per second: 28.840

```

## Details

This updates the existing PR rather than opening a duplicate. `tokenspeed_mla_min_split_kv` follows the other backend-specific split controls in `AttentionConfig`. The backend reads it once during initialization for both kernel dispatch and workspace sizing, and passes `min_split_kv=self._min_split_kv` directly; the proposed env var is removed. The pinned `tokenspeed-mla==0.2.15` supports this keyword, including the default value `1`. Changes to `tests/test_config.py` were removed. Increasing the floor may increase workspace memory.

title: [Kernel] Integrate FA4 SM90 FP8 MMA for Gemma-4 full attention
author: katec846
body:
## Overview

Enable FP8 MMA in the SM90 FA4 full-attention kernel ([PR199](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/199)) for Gemma-4 while retaining FP8 KV-cache storage.

Gemma-4 uses head dimension 512 for full attention and 256 for sliding-window attention. This change compares FP8 MMA against the existing path that reads FP8 KV, dequantizes it, and performs FP16 MMA.

On H200, FP8 full attention uses FA4, while FP8 sliding-window attention continues to use FA3. FA4 FP8 sliding-window attention with head dimension 256 is currently unsupported.

## Claims

- Integrate the SM90 d512 FP8-MMA kernel while preserving native FP16/BF16 queries and supported FA3 sliding-window routing.
- Gate unsupported kernel combinations and normalize descale layouts.
- Allow FA4 full-attention layers to select splits automatically, removing the previous CUDA-graph cap of 32 for these layers; retain the cap for FA3.
- Report measured gains over the KV-dequantization baseline and the remaining regression against BF16 KV/MMA.

## Validation
The MMA labels describe the **full-attention path**. Both FP8-KV configurations use FA3 FP8 sliding-window attention; the BF16-KV reference uses FA4 BF16 sliding-window attention.

Serving setup:

- Gemma-4-31B-it-FP8 weights for all configurations.
- Four H200 GPUs on one node; TP4.
- Approximately 25K shared prefix plus 3K unique input tokens.
- 128 requests, 200 output tokens per request.
- MTP enabled with three speculative tokens.
- Prefix-cache reuse enabled.
- Concurrency 1–64; median of three rounds.

### Serving performance
The `8k-in-1k-out` benchmark of [`gemma_4_31b_it_h200`](https://github.com/vllm-project/perf-eval/blob/main/workloads/gemma_4_31b_it_h200.yaml) on one H200 at TP=1, with GPU clocks locked. Each number is the median of 3 repetitions, as perf-eval aggregates them; no request failed.

| | Output tok/s | Mean TPOT (ms) | Median ITL (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Before (`5d35ce3934` + FA `b273a02`) | 796.5 | 126.5 | 75.1 |
| This PR + vllm-project/flash-attention#199 | **831.1 (1.04x)** | **123.2** | **69.3** |
| Delta | +4.3% | -2.6% | -7.8% |

<details><summary>Reproduce</summary>

- Before is this PR's base, `5d35ce3934`, with FlashAttention at vllm-project/flash-attention#199's base, `b273a02`. After is this PR's head, `237043eee6`, with #199's head, `2648f1b`.
- Neither PR changes C++. Both runs use one editable build of `237043eee6` with `VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_SRC_DIR` set to the FlashAttention checkout, and differ only in Python sources.
- The model is a local copy of `RedHatAI/gemma-4-31B-it-FP8-dynamic`. Server and benchmark match perf-eval@5f4e445 (`lib/server.sh`, `lib/run_vllm_bench.sh`, `lib/aggregate_perf.py`).

```bash
VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip VLLM_ENGINE_READY_TIMEOUT_S=3600 \
vllm serve $MODEL --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --enable-auto-tool-choice

# 3 repetitions against the same server; median of each metric
vllm bench serve --backend openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --model $MODEL \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 8192 --random-output-len 1024 --ignore-eos \
  --num-prompts 512 --max-concurrency 128 --num-warmups 128
```

</details>

### Model evaluation
Accuracy scores are percentages. **87.19% for AIME 2025, 85.73% for GPQA Diamond (avg@16), and 86.86% for MMLU-Pro are measured in this PR; the two reference columns are reported baselines from [PR #48666](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48666).**

| Benchmark | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA ([PR199](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/199)) | FP8 KV + FP16 MMA (reference FA4) | 	BF16 TRITON |
|---|---|---|---|
| AIME 2025 (avg@64) | 87.19 | 86.88 | 87.29 |
| GPQA Diamond (avg@16) | 85.73* | 86.55 | 85.42 |
| MMLU-Pro | 86.86  | 86.64 | 86.44 |

\* Note that in a paird GPQA Diamond comparison using the same 198 questions and 16 seeds, FP8 MMA scored 85.73% versus 85.32% for the FP8 KV + FP16 MMA. The difference was +0.41 percentage points, with a paired question-bootstrap 95% interval of [−0.51, +1.36] points. Both runs had zero invalid or truncated answers. The table’s 86.55% reference is imported from PR [#48666](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48666) and is separate from this matched control.

### MTP speculative decoding

Mean acceptance length (**AL**), median of three rounds, from the same sweep as the serving-performance table above. All configurations use FP8 model weights, TP4 on four H200 GPUs, three speculative tokens, and prefix-cache reuse enabled. Each measurement completed **128/128 requests without errors**. AL includes the bonus token emitted per speculative step.

| Configuration | cc1 | cc2 | cc4 | cc8 | cc16 | cc32 | cc64 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | 2.9830 | 2.9932 | 3.0002 | 2.9640 | 2.9849 | 2.9860 | 2.9793 |
| FP8 KV + FP16 MMA | 2.9924 | 2.9691 | 3.0130 | 2.9995 | 2.9993 | 2.9857 | 2.9979 |
| BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | 3.0053 | 2.9823 | 2.9940 | 2.9935 | 2.9995 | 3.0002 | 2.9982 |

## Reproduction commands
The Hopper FP8 MMA path supports text-only workloads. The commands use --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' to disable Gemma-4’s bidirectional/mm-prefix attention. Multimodal Gemma-4 with FP8 KV uses Triton instead of this kernel. FP8 sliding-window layers use FA3, so do not force FA4 globally.

Serve and benchmark: 25K shared prefix, TP4, MTP3, cache reuse on

* FP8 KV + FP8 MMA (this PR):

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

* FP8 KV + FP16 MMA (PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) baseline kernel environment):
(The two FP8-KV serving commands are identical because MMA selection depends on the FlashAttention kernel source, not a CLI flag. For the control, we kept the same vLLM integration but replaced its vendored CuTe sources with the PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) dequantizing kernel, including the baseline safety fixes, then restarted the server. --kv-cache-dtype fp8 selects FP8 cache storage in both cases)

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

* BF16 KV + BF16 MMA:

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" \
  --max-num-seqs 64 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 --trust-remote-code --async-scheduling \
  --enable-prefix-caching --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --max-cudagraph-capture-size 256 --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \
  --compilation-config '{"use_inductor_graph_partition":1,"pass_config":{"eliminate_noops":true,"fuse_allreduce_rms":true}}' \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}' \
  --speculative-config "{\"model\":\"$ASSISTANT\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":3}"
```

These recorded runs left the FA version unset. The dequantized control uses the PR [#164](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/164) baseline kernel environment.

Benchmark:

```bash
aiperf profile \
  --model "$MODEL" --tokenizer "$MODEL" --tokenizer-trust-remote-code \
  --endpoint-type chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --streaming \
  --use-legacy-max-tokens --url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
  --input-file "$DATASET" \
  --extra-inputs max_tokens:200 --extra-inputs min_tokens:200 \
  --extra-inputs ignore_eos:true --extra-inputs skip_special_tokens:false \
  --random-seed 1234 --use-server-token-count \
  --concurrency 16 --request-count 128 --num-dataset-entries 128
```

Run at concurrency 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64; report the median of three rounds.

<details>
<summary>Evaluation commands</summary>

Evaluation server on four H200 GPUs. AIME and GPQA use `--max-num-seqs 16`; MMLU-Pro uses `32`. No MTP.

```bash
vllm serve "$MODEL" --served-model-name gemma \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --data-parallel-size 4 \
  --max-model-len 262144 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --kv-cache-memory-bytes 101716968203 --enforce-eager \
  --trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --attention-backend FLASH_ATTN \
  --attention-config.flash_attn_version=3 --block-size 64 \
  --kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune=false \
  --kernel-config.enable_cutedsl_warmup=false \
  --hf-overrides '{"text_config":{"use_bidirectional_attention":null}}'
```

**AIME 2025, avg@64**

Use `aime.yaml` with 64 samples per problem, temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, and the GPT-4.1 judge configuration. Export `INFERENCE_API_KEY`.

```bash
docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=100g \
  -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e INFERENCE_API_KEY \
  -v "$PWD/aime.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/aime-results:/results" \
  --entrypoint bash nvcr.io/nvidia/eval-factory/simple-evals:26.03 \
  -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml'
```

**GPQA Diamond, avg@16**

Use `gpqa.yaml` with all 198 questions, the `eval/aai/mcq-4choices` prompt, temperature 1.0, and top-p 0.95. Run seeds 0–15.

```bash
pids=()
for seed in $(seq 0 15); do
  docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=4g \
    -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e HF_TOKEN \
    -e NEMO_EVALUATOR_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=0 -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
    -v "$PWD/gpqa.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
    -v "$PWD/gpqa-results/seed-$seed:/results" \
    --entrypoint bash "$EVAL_IMAGE" \
    -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml "$@"' \
    -- --overrides "config.params.extra.args=++prompt_config=eval/aai/mcq-4choices ++inference.random_seed=$seed" &
  pids+=("$!")
done

status=0
for pid in "${pids[@]}"; do
  wait "$pid" || status=1
done
test "$status" -eq 0
```

**MMLU-Pro**

Restart the evaluation server with `--max-num-seqs 32`. Use `mmlu.yaml` with all 12,032 questions, one sample per question, the `eval/aai/mcq-10choices-boxed` prompt, temperature 1.0, and top-p 0.95.

```bash
mkdir -p mmlu-results
chmod 777 mmlu-results

docker run --rm --network host --shm-size=4g \
  -e DUMMY_API_KEY=dummy -e HF_TOKEN \
  -e NEMO_EVALUATOR_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=0 -e OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  -v "$PWD/mmlu.yaml:/config.yaml:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/mmlu-results:/results" \
  --entrypoint bash "$EVAL_IMAGE" \
  -lc 'runner=$(command -v nemo-evaluator || command -v eval-factory); exec "$runner" run_eval --run_config /config.yaml'
```

</details>

## Details

### Why FP8 is slower than BF16

Nsight shows that faster FP8 full attention does not necessarily produce faster end-to-end execution.

#### Sliding-window attention and KV-cache operations offset full-attention gains

The profiling setup uses 25K inputs, TP4, MTP enabled, prefix reuse enabled, and offered concurrency 64.

| Target-model kernel work | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | FP8 time reduction vs. BF16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | **6.681 ms** | 7.584 ms | **+11.9%** |
| Sliding-window attention | 5.482 ms | **4.206 ms** | −30.3% |
| KV-cache writes | 0.261 ms | **0.157 ms** | −66.2% |
| Attention preparation | 0.105 ms | 0 | N/A |
| Whole-cycle GPU span | 29.879 ms | **29.391 ms** | −1.7% |

Time reduction is `100 × (BF16 time − FP8 time) / BF16 time`, calculated from the displayed times. Positive values mean less time (faster); negative values mean more time (slower). 

Full attention is approximately **12% faster**, but sliding-window attention is approximately **30% slower**, with additional KV-write, preparation, and combine work.

KV-write overhead refers to the kernels that reshape and write newly generated keys and values into the paged cache, including the FP8 conversion/quantization path. Attention reads and prefix-cache reuse accounting are separate from this kernel category.

Reuse-off profiles show the same pattern.
The following comparison uses **cc16**, 25K inputs, TP4, MTP enabled, and prefix-cache reuse disabled. These matched pure-decode cycles process **16 active requests per target step**. Values are medians across four GPU ranks of each rank's per-cycle medians, with 69 matched cycles per rank for BF16 and 87 for FP8.

| Target-model kernel work | FP8 KV + FP8 MMA | BF16 KV + BF16 MMA | FP8 time reduction vs. BF16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | **1.9670 ms** | 2.4358 ms | **+19.2%** |
| Sliding-window attention | 1.9593 ms | **1.3867 ms** | −41.3% |
| KV-cache writes | 0.2551 ms | **0.1413 ms** | −80.5% |
| Attention preparation | 0.1098 ms | 0 | N/A |
| Whole-cycle GPU span | 14.6594 ms | **14.2903 ms** | −2.6% |

Full attention is faster, but SWA, KV-cache writes, and attention preparation/combine offset the gain. The whole-cycle GPU span is **2.6% longer** for FP8. This is a profiling comparison, not an unprofiled end-to-end throughput measurement.

title: [Bugfix][KV Offload][P2P] Report NIXL submission failures and escalate persistent faults to session teardown
author: liranschour
body:
## Overview

This PR fixes two P2P data-plane failures and adds a reconnect backoff. Each part is its own commit (the backoff plus a follow-up that counts faults in its log, then a commit addressing review), so they can be reviewed, or split, independently:

1. **Submission failures are reported to the fetching peer** (fixes #60204). A NIXL error raised while submitting a fetch's WRITE escaped to the session dispatcher, so the peer waited its full 30 s load timeout before recomputing.
2. **Persistent NIXL faults end the session** (fixes #60205 together with #60279). A peer with a stale NIXL registration but a healthy control plane failed every WRITE for the rest of the process. This also answers @snadampal's review question on this PR about recovering the peer instead of fast-failing forever.
3. **Reconnect backoff.** A peer that faults again right after each re-handshake backs off before the next reconnect, as the NixlConnector does for invalid peers.

#61500 independently traces the same root cause in NIXL 1.5.0 for the NixlConnector's pull path: after one `REMOTE_DISCONNECT`, the UCX endpoint stays `FAILED` until the remote agent is re-added. Its production numbers show the before/after effect.

Replaces #55553 (closed in favour of this, by @Etelis). Together with #60279 it covers #55181.

## Claims

**Commit 1 (transfer scope)**
- An error from `make_prepped_xfer` / `transfer` takes the existing fail-fast path. The round fails, the peer gets `TransferDoneMsg(success=False)`, the store job fails at once, and the created handle is released.
- `transfer()` returning `"ERR"` (how the bindings report a failed post) is a failed submission. Previously it was ignored and the handle parked inflight.
- `on_fetch` no longer finalizes a round a second time after a failed submission. That raised `KeyError` in the store-first and finish-before-fetch orderings.

**Commit 2 (escalation)**
- `NixlTransport` classifies each NIXL failure in one place:
  - `nixlRemoteDisconnectError` / `nixlNotFoundError` fault the peer at once.
  - A `check_xfer_state` that raises faults the peer at once (commit 5). NIXL's binding raises for every error status (only `SUCCESS` / `IN_PROG` are returned), so a raise is how a failed WRITE is reported, e.g. `nixlBackendError` for a UCX error.
  - Any other failure (a failed submission, or a transfer in state `"ERR"`) is a strike, and 3 consecutive strikes with no success between them fault the peer. Strikes from one `poll()` batch are applied after the batch is classified, so a `DONE` for the peer anywhere in it counts as the success between (commit 5).
  - Only `nixlRemoteDisconnectError` ends a transfer whose state check raised. Any other raise keeps it inflight, because its WRITE may still be landing (#59790 measured bytes landing while the handle raised `nixlNotFoundError`); the peer fault and the drain cap below bound it.
  - The fault is reported through a new `PollResult.peer_fault`.
- After a fault, no new WRITE goes to that peer. Once its inflight WRITEs drain (capped at 10 s), the session sends `DisconnectMsg`. The existing reap then tears down both sides, and the next request re-registers them.
- Every session death records a reason, and the manager's `peer X down (<reason>)` log reports it. Examples: `data plane: NIXL_ERR_REMOTE_DISCONNECT`, `protocol error: …`, `handshake timed out`, `lookup response timed out`, `control connection lost`.

**Commits 3–4 (reconnect backoff)**
- After reaping a session that ended on a data-plane fault, the faulting side records a per-peer backoff. The first fault reconnects at once. A repeat fault within 60 s of the previous wait expiring doubles the wait, from 1 s up to 60 s, as in the NixlConnector (#55471, #61500). Expiry is by time alone: no successful transfer is required, so a peer that is only idle for 60 s starts over at an immediate reconnect. Control-plane deaths don't back off.
- During the wait, outbound connects to the peer are skipped, so lookups fall back to local prefill. An inbound connect from the peer gets `DisconnectMsg` and is closed, so the peer falls back at once instead of waiting for its handshake deadline. There is no protocol change.
- The peer-down log carries a per-peer lifetime count of data-plane faults, e.g. `peer X down (data plane: …); data-plane fault #7; reconnect backoff 8s`. Unlike the backoff it never expires, so a peer that keeps faulting under traffic too sparse to escalate shows up as a rising count rather than as a series of unrelated faults.

## Validation

```
pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/ -q    # 308 passed (commit 1 alone: 281)
pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/ -q        # 554 passed, 12 skipped
pre-commit run --files <changed files>        # passed, incl. mypy
```

| Scenario | Before | After | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `transfer` / `make_prepped_xfer` raises, including when the release also fails | escapes to the dispatcher; no `TransferDoneMsg`; round stays alive | `None`, handle released, no inflight leak | `test_write_blocks_submission_exception_returns_failure` |
| `transfer()` returns `"ERR"` | handle parked inflight | `None`, handle released | `test_write_blocks_transfer_err_status_returns_failure` |
| Failed submit, store-first or finish-before-fetch | `KeyError` from double finalize | one finalize, one `TransferDoneMsg(False)` | `test_write_blocks_failure_finalizes_with_failure[*]`; fails without the `on_fetch` change |
| 3 failed WRITEs to a peer whose control plane is healthy (#60205) | every later WRITE fails, session never ends | peer faulted → drain → `DisconnectMsg` → reap | `TestNixlPeerFaults`, `TestPeerFaultEscalation` |
| `check_xfer_state` raises (`nixlBackendError`) while other WRITEs to the peer succeed | one strike, reset by the successes; transfer stays inflight for good: ~40 s consumer stall, pins and session held | peer faulted at once; transfer kept until it drains or the 10 s drain cap, then reaped | `test_raising_state_check_faults_the_peer_and_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_raise_faults_despite_a_success_in_the_batch` |
| `check_xfer_state` raises `nixlNotFoundError` | peer faulted; transfer kept, warning on every poll | peer faulted; transfer kept (not terminal, per #59790); warns once | `test_not_found_state_check_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_not_found_in_cancel_keeps_the_transfer`, `test_raising_state_check_warns_once` |
| strikes=2, one poll batch with `ERR` iterated before 3 `DONE`s | peer faulted, session torn down | strikes reset, no fault | `test_success_in_the_same_batch_prevents_the_fault`; fails on the previous code |
| Fault while WRITEs are inflight | — | new rounds fail fast; disconnect only after the drain or the 10 s cap | `test_fault_waits_for_inflight_then_disconnects`, `test_fault_disconnects_after_drain_deadline` |
| Peer faults again right after each re-handshake | reconnect, register and fail on every request | waits 0, 1, 2, 4 … 60 s; outbound skipped, inbound told to disconnect; resets 60 s after the last wait expires; the logged fault count keeps growing across the reset | `TestReconnectBackoff` |

**End to end on real NIXL** (two H200 pods, PDConnector + P2P tier, Llama-3.2-1B, NIXL 1.5.0, commit dc2d0b94fc). Happy path in both proxy modes: correct output and a 95–96 % external prefix-cache hit rate (240 of 254 prompt tokens pulled per request). A persistent fault was then forced with a test-only hook (not in this PR) that makes the prefiller's `transfer()` return `"ERR"` while a flag file exists:
- Every fetch failed fast: 20 consecutive requests finished in 1.6–2.3 s with correct output (recomputed locally), with no 30 s load timeout.
- Each 3 strikes ended the session: prefiller `peer D down (data plane: 3 consecutive transfer failures …); data-plane fault #1 … #6`, decoder `peer P down (peer disconnected)`; both sides re-registered on the next request.
- The backoff grew 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s; during the 8 s and 16 s waits the prefiller logged `rejecting inbound peer … (2.5s / 10.6s left)` and the decoder fell back at once.
- After the flag was cleared, hits returned (240/254) on the fresh session, with no crash, `KeyError` or segfault on either side.

**State-check faults, end to end** (same setup, commit a1cc819cb6). A second test-only hook makes the prefiller's `check_xfer_state` raise an exception named after the real binding class while a flag file exists. That is how NIXL 1.5.0 reports a failed WRITE: the binding raises for every error status.

| Injected fault | Faulted request | Prefiller log | After clearing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| every check raises `nixlBackendError` | 11.7–11.9 s, correct output (recomputed) | peer faulted on the first raise; `disconnecting once inflight transfers drain`; `peer D down (data plane: check_xfer_state raised nixlBackendError …)` exactly 10 s later; backoff 0, 1, 2 s over three faults | 240/254 hits |
| every check raises `nixlNotFoundError` | 11.6–11.8 s, correct output | peer faulted (`NIXL_ERR_NOT_FOUND`); the transfer stays inflight (not terminal, per #59790) until the 10 s drain cap, then teardown | 256/256 hits |
| one transfer keeps raising while all others succeed | 12.2 s for that request; the next two 1.8 s with 240/254 hits | one fault, teardown at the 10 s cap, reconnect 6 s later | 256/256 hits |

- The last row is the case the previous revision left unbounded: its single strike was reset by the other successes, so the transfer stayed inflight for good, holding its pins and session. It is now torn down within the 10 s drain cap. Each faulted request costs the cap plus normal latency, versus an expected ~40 s (load timeout plus abort-ack timeout) before; that before-number was not measured.
- One `check_xfer_state failed` warning per transfer, not one per poll.
- One EngineCore per pod throughout; no crash, `KeyError` or segfault. Happy path afterwards in PD mode with the hook removed: 95.9 % hit rate.

These exercise faults that leave both processes alive. A genuinely restarted peer still can't be tested here: restarting either P2P peer segfaults the survivor in NIXL `loadRemoteMD`, a pre-existing problem (see #60205).

## Details

**Root cause (commit 1).** `_submit_transfer` fails fast only when `write_blocks` *returns* `None`. `NixlTransport.write_blocks` caught nothing, so a NIXL error reached `P2PSession._on_message`, which only logs. The dispatcher's disconnect-after-5-errors guard doesn't fire either, because successful messages in between reset its counter.

**Root cause (commit 2).** Only control-plane signals can mark a peer dead: heartbeat, protocol error, handshake, registration, and lookup timeout (#56836). Data-plane failures were never an input. In #60205 the heartbeats and lookups stay healthy while NIXL's endpoints for the peer are stale.

**Flow after a persistent fault (prefiller P writes into decoder D):**
1. D sends `FetchMsg`. P's `write_blocks` fails, or `check_xfer_state` raises in `poll`. The round fails with `TransferDone(False)` and D recomputes.
2. After 3 strikes, or one decisive error, P's `poll(D)` returns `peer_fault`. P's server role stops submitting, so later fetches from D fail fast.
3. Once P's inflight WRITEs to D drain, P sends `DisconnectMsg` and marks the connection dead with reason `data plane: …`.
4. P's manager reaps the session: it fails its jobs and calls `remove_remote_peer(D)`. D receives `DisconnectMsg` and runs the same reap for P.
5. D's next request opens a new connection, `ConnectMsg` goes both ways, and both sides register fresh. The registration generation keeps a late async registration from reviving the old peer.

**Design choice: one death path.** A data-plane fault ends a peer the same way a control-plane fault does. The transport never re-registers a peer in place. The alternative was `remove_remote_peer` after N failures, inside the transport. That tears down only one side: the session still believes the peer is registered, and the peer keeps *our* stale registration. It also cannot work for a restarted peer. Reusing the reap means no new teardown code.

**Tradeoffs and limitations.**
- A `check_xfer_state` that raises with anything but `REMOTE_DISCONNECT` stays inflight, as #59790 established: it isn't provably terminal, and its WRITE may still be landing. It faults the peer at once, so the session's 10 s drain cap bounds how long it can last. The cost is that one failed state check tears down a peer that is otherwise working (a re-handshake, plus the backoff if it repeats). Treating `nixlBackendError` / `nixlCancelledError` as terminal (the UCX request finished with an error) would avoid the drain wait, but needs evidence that NIXL's UCX backend reports a handle's error only once all of its requests are done; left for a follow-up.
- The disconnect waits for inflight WRITEs because D frees their destination blocks on `DisconnectMsg`. The 10 s cap trades that guarantee for not hanging on a stuck transfer, the same exposure a heartbeat death has today.
- The thresholds (3 strikes, 10 s drain, 1→60 s backoff) are conservative constants, not measured values. The backoff uses the NixlConnector's numbers.
- The backoff forgets a peer by time, not by a successful transfer, matching the NixlConnector. Under sparse traffic a persistently broken peer therefore cycles at a 0 s backoff (3 fast-failing requests that recompute locally, plus one re-registration per cycle); the fault count in the log makes that visible. Requiring a success before forgetting would close the gap but needs a transport→manager success signal, and is better done for both connectors together.
- Only the faulting side knows about the backoff. During the wait, the other peer still tries to connect on each new request and is turned away within one round trip; concurrent requests share the pending attempt. A retry-after hint in `DisconnectMsg` would remove that, at the cost of a protocol change.

**Relation to other PRs.**
- #59790 (merged) provides the sibling drain before `TransferDone(False)`; this PR builds on it.
- #60279 (narrowed to `remove_remote_peer` teardown robustness) is complementary. Expect a one-line conflict in `remove_remote_peer` for whichever lands second.
- #61500 (NixlConnector, pull mode) releases a peer after a failed read, with the same backoff. It touches no shared code. That connector's teardown is one-sided because only the decoder holds the remote registration; P2P registers both ways, so here both sides tear down.
- #49632 marks any `check_xfer_state` raise as failed and releases the handle, which can free a handle whose WRITE is still landing. Here such a transfer stays inflight and is bounded by the escalation instead.

**Changes since the previous revision.**
- Rebased onto main, which now includes #59790, #56836 and #58168.
- Dropped the `try/except` around `write_blocks` in `_submit_transfer`, and its test. The contract, now documented in `data/base.py`, is that transports don't raise for NIXL errors.
- Added commits 2–5. Commit 4 adds the per-peer fault count to the peer-down log and corrects the description of when the backoff resets (time since the last wait expired, not time healthy); behaviour is unchanged. Commit 5 addresses review of `poll()`: strikes per batch, and any raising state check faults the peer (`NOT_FOUND` is deliberately not terminal; see the review thread).
- About 330 source lines are added, comments and docstrings included: roughly 30 in commit 1, 190 in commit 2, 60 in commit 3, 20 in commit 4 and 30 in commit 5. Each commit stands alone, so the PR can be split along those lines if reviewers prefer.
