title: [Bugfix] Fix int32 token offset overflows in Qwen3.5 attention and GDN prefill kernels
author: simon-veitner-redhat
body:
_Requested by **Simon**_ ## Overview Fixes #63759. Several Triton kernels on the Qwen3.5 prefill path multiply an int32 token index by a row stride before adding it to a pointer. Triton passes integer arguments below 2^31 as int32, and `tl.program_id`, `tl.arange` and the int32 `query_start_loc` are int32 too, so the offset wraps once `token * stride >= 2^31`. The result is wrong outputs or an illegal memory access. This PR computes those offsets in int64, one commit per kernel, each with a regression test. | Kernel | Triggers when (Qwen3.5-9B unless noted) | Fix | |---|---|---| | `_fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope_gate_kernel` (`fused_qk_norm_rope.py`) | token index >= 209,716 (qkv row stride 10,240), i.e. a 209,717-token step; hit in the startup profile run | `tl.program_id(0).to(tl.int64)` | | `store_cache_checkpoints_kernel` (`mamba/checkpoint.py`) | token index >= 174,763 (qkvz stride 12,288); real prefills with prefix caching only | int64 `token_idx` before `* x_stride_0` | | `_fused_post_conv_kernel` (`fused_gdn_prefill_post_conv.py`) | token index >= 262,144 (conv row stride 8,192) | int64 per-block base offset, int32 in-block offsets | | `chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_kernel_h_blockdim64` (`chunk_delta_h.py`), spotted by reviewer Roberto (`LopezCastroRoberto`) | H=64: 2+ sequences with a later one starting at token >= 131,072 | int64 before `* V * K` (as `chunk_o.py`), also h0/ht | | `solve_tril` merge kernels (`solve_tril.py`) | H=64: a sequence with rows past 524,288, or one starting at >= 524,288 | int64 base offset and row index (16/32/64 kernels) | | `layer_norm_fwd_kernel` for `RMSNormGated` (`layernorm_guard.py`) | H=64: 262,145 tokens (`num_tokens * H * 128 >= 2^31`), when the `rms_norm_gated` custom op is enabled, e.g. `--enforce-eager` | int64 first row of each block | For the last three, thresholds double at H=32. The rest of the path (`causal_conv1d`, `layernorm_gated`, `gather_initial_states`, `scatter_states`, Mamba2 `ssd_checkpoint`, FlashInfer GDN prefill) already uses int64 offsets. The KDA and Qwen4Exp PLE exporters share the fixed checkpoint kernel. Related: #43166 (closed) fixed the same overflow in the CUDA `fused_qk_norm_rope` kernel; #51406 (open) enables the first kernel on ROCm, so ROCm gets the bug and this fix. ## Claims - On main, `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B --max-num-batched-tokens 209717` (or 263,168) fails in the startup profile run with an illegal memory access in `_fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope_gate_kernel`. With this PR it starts and serves correctly. - With prefix caching, one prefill step can fill the budget. At 263,168, a 258,798-token prompt and a 262,784-token two-prompt batch serve correctly; without the checkpoint and post-conv commits they crash in those kernels. - Each kernel matches its previous output below its threshold and the reference above it. - Perf: about +1% on the gate kernel (141.2 vs 139.7 us at 8,192 tokens), +2.2% on post-conv, 0.2 us on the checkpoint export, and 0 to 3% on the follow-ups (`chunk_delta_h` 0% / -3.0%, `solve_tril` +1.1%, `rmsnorm_gated` +2.4 to +3.1%). ## Validation 1x B200, torch 2.14.0+cu132, Triton 3.8.0, FlashInfer 0.7.2.post1, main `ffcabb8c7a`, `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` at `c202236235`. "Base" is main plus only the new tests. ```bash pytest -v tests/kernels/test_fused_qk_norm_rope_gate.py -k int64_row_offset pytest -v tests/kernels/mamba/test_checkpoint_exporter.py -k int64_token_offset pytest -v tests/kernels/fla/test_fused_gdn_post_conv.py -k int64_token_offset pytest -v tests/kernels/fla/test_chunk_int64_offsets.py pytest -v tests/kernels/fla/test_fla_layernorm_guard.py -k int64_row_offset ``` - Every new test fails on base (77.1% / 93.4% of q mismatched for the gate and post-conv kernels, illegal memory access for the other four) and passes with this PR. Existing tests in these files, `tests/kernels/fla`, `test_gdn_prefill_flashinfer.py` and `test_gdn_output_projection.py` pass. - Server (`--max-num-batched-tokens` 209,717 and 263,168, prefix caching on, compiled and eager): base fails in the profile run; this PR finds needles near the start and end of a 196,883 / 258,798-token prompt, answers both prompts of the 262,784-token batch, scores gsm 8/8, and matches base outputs at the default budget of 16,384. - Latency: kernels timed side by side with `triton.testing.do_bench_cudagraph` (follow-ups with `do_bench`), median of alternating rounds; a base-vs-base control gave 1.000 and outputs are bitwise equal to base. ## Details - Tests run each kernel just past its boundary on a realistic layout (packed qkv/qkvz buffers, contiguous conv output) and compare those rows with a reference. They need about 4 to 21 GB, skip when free device memory is short, and take a few seconds each. The gate test's CI step did not list `fused_qk_norm_rope.py` in `source_file_dependencies`, so this PR adds it there and to the AMD mirror; the other tests run in steps that already depend on their kernels. - Post-conv: an int64 per-token offset vector is a one-line change but costs 4.4% instead of 2.2%, so the PR uses an int64 base pointer. For `rmsnorm_gated` and `solve_tril` both approaches timed the same, so the simpler diff is kept. - Not fixed here: at these budgets Qwen3.5-9B needs a lower `--gpu-memory-utilization` than 0.92, with or without this PR (FlashInfer autotune and compiled-graph OOMs). The runs above used 0.88 at 209,717 and 0.84 at 263,168. ---

title: [KV Offload][P2P] Fail faster: per-mode load timeout, shorter abort-ack and lookup timeouts
author: liranschour
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Part of #63602: the P2P KV offload tier fails faster on a stuck peer. Symmetric-P2P loads time out after 10s instead of 30s, PD loads keep 30s, the abort-ack timeout drops from 10s to 5s, and the lookup no-progress timeout drops from 30s to 8s.

## Claims

- A stuck symmetric-P2P fetch is surfaced as failed (and recomputed locally) after ~15s (10s load + 5s abort-ack) instead of ~40s.
- A stuck PD fetch fails after ~35s (30s load + 5s abort-ack) instead of ~40s; the PD load timeout itself is unchanged.
- An unanswered symmetric-P2P lookup expires the session after 8s without progress instead of 30s.

## Validation

- `pytest tests/v1/kv_offload/tiering/p2p/`: 325 passed.
- New `test_load_timeout_depends_on_mode`: a probed (P2P) load and an unprobed (PD) load are both backdated past the P2P timeout; only the P2P one aborts.

**E2E, two pods (1×H200 each, `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B`, `OffloadingConnector` + `TieringOffloadingSpec` with a `p2p` secondary tier, `p2p_connector_proxy.py`).** Each fault was injected with a temporary pod-only hook (not part of this PR) that drops one inbound message type on the producer while the ZMQ session stays healthy. Each case is one request with a fresh, unique ~600-token prompt, `max_tokens=16`, `temperature=0`; latency is curl `time_total` on the pod.

| Case | Dropped on producer | Path | Request latency | Decoder log |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | – | PD via proxy / P2P `remote_kv_source` | 1.80 s / 1.75 s (first request, cold) | – |
| P2P load timeout | `fetch` | P2P | **10.12 s** | `timed out, sending abort` → failure after abort, local recompute |
| PD load timeout | `fetch` | PD | **30.13 s** | same, at 30 s (unchanged) |
| Abort-ack timeout | `fetch` + `abort_fetch` | P2P | **15.11 s** (10 + 5) | `abort_ack timed out` 5 s after the abort |
| Lookup timeout | `lookup` | P2P | **8.11 s** | `lookup response timed out ... after 8.0s without progress`, peer down |
| Recovery | – | P2P / PD | 0.18 s / 0.13 s | KV pulled again, ~0.8 prompt tok/s computed locally |

- Every faulted request still returned the same greedy text as the baseline (it fell back to local prefill); there were no tracebacks, engine deaths or segfaults on either pod.
- Deploy sanity on the branch: French-Revolution prompt (254 tokens) gives coherent text, the counting prompt continues with `30`, and the decoder reports an external prefix cache hit rate of 96%.

## Details

- **Per-mode load timeout.** `_InboundLoadState` gets a `timeout_s` fixed at `request_blocks` time: `_P2P_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S` (10s) when the id ran the lookup phase (`st.probed`), otherwise `_PD_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S` (30s). A symmetric fetch only goes out for keys the peer has already confirmed it holds, so a fetch that has not landed after 10s is stuck. A PD prefiller may still be computing the blocks when the fetch arrives, so PD keeps room for a full prefill.
- **Abort-ack 5s** applies to both modes. Once we have sent `AbortFetchMsg`, waiting longer for the ack does not depend on whether the blocks needed computing.
- **Lookup 8s** stays above the producer's `_LOOKUP_PENDING_TIMEOUT_S` (5s), so a producer holding a `HIT_PENDING` key answers MISS before the consumer gives up.
- `_REAPED_ID_RETENTION_S` (60s) still exceeds the longest load timeout (30s).
- Tradeoff: on a slow but healthy data plane (e.g. very large symmetric fetches over degraded NICs), a fetch that genuinely needs >10s now aborts and falls back to local recompute. The timeouts remain module constants; they are not made configurable here.

title: [Perf] Drop BasevLLMParameter's Python `__torch_function__`
author: NickLucche
body: ## Overview `BasevLLMParameter` overrides `__torch_function__` with a Python classmethod. The override only forwards to `Parameter`'s disabled implementation. Since #62326, quantized weights and scales stay `BasevLLMParameter` subclasses after `process_weights_after_loading`. As a result, every eager op that takes one of them goes through Python `handle_torch_function`. This PR removes the override. The subclasses then inherit `torch._C._disabled_torch_function_impl` from `Parameter`, which torch short-circuits in C++. ## Claims - Fixes a host-side regression from #62326 on steps that run outside full CUDA graphs: prefill and mixed prefill+decode steps. - GLM-5.2-FP8, TP4 on one GB300 node, same-node A/B against main on 3 nodes: - c1 TTFT for 1024-token prompts drops from 220.4 to 207.0 ms (-6.1%); - worker `execute_model` host time drops 8.7 ms per prefill step (-4.5%) and 11.2 ms per mixed step (-4.4%); - TPOT is unchanged: pure decode replays full CUDA graphs and dispatches no ops. - No behavior change: - #62326's guarantees are untouched: the same parameter objects, classes, loader attributes and `data_ptr`; - op results were plain tensors before (`super().__torch_function__` is the disabled implementation) and still are; - greedy outputs are identical and GSM8K is within run-to-run noise. ## Validation ### Serving: GLM-5.2-FP8 (`zai-org/GLM-5.2-FP8`) Setup: - TP4, one GB300 node, MRV2, default torch.compile and CUDA graphs; - `--attention-backend FLASHMLA_SPARSE --kv-cache-dtype fp8_ds_mla`, `VLLM_FLASHINFER_ALLREDUCE_BACKEND=mnnvl`; - `--max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 64 --no-enable-prefix-caching`; - `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --ignore-eos`. At c8/c32, new prompts arrive while others decode, so those runs mix prefill and decode steps. Method: - Each Slurm job runs on one node. It first starts a throwaway server: the first server on a node is 10-15 ms slower at c1 TTFT, so it is excluded. - It then interleaves `main`, `this PR` and two other variants not covered here, twice each. - Values are the mean of each variant's 2 runs on that node; the delta is against `main` on the same node. Median TTFT (ms): | node / job | workload | main | this PR | delta | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | c1, 24 prompts | 223.5 | **204.7** | **-18.7** | | 2 | c1 | 220.5 | **210.5** | **-10.1** | | 3 | c1 | 217.3 | **205.7** | **-11.6** | | **mean** | **c1** | **220.4** | **207.0** | **-13.5 (-6.1%)** | | mean | c8, 160 prompts | 465.7 | **453.1** | **-12.6** | | mean | c32, 320 prompts | 810.2 | **762.1** | **-48 (noisy)** | Median TPOT (ms): c1 9.70 vs 9.69, c8 14.30 vs 14.27, c32 25.80 vs 25.77. Host time of the worker's `GPUModelRunner.execute_model`: a `perf_counter` wrapper, with steps split by kind. Values are the p50 per rank, averaged over the 4 ranks, from the same runs (c1 + c8 workloads): | node / job | prefill-only step: main | this PR | delta | mixed step: main | this PR | delta | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 189.8 | **181.0** | **-8.8** | 254.5 | **239.3** | **-15.2** | | 2 | 192.5 | **184.2** | **-8.3** | 257.4 | **248.6** | **-8.8** | | 3 | 191.7 | **182.8** | **-8.9** | 254.0 | **244.5** | **-9.6** | An earlier stack-sampling profile of the prefill step put about 14% of its host time in `parameter.py:__torch_function__`. It was called from the FP8 linear apply, the DeepGEMM / per-token-group quant wrappers and the FlashInfer TRT-LLM FP8 MoE calls. Dense BF16 model (Qwen3-0.6B, TP1): no measurable change (c1 TTFT 22.4 vs 22.3/23.3 ms, c32 within noise). Its unquantized weights were already `ModelWeightParameter` before #62326, and its steps are less host-bound. ### Correctness - Greedy, `temperature=0`, 34 fixed prompts with 128 tokens each at c1: outputs are byte-identical to `main` in 3/3 runs on 3 nodes. - GSM8K (`tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py`, 1319 questions, 5-shot, completions, max concurrency 64): | | runs | accuracy | |---|---|---| | main | 5 | 95.0, 94.2, 94.2, 94.9, 94.8 | | this PR | 3 | 94.5, 94.1, 94.2 | The kernels and their inputs are unchanged, so the spread is batch-composition noise at concurrency 64. Main alone spans 94.2 to 95.0. - The serving runs use torch.compile (Dynamo traces modules with these parameters) and CUDA graphs. They start and produce identical outputs without the override. ### Tests ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/test_utils.py \ tests/quantization/test_keep_param_objects.py \ tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py -k "not test_reload_weights" .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/model_executor/model_loader/test_reload.py \ -k "test_reload_weights and (FP8_BLOCK or FP8_DYNAMIC)" pre-commit run --files vllm/model_executor/parameter.py tests/model_executor/test_utils.py ``` Results on GB300 (this PR vs `main`, same commands): | test | this PR | main | |---|---|---| | `tests/model_executor/test_utils.py` | 14 passed (incl. the new test) | 13 passed | | `tests/quantization/test_keep_param_objects.py` | 10 passed | 10 passed | | `test_reload.py -k "not test_reload_weights"` | 70 passed, 2 xpassed, 2 failed | same 2 failures | | `test_reload_weights` FP8_BLOCK / FP8_DYNAMIC (TP1, TP2) | 4 passed, 4 skipped | 4 passed, 4 skipped | | `pre-commit` | all hooks pass | | Both `test_reload.py` failures also fail on `main` and are unrelated: - `test_kv_scale_reload`: perplexity 6575.09 after reload, identical on `main`. - `test_online_quantize_reload[...Qwen3-0.6B...fp8_per_tensor-1]`: when it runs after that failure in the same session, the forked engine core hits `CUDA error: initialization error`. This also happens on `main`. The test passes when run alone on both trees. New test `test_kept_param_ops_skip_python_torch_function`: - it checks that a param kept by `replace_parameter` keeps its class; - that `torch.overrides.has_torch_function` is false for it, so eager ops dispatch in C++; - and that op results are still plain tensors. ## Details **Root cause.** - #23036 added the override, together with a torch-2.7-only `traceable_tensor_subclasses` Dynamo workaround (`_torch27_patch_tensor_subclasses`). - #33209 removed the workaround when torch < 2.8 support was dropped, but left the override. - The override does nothing at runtime: it calls `super().__torch_function__`, i.e. `Parameter`'s `_disabled_torch_function_impl`. Its presence still makes torch treat these parameters as having a Python torch function. Every op, and every Python-level `Tensor` method or property access on them, then goes through `handle_torch_function` and the classmethod. - Before #62326, most quantization methods re-registered plain `Parameter`s in `process_weights_after_loading`, so FP8/FP4 weights and scales did not pay this cost. - #62326 keeps the original objects so that reload and RL refit keep their loader metadata. The quantized weights and scales of every linear and MoE layer now pay this cost on every eager op. **Fix.** Delete the override. `BasevLLMParameter` then behaves like `torch.nn.Parameter`: - `__torch_function__` is the disabled implementation; - `isinstance`, class, attributes and object identity are unchanged; - op results stay plain tensors. This keeps everything #62326 relies on. A global monkey-patch or unwrapping params after loading would undo #62326's goal. **Scope.** - Only steps that dispatch ops eagerly benefit: prefill, mixed and piecewise steps. Full-CUDA-graph decode is unchanged. - The gain grows with the number of quantized layers and ops per step. ## Why this is not a duplicate - `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open` searches found no PR that touches `BasevLLMParameter.__torch_function__` or the overhead from #62326. Search terms: `__torch_function__`, `BasevLLMParameter`, `replace_parameter`, `62326`, `torch_function overhead`, `handle_torch_function`, `ModelWeightParameter overhead`. - #62407 (part 3 of the #62326 series, open) changes which params stay registered and does not touch `parameter.py`. This PR is independent of it and helps it as well. - The only earlier change to the override is #25613, reverted by #25681. It returned `NotImplemented` on torch < 2.8 for a Dynamo bug and did not remove the dispatch. - No upstream issue covers it. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate the regression, write the change and its test, and run the benchmarks and evals above. The submitter reviewed every changed line and the measurements. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

title: [Bugfix][Attention] FlashInfer sparse MLA: launch at most 65535 tokens per trtllm-gen call
author: suiyoubi
body:
## Overview The FlashInfer sparse MLA kernel silently skips attention for every token of a forward pass with more than 65535 tokens (e.g. any full prefill step at `--max-num-batched-tokens 65536`), returning uninitialized memory. This PR launches it in chunks of at most 65535 tokens that write into one preallocated output. Root cause on the FlashInfer side: flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3125. ## Claims - Fixes the silent skip for `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE` (**DeepSeek-V3.2 / GLM-5 / GLM-5.3 DSA layers**) and for the prefill of `FLASHATTN_MLA_SPARSE` (FA4), which delegates prefill to the same kernel. Covers prefill, decode, mixed steps and DCP. - Steps with <= 65535 tokens issue the same single launch as before (decode and CUDA graphs are unchanged). - No extra memory: chunks write into slices of one output (and LSE) buffer. - The DCP softmax-stats workspace is sized for one launch (<= 65535 tokens) instead of `max_num_batched_tokens`. ## Validation | Check | Base (main) | This PR | |---|---|---| | New `test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_attends_tokens_past_grid_limit` (69635 tokens, rope and no-rope), SM10x | 2/2 fail (NaN past token 65535) | 2/2 pass | | 40-shot GSM8K, GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4, DEP2, `--max-num-batched-tokens 65536`, 2 greedy runs | ~3 points below the unaffected baseline; server log full of `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE ... fmhaKernels.cuh` | at the unaffected baseline (within run-to-run spread); no launch errors | | 4 TP1 prefill workers at `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` + DEP4 decode, 8K/1K sa-bench, C512/C1024 | prefill OOM with an earlier chunk + `torch.cat` version of this fix | no OOM; throughput at parity with that version, median TTFT slightly lower | | RULER-64K (NeMo-Skills, 13 tasks x 100), same server shape, `--max-model-len 131072` | overall ~35 points below this PR; NIAH / variable tracking 11-82 points lower per task; ~7.7K `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE ... fmhaKernels.cuh` lines while serving | NIAH (8 tasks) and variable tracking all at or near 100%; no launch errors | Run on SM107 GPUs; end-to-end results are relative. - The 40-shot GSM8K prompts are 7-8K tokens, above the DSA top-k, so sparse MLA runs. 5-shot GSM8K does not show the bug, because short prompts take the dense MHA prefill path. - The DCP/LSE path (one launch per chunk with an `lse` slice) was also checked against a PyTorch reference at 69635 tokens. That ran outside the committed tests, because DCP needs more than one GPU. ```bash pytest tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py tests/v1/attention/test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_workspace.py \ -k "past_grid_limit or model_scale or workspace or dcp_size" ```
Before / after test output Base (main 51d2a8559): ``` E Mismatched elements: 6884 / 8192 (84.0%) E Greatest absolute difference: nan at index (0, 52) (up to 0.02 allowed) E Mismatched elements: 6850 / 8192 (83.6%) E Greatest absolute difference: nan at index (0, 282) (up to 0.02 allowed) FAILED tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py::test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_attends_tokens_past_grid_limit[128-64-128] FAILED tests/v1/attention/test_sparse_mla_backends.py::test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_attends_tokens_past_grid_limit[256-0-256] FAILED tests/v1/attention/test_flashinfer_sparse_mla_workspace.py::test_dcp_size_is_capped_at_one_launch 3 failed, 20 passed, 1883 deselected, 18 warnings in 52.12s ``` This PR: ``` 23 passed, 1883 deselected, 18 warnings in 52.08s ```
Why not FlashInfer's cum_seq_lens_q (#3131 / #3238)? Measured at kernel level (FP8 KV, top-k 2048, 16 and 64 heads, 1 to 131072 tokens): - trtllm-gen cannot return the LSE with `cum_seq_lens_q`, and DCP needs it. - `seq_lens` becomes per request. The static-sparse (rope) path uses it as each token's active top-k length, so rows shorter than the top-k width attend the `-1` padding and give wrong outputs. - Grouping tokens by real request launches `num_reqs x max_q_len` CTAs: one long prefill plus 511 decodes ran ~9.5x slower. - Packing tokens into uniform pseudo-requests (no-rope, no LSE) is bit-exact but no faster (within 1%): the MLA generation kernels still run one CTA per token. - For comparison, chunked launches cost the same per token as one launch. Chunk + `torch.cat` is 2-11% slower, and its extra output copy (8 GiB at 65536 tokens with 64 heads) is outside vLLM's memory profile.
## Details **Root cause.** `FlashInferMLASparseImpl._forward_mqa_kernel` passes every query token to `trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache_mla` as its own request (`q.unsqueeze(1)`, `topk_indices.unsqueeze(1)`), and trtllm-gen maps requests to `gridDim.z`, whose CUDA limit is 65535. A larger launch makes `cuLaunchKernelEx` return `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`, which FlashInfer only prints to stderr. Found with a profile that showed zero sparse-MLA kernels in every 65536-token step. **Fix.** Allocate `out` (and `lse`) once and call the kernel on row slices of at most 65535 tokens, passing the matching `out` / `lse` slices. FlashInfer accepts caller-owned output, so no copy is needed. The trtllm-gen softmax-stats slab is carved per launch, so the DCP workspace only needs to cover one launch. **Limitations.** Steps with more than 65535 tokens issue one extra kernel launch per additional chunk. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to investigate and write this change. The submitter reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above. Not a duplicate: no open vLLM PR touches this backend's 65535-token limit (searched "flashinfer_mla_sparse", "65535 flashinfer", "cum_seq_lens_q"). ---

title: [Spec Decode] DSpark: sliding-window MLA draft layers
author: NickLucche
body:
## Overview Extends DSpark speculative decoding with sliding-window MLA draft layers. Draft layers with an attention window now decode through the Triton MLA backend's windowed path, get a dedicated KV cache group, and can be driven by recurrent Markov heads whose state carries across the positions of one proposal. Not a duplicate: I searched open PRs for DSpark / DCP / sliding-window work. Adjacent but distinct: #62410 (GLM-5.3 MLA DSpark drafts, model-specific enablement), #61464 (DBO with spec + DCP), #56694 / #62958 (Markov walk perf kernels). None cover windowed MLA draft layers, their KV cache layout, or the recurrent-head speculator hook. ## Claims - Triton MLA backend: sliding-window decode in both kernel stages. - Non-causal multi-token decode flag on the MLA KV cache spec and a separate KV cache group for windowed MLA draft layers. - Speculator hook for recurrent Markov heads that carry a state across the positions of one proposal. ## Validation - `python -m pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_decode_attention.py tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_planning.py -v` — both extended by this change and wired into CI on CUDA. - The windowed decode path was exercised end-to-end during bring-up of the spec-decode stack this change originates from. ## Details - The windowed decode is implemented inside the Triton MLA kernel stages so a windowed draft layer costs no extra launches relative to the full-attention draft path. - The non-causal multi-token flag distinguishes speculative draft rows from target rows inside the same group, which is what lets windowed drafts share the MLA cache infrastructure instead of growing a parallel layout. - The recurrent Markov-head hook keeps proposal state out of the per-position interfaces: the speculator owns the state and re-enters the head per position.

title: [Perf][HiSparse] Prefetch speculative groups with bounded copy workers
author: zhenwenqi2024
body:
## Overview

Extend HiSparse's existing shared-index group prefetch to multi-token speculative verification, including MTP, and bound the CUDA compact-gather launch as verification expands the batch.

Related: #60072. This is separate from the platform-interface PR #62592. It composes with #60103; slot-invalidation fusion, padding-mask fusion and the all-resident resolver optimization remain in that PR and are not duplicated here.

## Claims

- Eligible pure-decode verification batches can stage follower layers' historical KV on the existing group copy stream, with a separate completion event for each layer.
- Prefetch eligibility is separate from the single-token resident-write and host-mirror policy. Mixed/prefill batches keep per-layer staging.
- Compact gather launches at most 64 thread blocks. Additional rows are processed by the existing workers; batches of at most 64 rows retain their column parallelism.
- Add native payload/graph regression cases and a reusable gather benchmark. Scoped H200 serving and profiling results are reported below; no model accuracy or acceptance improvement is claimed.

## Performance results

Measured on 8 x NVIDIA H200 with GLM-5.2-FP8, TP=8, MTP=3 and the V2 model runner. Both arms were rebuilt from frozen main `a1cfd2c1b584c4ac197db9cc9ac84a6d973d39df`; the candidate adds this PR's changes at `bb84fb5e976f941e9e2b8586f79930be64408a74`. Source/native-library pairs were checked. The table uses the original PR implementation.

Runtime: Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, driver 595.58.03; EvalScope 1.14.1 for unprofiled serving measurements.

- Workload: 65,536 input tokens, forced 4,096 or 8,192 output tokens, concurrency 32, 32 requests per case; temperature 0, ignore EOS. Frozen GSM8K-derived long prompts are a synthetic performance workload, not a natural long-reasoning accuracy evaluation. Request bodies match between arms and actual input/output lengths were audited.
- Both arms: `kv_cache_dtype=fp8_ds_mla`, 32 GiB GPU KV cache per rank, 128 GiB shared host pool, `max_model_len=73728`, `max_num_batched_tokens=8192`, `max_num_seqs=32`, prefix caching disabled, seed 42; FLASHMLA_SPARSE / DEEPSEEK_V32_INDEXER.
- Each initial process ran a separate C32 64K/128 warmup (excluded), then 4K output, 8K output and an 8K repeat. A separate PR process restart repeated warmup -> 4K -> 8K. The restart rows reuse the original main process's corresponding first measurements; they are not additional independent main restarts.
- TPOT is the mean of per-request `(latency - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1)`, not inter-chunk latency. TTFT includes queueing.

All arrows below are **main -> PR**. Throughput is aggregate output tokens/s; TPOT and TTFT are client means.

| Output / run | Output tok/s | Change | TPOT (ms/token) | Change | TTFT (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4K, first | 487.7481 -> 494.6458 | +1.41% | 38.14 -> 37.08 | -2.78% | 107.739 -> 107.676 |
| 8K, first | 780.2473 -> 802.4179 | +2.84% | 26.80 -> 25.35 | -5.41% | 107.713 -> 107.733 |
| 8K, same-process repeat | 782.5196 -> 800.9244 | +2.35% | 26.59 -> 25.50 | -4.10% | 107.541 -> 107.610 |
| 4K, PR restart | 487.7481 -> 495.4115 | +1.57% | 38.14 -> 36.87 | -3.33% | 107.739 -> 107.992 |
| 8K, PR restart | 780.2473 -> 803.6892 | +3.00% | 26.80 -> 25.43 | -5.11% | 107.713 -> 107.901 |

The 32 GiB series completed main 96/96, first PR process 96/96 and restarted PR process 64/64 measured requests, with **zero preemptions in both arms**. Earlier 24 GiB runs had capacity-driven preemptions; increasing capacity is a separate tuning change and its gain is not attributed to this PR.

These observations support a modest benefit for this workload: 8K-output throughput +2.35% to +3.00%, mean TPOT -4.10% to -5.41%, with essentially unchanged mean TTFT. They are not confidence intervals or a general performance guarantee. Host NUMA placement was not pinned; generated continuations and MTP acceptance can differ across processes. No accuracy or acceptance-rate improvement is claimed.

### Profiling

A separate Torch-profiler diagnostic run at 24 GiB GPU KV capacity selected pure-decode steps with 26 requests / 104 verification rows: 24 main steps versus 23 PR steps, excluding one mixed-prefill PR step. Values are medians across rank-level medians, not end-to-end serving results.

| Diagnostic metric | Main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPU pure-decode envelope per step | 63.0585 ms | 54.8721 ms |
| Total gather duration per step | 14.9948 ms | 16.3471 ms |
| Exposed / non-overlapped gather duration | 14.9948 ms | 5.3232 ms |
| Gather overlap fraction | 0% | 67.44% |

The trace supports the intended copy/compute overlap: exposed gather time falls about 64.5%, despite total gather duration increasing. The selected GPU interval is about 13.0% shorter; **this is not a 13% end-to-end speedup**. Tokens and cache hit/miss state may differ. HiSparse traffic counters publish every 2,000 worker calls, so their per-case deltas are not used to attribute transfer-volume changes.

#### Trace timeline: before and after

![HiSparse main versus PR: actual GPU trace timelines and 20–24 ms zoom](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhenwenqi2024/vllm/974d68aa2b97c604003a42163f3257d926f7c606/pr63801/overlap-before-after.png)

The figure is rendered from original GPU event timestamps and durations, grouping events into per-category interval unions. **Left: main. Right: main + this PR.** Orange shows HiSparse gather kernels reading mapped host KV; blue shows other GPU activity; purple is the measured time intersection of the two tracks. In the magnified main panel, gather occupies gaps between other GPU work. In the PR panel, gather runs concurrently with other kernels; the original events include sparse MLA attention, fused MoE and GEMM kernels in these overlapping intervals.

Both panels show **rank 0, 26 requests / 104 verification rows, 24 GiB GPU KV**. To select a representative example, each arm uses the pure-decode step nearest its own rank's median GPU envelope: main step 22 and PR step 21 (zero-based profiler indices). Each panel starts at its own first GPU event; the lower panels show the same relative 20–24 ms window in the separate executions.

| Metric in the displayed step | Main | PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| GPU envelope | 63.0919 ms | 54.8733 ms |
| Gather duration (interval union) | 15.0741 ms | 16.6993 ms |
| Gather overlapped with other GPU activity | 0 ms | 10.9321 ms |
| Gather without other GPU activity | 15.0741 ms | 5.7672 ms |
| Gather overlap fraction | 0% | 65.46% |

The gather duration itself increases in this example, while much of it executes alongside other GPU work. **65.46% is this single rank/step's overlap; 67.44% in the table above is the summary across rank-level medians.** Generated tokens and cache states can differ between executions. A time intersection is not a direct measurement of critical-path savings, and this 24 GiB diagnostic is separate from the unprofiled 32 GiB serving results.

## GSM8K accuracy and MTP acceptance

Full real-weight regression on the same 8 x H200, GLM-5.2-FP8, TP8/MTP3, V2 runner and 32 GiB KV configuration above, comparing frozen main `a1cfd2c1` with main + original PR `bb84fb5e`.

Protocol: EvalScope 1.14.1 / GSM8K adapter v1.1, standard `main/test` **all 1,319 questions**, first four training examples in fixed order, thinking enabled with `reasoning_effort=max`, temperature 0, top_p 1, seed 42, concurrency 32, `max_tokens=16384`, normal EOS, non-streaming, no retries. This is a custom greedy regression, not a reproduction of the official GLM model-card score. Dataset: `openai/grade-school-math@3101c7d5072418e28b9008a6636bde82a006892c`; test SHA256 `3730d312f6e3440559ace48831e51066acaca737f6eabec99bccb9e4b3c39d14`. The complete request bodies and model metadata hashes matched across arms.

| Metric | Main | Main + PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Unique questions / scored | 1,319 / 1,319 | 1,319 / 1,319 |
| Correct | 1,285 | 1,282 |
| Accuracy, all questions | 97.4223% | 97.1948% |
| Output-budget failures, scored zero | 14 | 8 |
| HTTP errors / missing / duplicate questions | 0 / 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 0 |
| Accepted / proposed draft tokens | 781,084 / 910,050 | 705,864 / 831,003 |
| Speculative steps | 303,350 | 277,001 |
| True draft-token acceptance | 85.8287% | 84.9412% |
| Mean acceptance length, including bonus token | 3.5749 | 3.5482 |
| Position 1 / 2 / 3 unconditional acceptance | 94.6313% / 86.1961% / 76.6586% | 94.3011% / 85.3723% / 75.1503% |
| Preemptions | 0 | 0 |

Accuracy changed by **-0.2274 percentage points (three fewer correct answers)**: 11 main-correct answers became wrong, and eight main-wrong answers became correct. All eight gains came from baseline output-budget failures; four of the 11 losses were PR output-budget failures. Every budget failure reached 16,384 tokens with reasoning but no final answer and remained a zero in the full denominator. This single pass does not establish accuracy equivalence or isolate the cause of the differences; no accuracy improvement is claimed.

Acceptance is `sum(accepted) / sum(proposed)`; mean acceptance length is `1 + sum(accepted) / sum(steps)`. All per-request counters, histograms and three position counts reconciled exactly with isolated Prometheus deltas. The table includes the budget failures and excludes the preceding 20-question smoke runs. It does not use EvalScope's streaming-chunk acceptance estimate.

As a secondary diagnostic, excluding the union of either arm's truncated questions leaves the **same 1,300 questions** in both arms: acceptance is 83.8127% -> 83.9579%. This illustrates sensitivity of the token-weighted aggregate to generated continuation lengths; it is not the primary metric or evidence of an acceptance improvement.

Raw responses, per-question reviews/reports, request hashes, metrics snapshots, source-patch hash and native-library identities were archived and audited. The baseline was re-audited without regenerating answers or changing scores after correcting the harness's classification of scored budget failures; the initial failed audit remains preserved. The model/PR implementation and frozen generation protocol were unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Full EvalScope command</summary>

`DATASET_DIR` contains the frozen official train/test JSONL files and the local `main` split mapping; `OUT` is a fresh directory for each variant. Port 18593 is the local raw-response audit proxy forwarding to the model on 18592.

```bash
evalscope eval \
  --model GLM-5.2-FP8 --eval-type openai_api \
  --api-url http://127.0.0.1:18593/v1 --api-key EMPTY \
  --datasets gsm8k \
  --dataset-args "{\"gsm8k\":{\"dataset_id\":\"$DATASET_DIR\",\"few_shot_num\":4,\"few_shot_random\":false,\"subset_list\":[\"main\"]}}" \
  --generation-config '{"temperature":0,"top_p":1,"max_tokens":16384,"seed":42,"timeout":7200,"stream":false,"n":1,"retries":0,"extra_body":{"chat_template_kwargs":{"enable_thinking":true,"reasoning_effort":"max"}}}' \
  --eval-batch-size 32 --seed 42 --work-dir "$OUT" --no-timestamp
```

</details>

These are standard short GSM8K prompts, not inputs padded to 64K. They do not alone validate long-history offload misses or establish performance gains; the separate 64K performance and byte-level device tests above address different aspects.

## Validation

### Rebase validation (2026-10-29)

Rebased the original PR commit `bb84fb5e976` onto main `914d61fc538a84e8487cb16fe8241a70f6f4bf9e`; the updated head is `fc1fd11a1d306ab5f7b2d00e12107d3076e188af`. The only textual conflict was two tests added at the same location in `tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py`. Both main's resident-gather stride/payload test and this PR's bounded-decode prefetch test were preserved unchanged, including their parametrization. A per-file comparison verified that all added/removed lines in the seven-file PR patch are identical to the original patch; only surrounding context changed.

- On the isolated rebased Python source, `python -m pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py -k 'hisparse_resident_gather_preserves_stride_and_payload or hisparse_group_prefetch_requires_bounded_decode_only'`: **10 passed, 55 deselected**. These are CPU tests run with the existing CUDA environment's import dependencies, not a rebuild or device validation of the new base.
- Applicable pre-commit checks passed: Ruff check/format, mypy, typos, Markdown formatting, Buildkite keys/test tethering, SPDX/import/config checks, boolean-context/remote-code checks, filenames and Docker ignore rules. The test-tethering check used UTF-8 on Windows. The Windows clang-format launcher failed, so the exact rebased CUDA source was checked on Linux with **clang-format 21.1.2 `--style=file --dry-run --Werror csrc/hisparse_kernels.cu`**, which passed. Python syntax and `git diff --check` also passed.

The performance, profiling, device-test and GSM8K measurements reported above/below remain results for frozen main `a1cfd2c1` plus the original PR `bb84fb5e`; they have **not** been rerun on the new main base.

Linux/CUDA native builds and H200 device checks have now run:

- `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/v1/worker/test_utils.py -k hisparse`: main **45 passed**, PR **53 passed** (12 deselected each).
- Attention HiSparse selection: **53 main / 67 PR passed using out-of-tree compatibility copies** that repaired stale fixtures while preserving assertions. The unmodified baseline selection had 6 fixture failures / 47 passes; this is not a claim that the unmodified checked-in attention suite passed.
- Supplemental `validation/test_pr63801_device_stress.py`: **2 main / 2 PR passed**, eager and CUDA Graph replay, exact independent CPU byte-level golden comparisons; 656-byte rows, top-k 2048, four layers, up to 32 requests x 4 verification rows with changing active counts. PR Compute Sanitizer memcheck: **2 passed, 0 errors**.
- Supplemental `validation/test_pr63801_stream_consumption.py`: **2 main / 2 PR passed**, eager and CUDA Graph, immediate compute-stream consumption of each layer while follower prefetch proceeds, 64K history and an explicit logical-index readiness event. PR memcheck independently on GPU 0 and GPU 1: **2 passed, 0 errors on each**. These supplemental local tests are not checked-in full-model accuracy tests.

The standard reduced-model E2E suite (`tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py`), real-weight accuracy under long-history offload misses, repeated accuracy runs and a broader concurrency / MTP-on-off sweep remain outstanding. The completed standard GSM8K regression above and byte-level device checks do not replace these.

Previously recorded local checks: the isolated CPU harness passed 10 contract cases (stand-in runtime owner); Ruff, syntax, whitespace, markdownlint, typos, SPDX/import checks, Buildkite test tethering and isolated Python 3.11 mypy passed. LLVM 21.1.2 WASM formatting produced identical CUDA source bytes; the native Windows formatter hook was skipped because its launcher failed. These are local results, not a claim of upstream CI success.

## Details

Group prefetch already exists for single-token decode. This extends its eligibility without adding a backend support flag, stream, buffer or CPU readback. Current verification KV remains resident and is written by each layer before its attention; only historical host misses are staged early.

The compact gather previously targeted 64 blocks but launched one block per row once the row count exceeded 64. For example, 32 requests with four verification rows produced a 128-block copy grid. Workers now loop over those rows within a 64-block launch. Miss-count clamping, invalid entries, out-of-range source zeroing and padded hot-page strides keep their existing behavior. Tests cover row counts around the boundary, empty plans, payload bytes and replay with updated inputs.

The launch bound may trade dense-copy bandwidth for compute overlap, as illustrated by the diagnostic trace above. A block-count bound does not reserve particular SMs.

An open-PR search found no equivalent speculative-group-prefetch or bounded-gather change. #60103 handles separate existing launch/resolver overhead; #61263 changes residency hash probing.

AI assistance was used for implementation, tests, performance/accuracy analysis and preparation of this update. Human review and the remaining validation items above are still outstanding.

title: [MRV2][Spec Decode] Close DFlash/DSpark and adaptive-verification JIT warmup gaps
author: mgoin
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Three Triton kernels on the MRV2 spec-decode path still JIT-compile during serving after warmup, triggering `Triton kernel JIT compilation during inference: ...` from the JIT monitor and a latency spike on that step (and a hard failure under `--jit-monitor-mode=error`). Seen while serving Muse-Spark-Open with a DSpark drafter; reproduced on small models.

## Claims

- `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` (DFlash/DSpark) compiles once instead of once per power-of-two prefill chunk bucket; decode-time kernel GPU time drops ~3x as a side effect.
- `_accumulate_kernel` (adaptive verification acceptance estimator) compiles once for all batch sizes.
- `_refit_kernel` is compiled at warmup instead of 100 steps into serving.
- No output changes: `prepare_dflash_inputs` outputs are bitwise identical; estimator statistics differ only by fp32 summation order.

## Validation

**End to end, `jit_monitor_verbose=True`, MRV2, B300** (repro script runs a battery of batch sizes / prompt lengths after warmup):

| Config | Runtime JIT before | Runtime JIT after |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-4B + `RedHatAI/Qwen3-4B-speculator.dspark`, k=7, prompts 5–3000 tokens | `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` `BLOCK_SIZE=128`, `BLOCK_SIZE=256` | none |
| Qwen3-8B + `z-lab/Qwen3-8B-DFlash-b16`, k=7, `enable_adaptive_verification`, `max_num_seqs=1024`, bs 1/200/300/600/1000, >100 steps | `_refit_kernel`, `_accumulate_kernel` `BLOCK_R=512` (bs=300) | none from these kernels |

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    speculative_config={"method": "dflash", "model": "z-lab/Qwen3-8B-DFlash-b16",
                        "num_speculative_tokens": 7, "draft_sample_method": "probabilistic",
                        "rejection_sample_method": "block",
                        "enable_adaptive_verification": True},
    jit_monitor_verbose=True, max_model_len=4096, max_num_seqs=1024,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.6,
)
for bs, max_tokens in ((1, 600), (200, 64), (300, 64), (600, 64), (1000, 64)):
    prompts = [{"prompt_token_ids": list(range(1000 + i, 1040 + i))} for i in range(bs)]
    llm.generate(prompts, SamplingParams(max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=0.8,
                                         ignore_eos=True), use_tqdm=False)
```
Run with `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`. The DSpark variant swaps in the DSpark model pair and varies prompt length.
</details>

**Kernel GPU time, `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`** (CUPTI, CUDA graph, cold L2, B300; k=7, sample-from-anchor, block-table stride 4096). All block-size policies produce bitwise-identical outputs on every case.

| max reqs / tokens | case | before (dynamic) | fixed 128 (this PR) | fixed 256 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 256 / 8192 | decode bs1 | 19.7 us | 7.5 | 7.8 |
| 256 / 8192 | decode bs256 | 14.3 | 5.3 | 5.6 |
| 256 / 8192 | mixed 1x2048 + 63 decode | 6.8 | 6.3 | 6.8 |
| 256 / 8192 | prefill 1x8192 | 8.0 | 7.7 | 7.9 |
| 1024 / 16384 | decode bs1 | 38.1 | 12.5 | 12.6 |
| 1024 / 16384 | decode bs256 | 33.4 | 9.6 | 10.1 |
| 1024 / 16384 | mixed 1x2048 + 63 decode | 11.2 | 10.8 | 11.3 |
| 1024 / 16384 | prefill 1x8192 | 13.0 | 13.1 | 12.9 |

Fixed 512 was slower on every row. 128 vs 256 is within ~0.5 us.

**Kernel GPU time, `_accumulate_kernel`** (k=7, `max_num_reqs=1024`): pinning `BLOCK_R=1024, num_warps=4` is within run-to-run noise (~±0.5 us on a ~4 us kernel) of the old per-batch sizing for bs 1–1024; max relative difference in the accumulated statistics is 1.6e-7. A tiled loop over a fixed 256-wide block was also tried and rejected: up to 2x slower at bs 1024.

**Tests**

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_acceptance_estimator.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py -q
# 14 passed
```

The two new compile-count tests fail on `main` and pass with this PR. `test_warmup_covers_every_batch_size_and_the_refit` also fails when only the `BLOCK_R` fix is reverted.

No model evals: the DFlash prep outputs are bitwise identical, and the estimator change only reorders an fp32 reduction.

## Details

**Root cause.** Each kernel had a `tl.constexpr` derived from the live batch, and warmup only reaches a few of its values:

- `prepare_dflash_inputs` set `BLOCK_SIZE = min(256, next_power_of_2(max_query_len + num_query_per_req))`. Warmup prefill/decode steps are tiny, so 128/256 (and, depending on config, smaller buckets) first compile on a real prefill chunk. A fixed `BLOCK_SIZE` with a variable `num_blocks` grid covers every span with one variant. It also fixes a perf cliff: the padding loops at the end of the kernel stride by `BLOCK_SIZE`, so at decode (`BLOCK_SIZE` 8/16) they walked `max_num_tokens` in 8- or 16-element steps.
- `_accumulate_kernel` used `BLOCK_R = max(256, next_power_of_2(num_reqs))`. Warmup reaches 256 and `max_num_seqs`, not the buckets in between. `BLOCK_R` is now computed once from `max_num_reqs`.
- `_refit_kernel` runs every `REFIT_INTERVAL` (100) steps. `OnlineAcceptanceEstimator.warmup()`, called at the end of `warmup_kernels`, clears the per-round statistics and runs a refit. With zero statistics the Newton step is exactly zero, so the coefficients don't move. This also stops dummy warmup observations from leaking into the first real refit round, which is a small behavior change.

**Scope.** The estimator is only active with adaptive verification and a drafter without a confidence head (e.g. DFlash). DSpark checkpoints with `enable_confidence_head` disable it.

**Related PRs.**
- #58559 also targets `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`, by explicitly launching every `BLOCK_SIZE` bucket at warmup. This PR removes the variant set instead: one compile, no warmup code, and faster decode. #58559 has merge conflicts and no review activity since September. Its DSv4 top-k part is unrelated to this PR.
- #58633 gives the padding loops a separate `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE`. It overlaps with the decode speedup here, and its `min(1024, next_power_of_2(pad_span))` sizing varies with batch size, so it could reintroduce runtime compiles.
- #56323 / #56654 added, then reverted, explicit JIT warmup for these MRV2 kernels.

**Known remaining gap, not addressed here.** `_gumbel_sample_kernel` (main sampler, `APPLY_TEMPERATURE=False, IS_DRAFTING=False`) still JITs on the first request that takes the non-fused sampling path: no top-k/top-p, or explicit seed, or processed logprobs. Warmup's sampled pass uses top-k/top-p, so it takes the fused FlashInfer sampler path, and its other pass is greedy.

AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for the investigation, implementation, benchmarks, and this description. I reviewed the changes and the results.

title: [Bugfix][Core] Defer async KV loads on HiSparse decoders until in-flight steps finish
author: vMaroon
body:
> **Edited by @MatthewBonanni:** per @LucasWilkinson's suggestion (vMaroon/vllm#2), every async load on a HiSparse decoder is now deferred until the in-flight step is processed; the reuse detection is gone. Overview, Claims, unit tests and Details are updated. The GLM-5.3 results were measured on the earlier revision, which deferred only loads into reused pages.

## Overview

Fixes KV corruption on HiSparse P/D decoders: a NIXL load can overwrite a GPU page while the previous step is still reading it. The request that was reading it emits garbage for the rest of its output. The fix makes the scheduler start every async load on a HiSparse decoder one step later, once the in-flight step is done.

Fixes #63811.

## When it happens

All four hold at once:

1. **HiSparse is on.** It returns a running request's clean resident pages to the GPU pool early; the request keeps reading them until the pool hands them out again.
2. **Async scheduling** (`max_concurrent_batches > 1`): step N is still on the GPU while step N+1 starts.
3. **KV arrives by an async load**: a P/D decoder with `NixlConnector` as consumer. NIXL posts its reads from the CPU, so nothing orders them after step N.
4. **In step N+1, the pool hands one of those returned pages to a new request whose KV comes through that load.**

NIXL then writes the new request's KV into the page while step N still reads it as the owner's KV. The owner's tokens from step N get wrong KV, later steps attend to them, and the output never recovers.

Unaffected: pages filled by a forward or a host restore (ordered on the CUDA stream), and engines without HiSparse or without an async KV load.

## Claims

- Fixes the symptom: output cuts mid-sentence into one repeated token (`locklocklock...` on GLM-5.3) until `max_tokens`, with MTP acceptance at 0.
- With HiSparse enabled, every async load is registered with the connector once the step in flight at its allocation is processed, normally on the next step. Other requests and steps run as before.
- Cost: each async-loaded request on a HiSparse decoder starts its load about one step later. No device sync, and no check for which pages were reused.
- Active only with HiSparse and `defer_block_free` (overlapping steps and a KV consumer); otherwise nothing is deferred.

## Validation

GLM-5.3 on H100, P/D. Decoder TP8 x DP2, MTP 3, MRV2, async scheduling, `MultiConnector` (`NixlConnector` + `HiSparseConnector`), 20,000-block GPU pool. Traffic from `benchmarks/multi_turn`: 46-77K token prompts, 2-4K token answers. Counts are answers with at least 1,024 tokens. The rig runs the production image, a vLLM fork at `110cf9dc12`; "this PR" is this change applied to that fork's scheduler, block pool and KV cache manager (it applies cleanly).

| Free-queue order | Engine | Answers | Page handed to a NIXL load while read | Collapsed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| default | base | 133 | 0 | 0 |
| released pages first | base | 162 | 90 | 81 |
| released pages first | this PR | 173 | 106 (load held) | 0 |

- "Released pages first" is the one-line test change in step 1 below. It makes condition 4 frequent. Any free-block order is valid for the allocator, so a correct engine keeps its output quality under it.
- Collapsed: under 1.3 tokens per step (MTP drafts stop matching) from some point to the end of the answer, for at least 512 tokens. On base, collapse starts a median 35 tokens after the overwrite.
- Holds with this PR: 151 loads, each registered in the pass where step N had been processed, none earlier.
- TTFT of later turns (prompt mostly cached on the decoder) in the stress run: p50 1.98 s base, 2.07 s this PR. First-turn TTFT is not comparable across these runs because the prefill pods' prefix cache state differed.
- Default order with long answers (12-16K tokens, KV pool up to 88% full, base engine): 0 of 5,215 reuses of returned pages went to a NIXL-filled group, so the hold would not have triggered.
- Unit tests in `tests/v1/core/test_deferred_block_free.py`: a deferred load is registered after the in-flight step, it records its prefix cache stats (with `hits_by_source`) when it starts, a load without deferral registers at once, and an abort while deferred frees the blocks after the in-flight step.

**How to reproduce**

1. In `BlockPool.unpin_blocks`, replace `self.free_block_queue.append_n(released)` with `self.free_block_queue.prepend_n(released)`.
2. Serve GLM-5.3 P/D with a decoder as above. Run `benchmarks/multi_turn/benchmark_serving_multi_turn.py --num-clients 4 --max-active-conversations 8` on a generated config: 20 conversations, 10-12 turns, 15K common plus 30-50K prefix tokens, 1-2.5K token user turns, 2-4K token answers. The tool rejects reasoning-only streams, so accept `reasoning` deltas.
3. On base, within minutes, answers end in a repeated token and the `SpecDecoding metrics` per-position acceptance falls toward 0. With this PR, no degenerate answers.

## Details

- `defer_async_loads` is set at init when `defer_block_free` is on and the KV cache config has a HiSparse host pool.
- With a step in flight, the scheduler puts an async load in `deferred_loads` with the fence `sched_step_seq` at allocation instead of calling `update_state_after_alloc`. `_drain_deferred_loads` starts it in `update_from_output`, next to `_drain_deferred_frees`, once `processed_step_seq` reaches the fence. The request stays in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` meanwhile.
- Connector prefix-cache stats for a deferred load are recorded in `_drain_deferred_loads` after `update_state_after_alloc`, so it keeps `hits_by_source` (the connector attributes tiers only after the load plan exists). The allocation-site stats code is unchanged from main apart from skipping deferred loads.
- Abort while deferred: no load was posted, so the scheduler frees the blocks itself, deferred to the same fence through `last_sched_seq`, which is set when the load is deferred. `NixlConnector.request_finished` already releases the remote blocks of a request it never registered.
- The scheduler already fences block reuse against async connector writes (`defer_block_free`), but only for freed requests' blocks; these pages still belong to a running request. Deferring the registration needs no device sync; the only HiSparse-specific line in the scheduler is the init flag.
- CI does not cover the GPU path (needs NIXL P/D on GPUs).

title: [ROCm][Perf][Bugfix] wvSplitK: launch tiles of their own for gfx1151 and gfx1150; fix bigType for A_CHUNK 16
author: roberteg16
body:
## Overview Faster wave32 `wvSplitK` on gfx1151 and gfx1150/gfx1152/gfx1153: one launch tile per arch, chosen from a sweep of every non-spilling launch configuration. Related: #63015 (gfx9 rows only), #62718 (moves these kernels to a header; textual conflict), #51511 (disables the skinny GEMM on gfx1151; this PR makes it faster there instead). ## Claims - bf16/fp16 `wvSplitK` kernel time against `main`: +0.8% to +4.9% on gfx1150, +1.8% to +4.1% on gfx1151; 99.3-99.8% of the per-shape best tile (`main`: 96-98%). - Fixes `bigType` for A_CHUNK = 16 (64 B instead of 32 B: reads past the activation row, overlapping LDS writes). - GSM8K unchanged within noise. ## Validation **Performance.** Interleaved A/B against `main`, cold caches, weights padded as at load, median of 5 rounds. 43 shapes x N = 1..5, bf16 and fp16; 13 shapes not used for tuning (odd M, K = 768/1000/2880 among them); bias on 4 shapes. | | gfx1150 | gfx1151 | |---|---:|---:| | Shapes used for tuning | +1.8% to +1.9% | +2.7% to +3.0% | | Other shapes | +0.8% to +4.9% | +1.8% to +3.2% | | With bias | +1.7% | +4.1% | Cells slower by more than 2%: at most 3 of 150 per dtype, none below 0.98x. **Accuracy.** GSM8K, full set, 5-shot, greedy, a 1.5B bf16 instruct model, `max_num_seqs=5` (decode batches N = 1..5 through `wvSplitK`), gfx1151: | | flexible-extract | strict-match | |---|---:|---:| | `main` | 0.5807 ± 0.0136 | 0.5307 ± 0.0137 | | this PR | 0.5785 ± 0.0136 | 0.5292 ± 0.0137 | 3 and 2 of 1319 answers differ: the tile changes the summation order and `v_dot2_f32_bf16` the rounding. ``` lm_eval --model vllm --model_args pretrained=Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct,dtype=bfloat16,max_num_seqs=5,max_model_len=4096,seed=0 \ --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size auto --gen_kwargs temperature=0 --seed 0 ``` **Tests.** - `pytest tests/kernels/quantization/test_rocm_skinny_gemms.py -k test_rocm_wvsplitk_kernel`: 126 passed on gfx1151, including new K % 16 != 0 and N = 5 cases. The file's other failures on gfx1151 (`test_rocm_wvsplitk_fp8_kernel`, `test_rocm_llmm1_kernel`) are the same 184 on `main`. - All 43 shapes x N = 1..5, bf16/fp16, with and without bias, against `torch.nn.functional.linear`: correct on gfx1150 and gfx1151. - `pre-commit` passes. ## Details 1. **`bigType` sized by A_CHUNK.** `half4` was (A_CHUNK / 2) x bf16; it is now 4 x bf16, the operand of its only consumer. No launch used A_CHUNK = 16 before this PR. 2. **bf16 `DOT2C` on gfx11/gfx12** issues `v_dot2_f32_bf16`, as fp16 issues `v_dot2_f32_f16`, instead of widening both operands to f32. 3. **Launch rows** (`WVSPLITK_CFG_AC` takes A_CHUNK; `WVSPLITK_CFG` keeps 8): - gfx1151: (YTILE 1, UNRL 4, A_CHUNK 16); (2, 4, 8) for K < 1024. - gfx1150, gfx1152, gfx1153: (2, 1, 16); (1, 2, 16) when M <= 32 * CUs. - A_CHUNK 8 when K % 16 != 0 (wider chunks give wrong results there). - Other archs: unchanged. The sweep covered YTILE 1-4, UNRL 1/2/4/8, A_CHUNK 8/16/32 and WvPrGrp 16/32, excluding configurations that spill. AI assistance was used. title: [GLM5.3 Perf] Enable dspark fp8 kv cache for draft model, 5.38 GB GPU Memory saved per rank
author: yewentao256
body:
## Overview

Enable dspark fp8 kv cache for draft model, perf nearly the same, but we save a lot of gpu memory

AI Analysis:

```bash
For RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-speculator.dspark at TP4, the three draft attention layers store 6,144 K/V values per token per GPU. That is 12 KiB in BF16 versus 6 KiB in FP8: a calculated saving of 6 KiB per cached token per GPU. At 8,192 cached tokens, the saving is 48 MiB per GPU.
An earlier run with the same FP8 DSpark behavior reported 940,736 KV cache slots and 47.18 GiB of cache per GPU. Holding that slot count and cache layout fixed, a BF16 draft would require approximately 52.56 GiB per GPU: 5.38 GiB more per GPU, or 21.53 GiB across TP4. At a fixed cache memory budget, this corresponds to approximately 11.4% more token slots.
```

So 5.38 GB saved each rank in the default config

vllm serve zai-org/GLM-5.3    --trust-remote-code     -tp 4     --load-format fastsafetensors     --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88     --enable-prefix-caching     --host 0.0.0.0     --port 9256     --max-model-len auto     --max-num-seqs 48     --speculative-config '{\"method\":\"dspark\",\"model\":\"RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-speculator.dspark\",\"num_speculative_tokens\":8}'

title: [Perf][Frontend] Compute prompt block hashes in the Rust frontend
author: njhill
body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Let the Rust frontend compute a request's prompt block hashes, so the engine's input thread no longer hashes long prompts while holding the GIL the engine loop needs. Revives the idea of #15652 for the Rust frontend; complementary to #63454 (cheaper engine-side hashing) and related to #43483 (frontend hashes for DP routing). Part of the long-context P/D CPU-overhead work in #63439.

## Claims

- The engine accepts frontend-computed prompt block hashes; prefix-cache hashes are unchanged (byte-identical), so cache hits, KV connectors and KV events are unaffected.
- The Rust frontend covers `sha256` and `sha256_cbor` for plain, LoRA, cache-salt and lookahead (EAGLE) requests; other requests are hashed by the engine as before.
- Removes the GIL-held prompt hashing from the engine's input thread (~50 ms per 227K-token prompt with `sha256`, ~150 ms with `sha256_cbor`), which otherwise stalls the engine loop: +9.6% decode throughput with `sha256` and +39% with `sha256_cbor` on a workload that admits long cached prompts during decode (below).

## Validation

- `pytest tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py`: 114 passed. `cargo test -p vllm-engine-core-client -p vllm-llm`: all passed, including known-answer vectors generated from the engine's own `Request` / `get_request_block_hasher`.
- E2E on GB300 with `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1`, using a test-only engine patch that recomputes the hashes of every request that arrives with frontend hashes and compares them:

| Config | Requests | Hash check | Cached tokens on repeat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-0.6B, `sha256`, LoRA | 12 (plain, salts incl. non-ASCII / 300-byte, short, LoRA, LoRA + salt) | 12/12 match | 5424/5427; a new salt or LoRA starts at 0 |
| Qwen3-0.6B, `sha256_cbor`, LoRA | 12 | 12/12 match | same |
| Qwen3-1.7B + EAGLE3 (lookahead 1) | 8 | 8/8 match | same |

Benchmark (GB300, `Qwen3-0.6B`, Rust frontend, CUDA graphs): 64 streaming decode requests while fully prefix-cached 30K-token prompts (token ids, `max_tokens=1`) arrive at 20/s for 40 s. This resembles a P/D decode instance admitting long prompts. Same binaries in both arms; the "engine" arm stops the engine from advertising `prefix_hash_config`. Mean of 2 interleaved rounds (each within 2%):

| Hash | Prompt hashing in | Decode tok/s | ITL mean / p90 / p99 (ms) | Long-request TTFT p50 / p99 (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sha256` | engine (main) | 16,870 | 3.77 / 8.36 / 10.10 | 27.6 / 46.1 |
| `sha256` | frontend (this PR) | 18,494 (+9.6%) | 3.44 / 6.51 / 9.83 | 25.6 / 37.8 |
| `sha256_cbor` | engine (main) | 13,244 | 4.80 / 10.41 / 15.64 | 34.9 / 61.1 |
| `sha256_cbor` | frontend (this PR) | 18,366 (+39%) | 3.46 / 6.45 / 10.04 | 25.6 / 35.5 |

The gain depends on how much of the engine loop the hashing displaces: a small model and a high arrival rate of long prompts make it large; larger models see a smaller relative gain.

<details>
<summary>Reproduce</summary>

Server (both arms): `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --max-model-len 32768 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.6 --max-num-seqs 256 --prefix-caching-hash-algo {sha256,sha256_cbor} --enable-prompt-tokens-details`. For the engine arm, set `self.prefix_hash_config = None` in `EngineCore.__init__`. Client: 64 concurrent streaming `/v1/completions` (32-token prompt, `max_tokens=2000`, `ignore_eos`), measuring inter-chunk gaps; after warming 8 distinct 30K-token-id prompts into the prefix cache, send them round-robin at 20 req/s with `max_tokens=1` for 40 s.
</details>

## Details

- `EngineCoreReadyResponse.prefix_hash_config` (algorithm, `hash_block_size`, `NONE_HASH`, lookahead) is set when the engine hashes blocks. Sending `NONE_HASH` means frontends needn't reproduce the seed logic.
- `EngineCoreRequest.block_hashes` seeds `Request.block_hashes`; the existing hasher continues from there. The engine only checks the count (`(prompt_len - lookahead) // hash_block_size`) and otherwise hashes the prompt itself.
- The Rust encoder writes pickle protocol 5 / canonical CBOR exactly. It leaves to the engine: multimodal and prompt-embeds requests, `xxhash*`, keys over one 64 KiB pickle frame, and the rare requests whose strings pickle could memoize by identity.
- The Python frontend doesn't send hashes yet.

title: [Perf] Tune the Triton packed GDN decode tile on SM90
author: Rockyeast
body:
## Overview

Use `BV = 4` for the Triton packed GDN decode kernel on SM90 (H100/H200) when the recurrent state is FP32,
the SM90 counterpart of #61355 (SM100). The kernel is unchanged; this adds one dispatch branch.

Not a duplicate: no open PR changes this kernel's SM90 tile (searched open PRs for "packed decode" and
"GDN decode"; #62961 only touches this kernel's tests). Sibling tunings: #61355 (SM100, merged), #61823
(SM89, open), #54181 (SM120, closed).

## Claims

- **1.02–2.16x faster kernel, 1.34x geometric mean** over 99 `(H, HV, batch)` points on H200 with an FP32
  state (cold L2, CUPTI). `BV = 4` is the fastest tile at all 99 points.
- **1.0–1.8% lower decode latency** serving Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (FP32 state is its checkpoint default),
  matching what the kernel saving predicts; throughput within noise.
- Output and updated recurrent state are **bitwise identical** to `BV = 32` at every measured point.
  BF16 state is unchanged.

## Validation

### Kernel (cold L2)

H200 NVL (132 SMs, 60 MiB L2), `K = V = 128`, BF16 qkv, QK L2-norm on. Each CUDA graph cycles through
enough disjoint state slots that the state touched between two uses of a slot is >= 4x L2 (240 MiB), so
the state is never L2-resident, as in a decode step. Kernel time from CUPTI (`torch.profiler`) over graph
replays; 7 rounds with the tile order shuffled each round, median reported (round-to-round spread <= 1.8%).
Speedup of `BV = 4` over `BV = 32`, FP32 state:

| (H, HV) | B=1 | B=2 | B=4 | B=8 | B=16 | B=32 | B=64 | B=128 | B=256 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| (16, 48) Qwen3.8-27B TP1 | 1.69 | 1.52 | 1.19 | 1.29 | 1.15 | 1.08 | 1.04 | 1.03 | 1.02 |
| (8, 24) TP2 | 1.86 | 1.70 | 1.52 | 1.21 | 1.29 | 1.17 | 1.09 | 1.04 | 1.03 |
| (4, 12) TP4 | 2.03 | 1.87 | 1.70 | 1.52 | 1.20 | 1.29 | 1.17 | 1.08 | 1.04 |
| (2, 6) TP8 | 2.11 | 2.04 | 1.86 | 1.71 | 1.52 | 1.24 | 1.26 | 1.15 | 1.08 |
| (16, 32) | 1.79 | 1.62 | 1.45 | 1.19 | 1.26 | 1.11 | 1.06 | 1.04 | 1.02 |
| (8, 16) | 1.95 | 1.79 | 1.63 | 1.45 | 1.19 | 1.24 | 1.11 | 1.06 | 1.04 |
| (4, 8) | 2.08 | 1.97 | 1.79 | 1.64 | 1.44 | 1.15 | 1.23 | 1.11 | 1.06 |
| (2, 4) | 2.16 | 2.11 | 1.97 | 1.80 | 1.60 | 1.46 | 1.23 | 1.24 | 1.12 |
| (16, 64) | 1.61 | 1.45 | 1.19 | 1.24 | 1.11 | 1.06 | 1.04 | 1.02 | 1.02 |
| (8, 32) | 1.78 | 1.63 | 1.45 | 1.19 | 1.26 | 1.12 | 1.06 | 1.04 | 1.02 |
| (4, 16) | 1.95 | 1.79 | 1.64 | 1.46 | 1.17 | 1.25 | 1.11 | 1.05 | 1.03 |

Absolute time for (16, 48), `BV = 32` → `4`: 6.65 → 3.94 us at B=1, 19.5 → 15.2 at B=8,
58.0 → 53.9 at B=32, 412.5 → 404.1 at B=256 (bandwidth-bound on the state, so the gain shrinks).
`BV` in {4, 8, 16, 32} gave bitwise-identical output and updated state at all 198 points (FP32 and BF16
state).

### End to end

Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (48 GDN layers), vLLM 0.32.0 with this rule applied, H200 NVL, `vllm bench serve`,
random 1024 in / 128 out, prefix caching off, `max_num_seqs 64`; unpatched and patched interleaved,
2 runs each (mean):

| concurrency | metric | unpatched | patched | change | predicted from kernel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | median TPOT | 10.78 ms | 10.65 ms | −1.2% | −1.2% |
| 8 | median ITL | 11.72 ms | 11.51 ms | −1.8% | −1.8% |
| 32 | median ITL | 14.60 ms | 14.45 ms | −1.0% | −1.4% |
| 1 / 8 / 32 | output tok/s | 86.1 / 503.7 / 1085.6 | 86.6 / 508.4 / 1088.0 | +0.5 / +0.9 / +0.2% | |

"Predicted" is the per-call kernel saving at that batch x 48 layers over the step time. The kernel is 3%
of a step at batch 1 and 19% at batch 32.

### Tests

```
pytest -q tests/kernels/fla/test_fused_recurrent_packed_decode.py   # 14 passed on H200 NVL
```

The FP32-state cases (`K = V = 128`) take the new branch on SM90.

<details>
<summary>Microbenchmark script</summary>

```python
"""Packed GDN decode kernel (vLLM's Triton fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode), cold L2:
time per call for each value-tile size BV, batch size and (H, HV) head layout, FP32 and BF16 state.

The wrapper is vLLM's own, with its fixed `BV = min(next_power_of_2(V), 32)` line replaced by a module
variable. Each CUDA graph cycles through enough disjoint state-slot sets that the state touched between
two uses of the same slot is at least 4x the L2 (a decode step touches each sequence's state once).
State slot 0 is the kernel's null slot (skipped), so real slots start at 1. Output and updated state
are compared bitwise with BV=32 at every point. Kernel time comes from CUPTI (torch.profiler) over graph
replays; CUDA-event time per call (which includes the gaps between graph nodes) is recorded too.
BV order is shuffled in each of ROUNDS rounds; reported values are medians over rounds.
usage: gdn_decode_bv_cold.py <out.json>
"""
import inspect, json, math, random, statistics, sys
import torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity
from vllm.third_party.flash_linear_attention.ops import fused_recurrent as fr

src = inspect.getsource(fr.fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode)
needle = 'BV = min(triton.next_power_of_2(V), 32)'
assert src.count(needle) == 1
ns = dict(fr.__dict__)
exec(compile(src.replace(needle, 'BV = _BV'), '<packed-decode-bv>', 'exec'), ns)
wrapper = ns['fused_recurrent_gated_delta_rule_packed_decode']

LAYOUTS = [(16, 48), (8, 24), (4, 12), (2, 6),      # HV/H = 3 (Qwen3.8-27B at TP1/2/4/8)
           (16, 32), (8, 16), (4, 8), (2, 4),       # HV/H = 2
           (16, 64), (8, 32), (4, 16)]              # HV/H = 4
BATCHES = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256]
BVS = [4, 8, 16, 32]
if __import__('os').environ.get('GDN_QUICK'):
    LAYOUTS, BATCHES = [(16, 48), (2, 6)], [1, 64]
K = V = 128
ROUNDS = 7
EVENT_REPS = 10
CUPTI_REPS = 3
dev = 'cuda'
props = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0)
L2 = props.L2_cache_size
FOOTPRINT = 4 * L2
torch.manual_seed(0)
random.seed(0)
print('DEVICE', torch.cuda.get_device_name(), 'SMs', props.multi_processor_count, 'L2', L2, flush=True)


def kernel_us(g, sets):
    """Mean CUPTI duration of one packed-decode kernel over CUPTI_REPS graph replays."""
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
        for _ in range(CUPTI_REPS):
            g.replay()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    durs = [e.device_time for e in prof.events()
            if 'packed_decode' in e.name and e.device_type == torch.autograd.DeviceType.CUDA]
    if not durs:
        durs = [e.cuda_time for e in prof.events() if 'packed_decode' in e.name and e.cuda_time > 0]
    return (sum(durs) / len(durs), len(durs)) if durs else (None, 0)


def event_us(g, sets):
    us = []
    for _ in range(EVENT_REPS):
        e0, e1 = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        e0.record(); g.replay(); e1.record(); e1.synchronize()
        us.append(e0.elapsed_time(e1) * 1000 / sets)
    return statistics.median(us)


rows = []
for state_dtype in (torch.float32, torch.bfloat16):
    for H, HV in LAYOUTS:
        A_log = torch.randn(HV, device=dev, dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1
        dt_bias = torch.randn(HV, device=dev, dtype=torch.float32) * 0.1
        for B in BATCHES:
            elsize = torch.empty((), dtype=state_dtype).element_size()
            set_bytes = B * HV * V * K * elsize
            sets = max(2, math.ceil(FOOTPRINT / set_bytes))
            pool = torch.randn(1 + B * sets, HV, V, K, device=dev, dtype=torch.float32).mul_(0.02).to(state_dtype)
            pristine = pool[:1 + B].clone()   # slot 0 (null) + set 0; timing updates `pool` in place
            qkv = torch.randn(B, 2 * H * K + HV * V, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
            a = torch.randn(B, HV, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
            b = torch.randn(B, HV, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
            idx = [torch.arange(1 + s * B, 1 + (s + 1) * B, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32) for s in range(sets)]
            out = torch.empty(B, 1, HV, V, device=dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
            real = torch.arange(1, 1 + B, device=dev, dtype=torch.int32)
            res, graphs = {}, {}
            for bv in BVS:
                ns['_BV'] = bv
                st = pristine.clone()
                wrapper(qkv, a, b, A_log, dt_bias, K ** -0.5, st, out, real, True)
                res[bv] = dict(out=out.clone(), state=st[1:].clone(), ev=[], cu=[])
                def step(bv=bv):
                    ns['_BV'] = bv
                    for s in range(sets):
                        wrapper(qkv, a, b, A_log, dt_bias, K ** -0.5, pool, out, idx[s], True)
                stream = torch.cuda.Stream(); stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
                with torch.cuda.stream(stream):
                    step()
                torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(stream)
                g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
                with torch.cuda.graph(g):
                    step()
                g.replay()
                graphs[bv] = g
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            ncupti = {}
            for _ in range(ROUNDS):
                order = BVS[:]
                random.shuffle(order)
                for bv in order:
                    res[bv]['ev'].append(event_us(graphs[bv], sets))
                    cu, n = kernel_us(graphs[bv], sets)
                    ncupti[bv] = n
                    if cu is not None:
                        res[bv]['cu'].append(cu)
            ref = res[32]
            us_ev = {v: round(statistics.median(res[v]['ev']), 3) for v in BVS}
            us_cu = {v: (round(statistics.median(res[v]['cu']), 3) if res[v]['cu'] else None) for v in BVS}
            have_cu = all(us_cu[v] is not None for v in BVS)
            basis = us_cu if have_cu else us_ev
            row = dict(state=str(state_dtype).split('.')[-1], H=H, HV=HV, B=B,
                       sets=sets, footprint_MB=round(sets * set_bytes / 2**20, 1), L2_MB=round(L2 / 2**20, 1),
                       us_cupti=us_cu, us_event=us_ev, cupti_kernels_per_bv=ncupti,
                       speedup_bv4_cupti=(round(us_cu[32] / us_cu[4], 3) if have_cu else None),
                       speedup_bv4_event=round(us_ev[32] / us_ev[4], 3),
                       best_bv=min(BVS, key=lambda v: basis[v]),
                       round_spread_bv4_cupti=(round((max(res[4]['cu']) - min(res[4]['cu'])) / us_cu[4], 3) if have_cu else None),
                       out_abs_max=float(ref['out'].float().abs().max()),
                       out_nonzero_rows=int((ref['out'].float().abs().amax(dim=(1, 2, 3)) > 0).sum()),
                       bitwise_out={v: bool(torch.equal(res[v]['out'], ref['out'])) for v in BVS},
                       bitwise_state={v: bool(torch.equal(res[v]['state'], ref['state'])) for v in BVS})
            rows.append(row)
            print('ROW', json.dumps(row), flush=True)
            del graphs, pool, res
            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
json.dump(dict(device=torch.cuda.get_device_name(), sms=props.multi_processor_count, l2_bytes=L2,
               footprint_bytes=FOOTPRINT, rounds=ROUNDS, rows=rows), open(sys.argv[1], 'w'), indent=1)
print('DONE', flush=True)
```
</details>

## Details

- The rule is batch-independent, so on SM90 with an FP32 state only one tile variant is reachable and
  graph capture compiles it; there is no batch-size boundary to warm up.
- BF16 state keeps `BV = 32`: no single rule wins everywhere on SM90 (the best, `4` for `B*HV <= 96`
  else `16`, is 1.18x geometric mean but up to 6% slower, and >2% slower at 7/99 points).
- Measured on H200 NVL only. The branch also covers H100 and H20 (fewer SMs, lower bandwidth), where I
  have not measured it.
- CI: `kernels/fla` runs on B200 and MI355 only, so CI does not reach this SM90 branch. The test above was
  run on H200 against this change.
- No new host synchronization: the branch reads only the state dtype and the device capability, like the
  SM100 branch above it.

title: [Bugfix][Bench] Support Muse balanced routing
author: WoosukKwon
body:
## Overview

Fix Muse Spark forward benchmarks with dummy weights and the default `--routing auto`, which already selects balanced routing. No explicit routing flag is needed.

## Claims

- `BalancedRouting` discovers Muse's gate and suppresses expert selection bias while its synthetic routing fixture is installed.
- Removing the fixture restores the original bias and real model routing.

## Validation

GB200 validation of the retained tests: 2 cases passed (native CLI and router/bias behavior). All targeted pre-commit checks pass.

On GB200, using `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/benchmarks/test_forward_cli.py -k test_balanced_routing_restores_expert_bias -v`:

| Configuration | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Muse `router` / `expert_bias` layout | `ValueError: No MoE gates found; use --routing real.` | Pass |

The test uses a real GateLinear and Muse router, checks exact per-rank balance despite a large expert-selection bias, and verifies bias restoration and subsequent real routing. Targeted pre-commit hooks passed. The existing Benchmarks CLI Buildkite step selects the layer regression; the B200 Quantized MoE step explicitly selects the native Muse CLI test.

The BF16 TRTLLM test passes without the separate MegaMoE initialization fix. The added `test_bench_forward_muse_balanced_routing` regression fails before the routing fix with `ValueError: No MoE gates found; use --routing real.`. It uses a one-layer Muse text config (512 hidden, 8 experts, top-2) on one GB200, BF16 FlashInfer TRTLLM, balanced routing, and prefill32/decode2@32. Both CUDA graph cases completed and matched eager output exactly (relative RMS 0). Two timing samples are a smoke check, not a speedup claim. Reproduce with `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/benchmarks/test_forward_cli.py -k "test_bench_forward_muse_balanced_routing or test_balanced_routing_restores_expert_bias" -v`. The CLI registers the native text class through ModelRegistry because public Muse checkpoints use the multimodal architecture wrapper.


## Details

Gate discovery previously recognized only `gate`, and bias handling recognized only `e_score_correction_bias`. Add fallbacks for Muse's existing names while reusing fixture generation, forward hooks, and bias restoration. This changes only benchmark fixtures; real serving routing is unaffected.

Open-PR searches for `"balanced routing"`, `"Muse" "dummy"`, and `"Muse" "finalize"` found no duplicate. #60217 concerns serving-time EMA routing penalties on ROCm, not synthetic forward-benchmark gate discovery. No associated issue number exists.
